0.title: The God Who Redeems: The Book of Exodus
0.overview:
Exodus is the great drama of redemption. If Genesis tells us how the world was made and how it fell, Exodus tells us how God comes down to rescue a people for himself. Here the God who walked in Eden, who called Abraham, who promised a multitude, now bends the heavens and bares his arm. He hears groaning. He remembers covenant. He descends in fire. "I have surely seen the affliction of my people," he says, "and I have come down to deliver them" (Ex. 3:7-8). That single sentence is the gospel in seed form: a holy God who sees, who hears, who remembers, and who comes down.

The book unfolds in three great movements. First, redemption accomplished (chs. 1-18): Israel groans in Egypt, Moses is raised up, the plagues fall, the Passover lamb is slain, and the people pass through the sea from death to life. Second, the covenant given (chs. 19-24): at Sinai the redeemed people receive the law, not as a ladder to climb to God but as the shape of life with the God who has already saved them. Third, the presence secured (chs. 25-40): the tabernacle is commanded, the golden calf nearly undoes everything, mercy triumphs, and at last the glory of the LORD fills the tent. The book that opens with a people enslaved in a foreign land ends with God himself dwelling in their midst.

Exodus is relentlessly about God. Israel does almost nothing to save itself; it cries out, it trembles, it grumbles, it sins. Salvation is the LORD's from beginning to end. As R.C. Sproul loved to insist, the central issue of Exodus is the character of God — his holiness, his faithfulness, his sovereignty, his steadfast love. When Moses asks to see his glory, God answers by proclaiming his name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (34:6). That is the heartbeat of the book.

And every page points to Christ. The Passover lamb without blemish is fulfilled when Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor. 5:7). The Red Sea is our baptism (1 Cor. 10:2); the manna is the bread of life (John 6); the rock struck in the desert is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4); the tabernacle anticipates the Word made flesh who "tabernacled among us" (John 1:14). Moses, the mediator who stands in the breach and offers his own life for the people, is a shadow of the one Mediator who actually gave his. To read Exodus rightly is to be led, step by step, out of bondage and up the mountain, until we see that the God who redeems is the God who in Jesus Christ came down to redeem us forever.

1.title: A People Multiplied in the Furnace
1.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household:<sup>2</sup>Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,<sup>3</sup>Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,<sup>4</sup>Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.<sup>5</sup>All the descendants of Jacob were seventy persons; Joseph was already in Egypt.<sup>6</sup>Then Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation.<sup>7</sup>But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.<sup>8</sup>Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.<sup>9</sup>And he said to his people, "Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us.<sup>10</sup>Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and, if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land."<sup>11</sup>Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses.<sup>12</sup>But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>So they ruthlessly made the people of Israel work as slaves<sup>14</sup>and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them work as slaves.<sup>15</sup>Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah,<sup>16</sup>"When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live."<sup>17</sup>But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.<sup>18</sup>So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this, and let the male children live?"<sup>19</sup>The midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them."<sup>20</sup>So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong.<sup>21</sup>And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.<sup>22</sup>Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live."
1.overview:
Exodus opens by tying itself back to Genesis: the names of the sons of Israel who came down to Egypt. The family of seventy has become a people. The command of Eden — "be fruitful and multiply" — and the promise to Abraham of descendants like the stars are quietly, irresistibly being fulfilled, even in a foreign land, even under the lash.

Then comes the ominous sentence: "there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph." The world turns. The favored guests become hated slaves. Pharaoh launches the first program of genocide in Scripture, and yet the more Egypt presses down, the more Israel spreads. As Alistair Begg notes, oppression cannot finally defeat the purposes of God; the bush burns but is not consumed. Into this furnace step two unlikely heroes, the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who fear God more than Pharaoh and so quietly defy the empire.

This chapter sets the theological stage for the whole book. God's people suffer, but God's promise advances. The growth of Israel under affliction is the first sign that a power greater than Pharaoh is at work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: The book opens with the Hebrew word for "and" — it begins mid-sentence, tied by a conjunction to the last verse of Genesis, and its Hebrew title is simply Shemot, "Names." These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, listed by their mothers, seventy persons in all, with Joseph already there.

Verses 6-7: A whole generation is buried in a sentence — Then Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation — and then five verbs pile up: the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them. It is the language of Genesis 1:28. In the soil of a foreign empire, God is growing a garden.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Deals in Names

Before there is a nation, a plague, a sea or a mountain, there is a list of names. God does not deal with populations; he deals with persons, and he knows each one — Issachar, Zebulun, Asher, men long dead and not forgotten. The Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). Everything that follows in this book grows out of promises made to named people.

Seventy is also the number of the nations in Genesis 10, and the echo is not idle: God has taken one family out of a world of seventy nations, and through that one family he intends to reach them all.

The Promise Never Depended on the Protector

Notice when the multiplying happens — not while Joseph lives and the family has a friend at court, but after every protector is in a tomb. Calvin observed that God multiplied them exactly where human reason expected them to dwindle. The promise to Abraham that his offspring would outnumber the stars (Gen. 15:5) marches forward in the dark, with no visible means of support and no one left who remembers why it should.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every witness to God's providence dies in verse 6, and the promise still has four centuries to wait. That is how God frequently works: the generation that saw the miracle is buried, nothing appears to be happening at all, and the word of God goes on keeping itself underground.

Now: Count the quiet faithfulness of God in the unremarkable growth of a family, a congregation, a life — births, ordinary years, people who will never be famous. The kingdom advances by generations far more often than by dramatic intervention, and the stretches that feel like nothing is happening are usually the stretches doing the most work.

The discouragement in verse 6 deserves naming too. There are seasons in which everyone who could remember the last time God clearly acted has died, and the people left are holding a promise on trust alone. Exodus opens there deliberately. It is not a failure of faith to find that hard; it is the situation the book was written for.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. All the descendants of Jacob were seventy persons; Joseph was already in Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exodus opens with the word "and" — in Hebrew, ve'elleh shemot, "And these are the names." It begins mid-sentence, as though someone had never stopped speaking. That is deliberate. This is not a new story; it is the next chapter of one, tied by a conjunction to the last verse of Genesis. The Hebrew title of the whole book is simply Shemot — "Names."

And what names. The twelve sons are listed by their mothers: Leah's six first, then Rachel's Benjamin, then the sons of the handmaids. Joseph needs no listing — he is "already in Egypt," which is the whole reason the family is there at all. Seventy persons in total (Gen 46:27): a household, a village, small enough to eat at one long table. Seventy is also the number of the nations in Genesis 10, and the coincidence is not idle. God has taken one family out of a world of seventy nations, and through that one family he intends to reach them all.

But feel the weight of the simple thing the chapter does first: before there is a nation, before there is a plague or a sea or a mountain, there is a list of names. God does not deal with populations. He deals with persons, and he knows each one by name — Issachar, Zebulun, Asher, men long dead and not forgotten. The Shepherd "calls his own sheep by name" (John 10:3). Everything that follows in this book — the blood on the doorposts, the water standing in walls, the glory filling the tent — grows out of a promise made to named people. He keeps his word to individuals.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation. But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A whole generation is buried in eleven words. Joseph dies; his brothers die; everyone who remembered dies. The man who read dreams before Pharaoh, who wept on his brothers' necks, who said "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" — gone. Every witness to God's providence is in a tomb, and the promise still has four hundred years to wait. This is how God often works: the generation that saw the miracle dies, and nothing appears to be happening at all.

Then verse 7, and the verbs come in a flood: fruitful, increased greatly, multiplied, grew exceedingly strong, the land was filled with them. Five of them, piled up, tumbling over one another. And every reader of Genesis knows exactly where that language comes from: "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth" (Gen 1:28). This is creation language. In the soil of a foreign empire, God is growing a garden. The seventy have become a swarm; the promise to Abraham that his offspring would outnumber the stars (Gen 15:5) is marching forward in the dark.

And notice when it happens: not while Joseph lives and the family has a protector at court, but after every protector is dead. Calvin observed that God multiplied them precisely where human reason expected them to dwindle. The promise never depended on Joseph. It never depends on the people we think are holding it up. When the last man who remembered is buried, the word of God is still keeping itself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-14 — The Pharaoh Who Did Not Know Joseph
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 8: The hinge of the chapter, and one sentence swings it — Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph. Everything before is blessing; everything after is bondage.

Verses 9-10: Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them. Pharaoh looks straight at the blessing of God and calls it a security problem.

Verses 11-12: The shrewdness becomes policy — taskmasters, heavy burdens, the store cities Pithom and Raamses — and it fails on the spot: But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.

Verses 13-14: The word for the labour is perech, crushing harshness, and it brackets the sentence at both ends. Their lives are made bitter — marar, the word Israel will taste every spring in the bitter herbs of Passover.
verseByVerse.theology:
Where Grace Is Forgotten, Hostility Follows

Did not know Joseph does not mean the king had never heard the name. The Hebrew yada is the verb of relationship and acknowledgement, not of information. Egypt owed its survival to a Hebrew who had read God's warning in a dream and stockpiled grain against the famine; the nation ate because Joseph lived. The new dynasty simply refuses the debt. A world that will not remember what it owes will turn, sooner or later, on the people it owes it to.

The Voice of Empire

Come, let us deal shrewdly is the language of Babel — Come, let us make bricks... Come, let us build ourselves a city (Gen. 11:3-4) — and the word for shrewd belongs to the serpent, more crafty than any other beast of the field (Gen. 3:1). Empire always says come, let us. By human calculation Pharaoh's logic is flawless: a large foreign population on the frontier an invader must use. He is a competent statesman and he is utterly blind. He is not fighting a minority; he is fighting Genesis 1:28. He who sits in the heavens laughs (Ps. 2:4).

God Does Not Minimise the Suffering

Four verbs of bitterness in verses 13-14 answer the five verbs of fruitfulness in verse 7. Scripture does not hurry past the affliction or reframe it as a growth opportunity. It records it, names it, and lets it stand on the page at full weight — and then, three verses into the next chapter, tells us he heard it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Pharaoh is pressing down on a spring. Every extra burden produces extra Hebrews, and the empire ends the passage in dread of its own slaves — a strong word, a sickened horror. The man with the armies is terrified of the men with the bricks, because underneath the politics he is contending with Someone he can neither see nor stop.

Now: Tertullian said it centuries later, watching the arenas fill: the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. Pressure has never yet reduced the people of God; it has only ever concentrated them. The world rarely sees the growth of God's people as a gift. It sees a demographic to be managed — and every measure taken to reduce them has so far multiplied them.

There is an irony in these verses that only hindsight can see. This nation, forced to make mortar and brick for a tyrant's storehouses, will one day be asked to build again — freely, out of gifts nobody compelled them to give — and what they build will be a tent for the living God to dwell in (Ex. 35-40). The slave camp is the training ground for the craftsmen of the sanctuary. But not yet. First they must learn, at the very bottom, to cry out.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hinge of the chapter, and one sentence swings it. Everything before is blessing; everything after is bondage.

"Did not know Joseph" does not mean he had never heard the name. The Hebrew yada is the verb of relationship and acknowledgement — the word for knowing a person, not a fact. This king refuses the debt. Egypt owed its very survival to a Hebrew who had read God's warning in a dream and stockpiled grain against the famine; the nation ate because Joseph lived. The new dynasty simply writes him out. Gratitude has a short memory in the palaces of the world.

And mark what the narrator does not tell us. He does not name this king. The mightiest man on earth, master of the Nile and its armies, is "a new king" — anonymous for the whole chapter. In a few verses two slave midwives will be named and remembered forever. God's economy of honour is the exact inverse of the world's.

Here is the pattern, and it has never changed: where grace is forgotten, hostility follows. A world that will not remember what it owes will turn, sooner or later, on the people it owes it to.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his people, "Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and, if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Too many and too mighty for us." Pharaoh is looking straight at the blessing of God and calling it a threat. The very fruitfulness that fulfils the promise to Abraham registers, to the eye of unbelief, as a security problem to be managed. It always does. The world rarely sees the growth of God's people as gift; it sees a demographic to be contained.

"Come, let us deal shrewdly with them." The word is worth stopping on. It is the language of the serpent, who was "more crafty than any other beast of the field" (Gen 3:1) — cunning, calculating, self-protective. And the opening phrase is the language of Babel: "Come, let us make bricks... Come, let us build ourselves a city" (Gen 11:3-4). Empire always says come, let us. It is the voice of men taking counsel together against a God they have not factored in.

By human calculation his logic is flawless. A large foreign population on your eastern frontier, in the corridor an invader must use — of course you act. He is a competent statesman, and he is utterly blind. He is not fighting a minority; he is fighting Genesis 1:28, and every measure he takes to reduce them will multiply them. "He who sits in the heavens laughs" (Ps 2:4). No one has ever won this fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses. But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shrewdness becomes policy. Taskmasters, heavy burdens, forced labour on state building projects — Pithom and Raamses, supply depots in the eastern delta where a Semitic population actually lived. The intent is not merely economic. Break a people's bodies and you break their birth rate: that was the calculation.

"But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad." There is the divine irony, stated flatly, without comment. The whip becomes the instrument of growth. Every extra burden produces extra Hebrews. Pharaoh is pressing down on a spring. Tertullian would say it centuries later watching the arenas fill: the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. Pressure has never yet reduced the people of God; it has only ever concentrated them.

And then the sentence that turns the whole scene upside down: "the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel." Dread is a strong word — a loathing, sickened horror. Who is afraid here? Not the slaves. The empire is afraid of the slaves. The man with the armies is terrified of the men with the bricks, because underneath the politics he is contending with Someone he cannot see and cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: So they ruthlessly made the people of Israel work as slaves and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them work as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word translated "ruthlessly" is perech — crushing harshness, the kind of labour designed to break a man rather than to build anything. It brackets the sentence at both ends, opening and closing it, so that you cannot read the verse without being hit twice. And their lives were made "bitter" — marar. Hold onto that word. Israel will taste it every spring at Passover in the bitter herbs (Exod 12:8), and they will taste it on purpose, forever, so that no generation forgets what God brought them out of.

Notice that Scripture does not hurry past this. Four verbs of bitterness answer the five verbs of fruitfulness in verse 7. God does not minimise his people's suffering or explain it away as a growth opportunity. He records it, names it, lets it stand on the page in all its weight. The God of the Exodus is no stranger to the groan of the oppressed — and in three verses' time we will be told that he heard it.

And there is an irony here that only hindsight can see. This nation, forced to make mortar and brick for a tyrant's storehouses, will one day be asked to build again — freely, joyfully, out of gifts they were not compelled to give — and what they build will be a tent for the living God to dwell in (Exod 35-40). The slave camp is the training ground for the craftsmen of the sanctuary. But not yet. First they must learn, at the bottom, to cry out to the God who hears.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-22 — The Fear of God Versus the Fear of Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 15-16: Oppression has failed, so Pharaoh escalates to murder and dresses it as a medical instruction: the midwives are to kill the boys on the birthstool. And the narrator does something extraordinary — he names them, Shiphrah and Puah, while the king of Egypt goes unnamed through the entire chapter.

Verse 17: But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them. One sentence, and an empire's policy dies in it.

Verses 18-19: Summoned to the throne to explain themselves, they answer that the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them.

Verses 20-21: So God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very strong; and because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.

Verse 22: The mask comes off — a public decree to all his people: Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fear of God Is Where Courage Comes From

Two fears meet in verse 17 and only one survives. In front of these women stands a king who can have them killed by lunchtime; above them stands a God they cannot see. They fear the One they cannot see more, and that is the whole secret. Fear the highest throne and every lower throne shrinks to its proper size. This is the first act of civil disobedience in Scripture, and God does not merely permit it — he rewards it. Believers are told to be subject to governing authorities (Rom. 13:1); they are never told to obey a command God forbids. We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29) was found by two slave midwives long before Peter said it aloud.

What the Text Commends, and What It Declines to Discuss

Was their answer in verse 19 true? Christians have differed honestly here, and the disagreement should be stated plainly: some hold it a straight falsehood God overlooked while blessing the faith behind it, some that it was true enough of hard-working women, some that it was a shrewd half-truth. What settles the matter is what the text itself chooses to say. It never comments on the answer. It comments on the motive — the midwives feared God — and it is for the fear of God, not for the sentence they spoke, that God rewards them. Rahab stands in exactly the same place a generation later and is treated exactly the same way: commended by name for her faith (Heb. 11:31; Jas. 2:25), never for her words.

God's Economy of Honour

The mightiest man on earth is "a new king," anonymous forever. Two slave midwives are written into Scripture by name and remembered three and a half thousand years later. That is how God keeps his books, and it is the exact inverse of the world's ledger.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Someone is always trying to kill the sons of Israel — Pharaoh here, Herod at Bethlehem, and behind both the dragon who stood before the woman... so that when she bore her child he might devour it (Rev. 12:4). Ever since Genesis 3:15 the serpent has known the promise runs through a seed, and he goes for the child every time.

Now: Look at how the evil is administered in verses 15-16 — quietly, through professionals, at the point of maximum vulnerability, with no soldiers and no record. That is how the great evils are usually run. And look at how it is resisted: not by an army but by two women with no power, no protection and no plan, who simply declined. God did not spare them the danger or remove the throne they had to stand before. He dealt well with them in it, which is usually how the kindness of God arrives — not as rescue from the hard place but as faithfulness inside it.

The reward fits the deed precisely: the women who risked everything to protect the households of Israel are given households of their own. The very thing Pharaoh strained to deny a nation, God quietly hands to the two who defied him. Nothing done in the fear of God is ever finally lost.

And keep an eye on the river. Pharaoh takes Egypt's source of life — its water, its harvest, its highway, worshipped as a god — and makes it a grave for children, which is precisely what sin always does with the gifts of God. But in a few verses that same water will carry a basket, and the deliverer will float safely down the river meant to kill him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah, "When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oppression has failed, so Pharaoh escalates to murder — and dresses it as a routine medical instruction. It is done quietly, through professionals, at the point of maximum vulnerability: "on the birthstool," the two stones on which a woman crouched to deliver. A newborn, a mother spent with labour, and a trained pair of hands that could make a death look like a stillbirth. No soldiers, no blood in the streets, no record. This is how the great evils are usually administered.

Why the boys and not the girls? Because boys grow into soldiers, and girls can be absorbed by marriage into Egypt. But look underneath the policy. Someone is always trying to kill the sons of Israel: Pharaoh here, Herod at Bethlehem, and behind both the dragon who "stood before the woman... so that when she bore her child he might devour it" (Rev 12:4). Ever since Genesis 3:15 the serpent has known the promise comes through a seed, and he goes for the child every time.

And now the narrator does something extraordinary. He names them: Shiphrah and Puah. Pharaoh — lord of the Nile, owner of armies, a god in his own theology — goes unnamed through this entire chapter. Two slave midwives are written into Scripture by name and remembered three and a half thousand years later. That is how God keeps his books.

verseByVerse.quote: But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But the midwives feared God." One sentence, and an empire's policy dies in it.

Two fears meet in this verse and only one survives. In front of these women stands the king of Egypt, who can have them killed by lunchtime. Above them stands God, whom they cannot see. They fear the One they cannot see more than the one they can — and that is the whole secret. The fear of God is not the enemy of courage; it is where courage comes from. Sinclair Ferguson puts it exactly: the fear of God liberates from the fear of man. Fear the highest throne and every lower throne shrinks to its proper size.

This is the first act of civil disobedience in the Bible, and God does not merely permit it — he rewards it. Scripture tells us to be subject to the governing authorities (Rom 13:1); it never tells us to obey a command God forbids. Where the two collide, the line is clear: "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). Two Hebrew midwives found that line long before Peter said it out loud, and they found it with no power, no army and no protection whatever — nothing but the fear of the LORD, which turned out to be enough.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this, and let the male children live?" The midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture it. Two slave women, summoned before the throne of the most powerful man alive, asked to explain why his order has not been carried out. "Why have you done this?" They know what the answer to that question usually costs.

Their reply is that the Hebrew women are vigorous and deliver before the midwife can get there. Was it true? Was it a lie? Christians have differed here honestly, and the disagreement should be stated plainly. Some hold it was a straight falsehood which God overlooked while blessing the faith behind it; others that it was true, or true enough, in a population of hard-working women; others that it was a shrewd half-truth. What settles the matter is what the text itself chooses to say. It never comments on the answer. It comments on the motive — "the midwives feared God" (v. 17) — and it is for the fear of God, not for the sentence they spoke, that God rewards them (v. 21). It is unwise to build a doctrine of lying on a verse that declines to discuss it, and unwise to miss what the verse is shouting.

Rahab will stand in exactly the same place a generation later, and Scripture will treat her exactly the same way: commended by name for her faith (Heb 11:31; Jas 2:25), never for her words. God is not endorsing everything his servants say under interrogation. He is honouring women who put their bodies between a tyrant and a child.

verseByVerse.quote: So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong. And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So God dealt well with the midwives." He did not spare them the danger; he did not remove the throne they had to stand before. He dealt well with them in it. That is usually how the kindness of God arrives — not as rescue from the hard place, but as faithfulness inside it.

And then the reward, and it fits the deed with a precision that should make you smile: "because the midwives feared God, he gave them families." The Hebrew says he made them houses. The women who risked everything to protect the households of Israel are given households of their own. The very thing Pharaoh was straining to deny an entire nation, God quietly hands to the two women who defied him. He is no man's debtor. Nothing done in the fear of God is ever finally lost.

And notice the sentence tucked between the two halves of their reward: "and the people multiplied and grew very strong." Pharaoh's second policy has failed as completely as his first. He has now tried labour and he has tried murder, and Israel is stronger after both.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the mask comes off. No more discreet orders to professionals behind a curtain — this is a public decree to "all his people," conscripting an entire nation into infanticide. Evil that begins in a private instruction ends as a civic duty.

And he chooses the Nile. Understand what that river was to Egypt: its water, its harvest, its highway, its life — and its god, worshipped as Hapi, the giver of all things. Pharaoh takes the river of life and makes it a grave for children. That is precisely what sin always does with the gifts of God: it takes the good thing given for life and turns it into an instrument of death.

So the chapter ends in the dark, with a river full of drowned sons and no deliverer in sight. But keep your eye on that river. In a few verses it will carry a basket, waterproofed with the same mortar and pitch these slaves had been forced to handle, and inside it the deliverer will float safely down the very water meant to kill him (2:3). In six chapters God will turn that river to blood (7:20). Pharaoh's instrument of death becomes the cradle of salvation — which is the pattern of everything God does, and which comes to its end on a Roman gallows, where the world's cruellest instrument of execution became the tree of life.

1.theology:
The faithfulness of God to his promises. The growth of Israel is the keeping of the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 12, 15). No empire can annul what God has sworn. The whole book rests on this bedrock: God remembers.

The fear of God. Shiphrah and Puah embody the truth that reverence for God is the root of moral courage. To fear God is to be set free from the tyranny of fear of man.

Suffering and providence. God's people are not promised ease but presence. Affliction is real, yet it is woven into a providence that advances, not defeats, God's purposes.
1.examples:
Then: A favored immigrant people became despised slaves under a regime that feared their numbers and sought their extinction — the first genocide recorded in Scripture, met by the quiet defiance of God-fearing women.

Now: Christians under pressure should not be surprised. The church grows where it is persecuted. And we are called, like the midwives, to a higher allegiance: to fear God so deeply that the threats of the powerful lose their grip on us.

2.title: Drawn Out of the Water
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman.<sup>2</sup>The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.<sup>3</sup>When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank.<sup>4</sup>And his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him.<sup>5</sup>Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it.<sup>6</sup>When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God.<sup>24</sup>And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.<sup>25</sup>God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
2.overview:
Against Pharaoh's death-decree, God begins his rescue not with armies but with a baby in a basket. A Levite woman hides her son, then entrusts him to the very river meant to drown him, in a little ark of bulrushes daubed with pitch — the same word used of Noah's ark. The deliverer is saved by water that should have killed him, and is drawn from it by the daughter of the very tyrant who ordered his death. Providence has a sense of irony and a sovereign hand.

Moses grows up in two worlds — nursed by his Hebrew mother, raised in Pharaoh's palace. As Hebrews 11 tells us, he will one day choose to be mistreated with the people of God rather than enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. But first comes his failed attempt to deliver by his own hand: he kills an Egyptian, is exposed, and flees to Midian. The man who tries to save Israel in his own strength must spend forty years in the wilderness learning that salvation belongs to the LORD.

The chapter closes with four of the most tender verbs in Scripture: God heard, God remembered, God saw, God knew. The silence of heaven is about to break.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Basket on the Nile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: Against a death decree, God begins his rescue with a baby. Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman, and when she saw that her son was a fine child, she hid him three months.

Verses 3-4: When hiding fails she builds him a basket made of bulrushes and daubs it with bitumen and pitch — the same word used of Noah's ark — and puts him in the reeds at the river's edge, with his sister standing at a distance to see what would happen.

Verses 5-6: Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, found the basket, opened it, and the baby was crying. She took pity on him.

Verses 7-9: The sister steps forward, and by the end of the exchange the child's own mother is being paid Egyptian wages to nurse her own son.

Verse 10: He is brought to Pharaoh's daughter, becomes her son, and is named Moses — Because I drew him out of the water.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Works Through the Smallest Things

There is no miracle in this passage. There is a basket, a mother's nerve, a sister's watchfulness, a princess's bath and a baby's cry at exactly the right moment — and out of those ordinary materials God bends Pharaoh's own household toward Israel's rescue. The empire's death decree is defeated by a woman with tar and reeds, and the tyrant ends up funding the upbringing of the man who will break him.

The Ark Word

The basket is a tevah — the word used of only one other object in the Hebrew Bible, Noah's ark. Both are waterproofed with pitch; both carry the hope of the world through the water of judgement; both land their occupant safely on the far side. The narrator is not being subtle. Salvation comes through the very waters meant to destroy, which is why the New Testament will read a drowned Egyptian army as baptism (1 Cor. 10:1-2) and Peter will read Noah's flood the same way (1 Pet. 3:20-21).

He Chooses the Weak to Shame the Strong

The people who defeat Pharaoh in these ten verses are all women, and not one of them holds any power: two midwives in the previous chapter, a Levite mother, a watching sister, and — the sharpest irony in the book — the tyrant's own daughter, who looks at a condemned Hebrew boy and feels pity. God's deliverance arrives through the compassion of an enemy's child.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A mother put her son into the river that had been declared his grave. Read verse 3 slowly and it is almost unbearable: she had hidden him three months, and hiding had run out, and the only thing left to do was to let him go into the very water the decree named. Hebrews calls that faith (Heb. 11:23). It did not feel like faith. It felt like a mother running out of options.

Now: The deliverer is saved by water that should have killed him, and drawn out by the daughter of the man who ordered his death. Nothing in the scene is dramatic and every piece of it is load-bearing. A great deal of God's work looks like this from the inside — a sequence of small decisions and lucky-looking timings, none of which announces itself, all of which turn out afterwards to have been holding the weight.

And there is a quiet mercy tucked into verses 7-9 that is easy to read past. The mother who had to give her baby away gets him back — legally, safely, and paid for it. She has him for the years that will matter most, long enough to tell him whose son he actually is. Forty years later, in a palace, with every door in Egypt open to him, he will choose the slave gang over the throne (Heb. 11:24-26), and this is where he learned it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman. The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 1 ended with a river full of drowned sons and no deliverer in sight. And God's answer to that begins — with a wedding. No angel, no announcement, no sign in the sky. "A man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman." The rescue of a nation starts in a bedroom in a slave quarter, and nobody notices.

Both of them are Levites, which the narrator mentions without comment. It will matter enormously later: this is the tribe that will carry the priesthood. Their names are held back until 6:20 — Amram and Jochebed — because at this moment they are nobody, two slaves under a death decree.

"When she saw that he was a fine child" — the Hebrew word is tov, "good." It is the word that tolls through Genesis 1: and God saw that it was good. A slave mother looks down at her newborn and, without knowing it, echoes the Creator surveying his work. Stephen says he was "beautiful in God's sight" (Acts 7:20).

"She hid him three months." Scripture has a name for that: "By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king's edict" (Heb 11:23). Not maternal instinct — faith. Two slaves with no rights whatever looked at the most powerful decree on earth and were not afraid of it. That is the fifth act of defiance in two chapters, and every one of them so far has been carried out by a woman.

verseByVerse.quote: When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank. And his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now watch the words, because the narrator is shouting and it is easy to walk past. The "basket" is a tevah. That word appears in only two stories in the entire Hebrew Bible: here, and Noah's ark. It is not the ordinary word for a box or a basket. And she "daubed it with bitumen and pitch" — exactly what Noah was told to do: "cover it inside and out with pitch" (Gen 6:14).

So this tiny boat is an ark, deliberately and unmistakably. Two vessels, both waterproofed with pitch, both carrying God's chosen through the very waters sent to destroy them. Noah's ark saved a family so that a world could go on. This ark saves a baby so that a nation could be born. And there is a bitter irony in the materials: bitumen, pitch, mortar — the very stuff of the slave labour that was crushing them (1:14). She takes the tools of her oppression and builds a rescue with them.

"Among the reeds by the river bank." The word for reeds is suph. Remember it. In thirteen chapters this nation will walk through the yam suph, the Sea of Reeds, and come out the other side alive. The baby is laid among the reeds; the people will be drawn through the reeds. His whole life is a rehearsal of theirs.

And then Miriam: "his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him." Faith does what it can and then it stands and watches. She has no plan. She cannot swim to him, cannot protect him, cannot control one thing that happens next. She stays anyway. There is a kind of love whose only remaining act is to refuse to look away.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it. When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. She took pity on him and said, "This is one of the Hebrews' children."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of every stretch of a river four thousand miles long, and every person in Egypt, the one who comes down to bathe at that spot on that morning is the daughter of the man who signed the death warrant. Call it coincidence and you have understood nothing. "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will" (Prov 21:1). God governs empires, and God governs a princess's decision about where to bathe.

"And behold, the baby was crying." The narrator makes us stop and look. And consider what the weapon is. Not an angel, not a plague, not a sign — a baby crying. That is what God brings against the might of Egypt at this moment, and it is enough. "God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong" (1 Cor 1:27). The tears of an infant move the heart of his executioner's daughter.

"She took pity on him." God can plant mercy in any heart he pleases, including inside the palace of the man who ordered the drownings. And do not miss what she says next: "This is one of the Hebrews' children." She knows. She knows the decree, she knows the child is under it, and she adopts him anyway. That is now four women who have defied Pharaoh — two midwives, a mother, and his own daughter. The great king is being dismantled from inside his own house, by people he never thought worth fearing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?" And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Go." So the girl went and called the child's mother. And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages." So the woman took the child and nursed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slave girl steps out of the reeds and addresses a princess of Egypt. It should have cost her everything. "Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women?" — spoken as if the thought had only just occurred to her.

"Go." One word, and the trap closes on the empire.

"So the girl went and called the child's mother." The narrator does not comment. He does not need to. And then the sentence that ought to make you put the book down: "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages." Jochebed is paid — out of Pharaoh's own treasury — to raise the son Pharaoh commanded to be drowned. The empire funds the rescue of the deliverer who will one day break it. The mother who could not keep her boy is handed him back, legally, safely, with a salary.

This is the laughter of Psalm 2: "He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision." It is not gentle laughter. Pharaoh's death decree has been turned, inside a fortnight, into a job offer for the mother of the man who will bury him.

And there is a quieter mercy in it. Those first years in his mother's arms are where Moses learns that he is a Hebrew, and learns the name of the God of Abraham. Egypt will give him his education. Jochebed gives him his identity. When he is forty and it comes to choosing, that is what he will choose.

verseByVerse.quote: When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, "Because," she said, "I drew him out of the water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"She brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son." She gives him up a second time, and this surrender is harder than the basket. The first time she was saving his life. This time she is simply keeping her word, and walking home without him.

"She named him Moses." The name is Egyptian — mose, "born of," the ending you hear in Thutmose and Rameses. But the princess reaches for a Hebrew meaning: mashah, to draw out. "Because I drew him out of the water." She names him after the one thing she did.

And in doing it she prophesies, without the faintest idea that she is doing it. The man drawn out of the water will draw a nation out of the water. What was done to him, he will do for them. Every deliverer God uses is first a delivered man; nobody leads anyone out of a place he has not been brought out of himself.

And there is a greater One standing behind this. Another baby, another king killing infant boys, another rescue in the night — and another child called out of Egypt: "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Hos 11:1; Matt 2:15). Moses is the shadow. The substance is coming.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-22 — The Failed Deliverer in Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11-12: When Moses had grown up — forty, Stephen tells us (Acts 7:23) — he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.

Verses 13-14: The next day he tries words instead of a fist and is thrown the question that ends everything: Who made you a prince and a judge over us? — and Then Moses was afraid.

Verse 15: Pharaoh seeks to kill him; Moses flees to Midian and sat down by a well.

Verses 16-17: Seven daughters of the priest of Midian come to water their father's flock, shepherds drive them away, and Moses stood up and saved them, and watered their flock.

Verses 18-20: Reuel asks why they are home early; they answer that an Egyptian delivered us — and he sends them back for the man.

Verses 21-22: Moses settles, marries Zipporah, and names his son Gershom: I have been a sojourner in a foreign land.
verseByVerse.theology:
Right Diagnosis, Wrong Hand

Moses is right that Israel is oppressed, right that a deliverer is needed, and right that he is the man. He is wrong about the method, the timing and who is in charge. He looked this way and that — and never looked up. He checked for witnesses and forgot the Witness; "seeing no one" was not true, and the sand hid nothing. Zeal running on its own clock is just violence with a good motive, and it will cost him forty years to learn the difference.

The Rejected One Is the Appointed One

Who made you a prince and a judge over us? is perfectly right and perfectly wrong: nobody had — not yet — but God would, and the man sneering the question is describing exactly what Moses will become, forty years early. Stephen saw what nobody else in Scripture stops to say: He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand (Acts 7:25) — and then drove it at the council about to stone him: This Moses, whom they rejected... this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer (Acts 7:35). He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). Moses is refused by his brothers before he can save them; so was Christ, and Christ was refused not for forty years but to the death.

The Fear of Man

The infant whose parents were not afraid of the king's edict (Heb. 11:23) is, at forty, afraid. The fear of man lays a snare (Prov. 29:25), and it catches the strongest. Moses will need a burning bush before he is free of it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: One day, and everything is gone — position, education, standing, and the plan for rescuing Israel — in the time it takes a rumour to cross a courtyard. He is not a prince; he is a wanted man. And in Midian he does the same thing he did in Egypt: he sees people being pushed around and he stands up for them. The instinct was never the problem.

Now: There is a particular kind of failure in view here, and it should be named, because it is common among people who love God: the failure that comes not from indifference but from running ahead. Moses' compassion in verse 11 is the very thing God will say of himself two chapters later — I have surely seen the affliction of my people (3:7). He was beginning to see what God sees. What he had not learned was that seeing what God sees does not authorise acting in God's place.

Then he sat down by a well, and any reader of Genesis feels it land. Wells are where covenant history turns: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah at one (Gen. 24), Jacob meets Rachel at one (Gen. 29). When an emptied man sits down by a well in this book, God is about to hand him a life. Moses thinks he is resting. He is arriving.

And he names his son sojourner in a foreign land — which is the honest confession of a man who has stopped expecting anything. He is not waiting for a burning bush. He has settled. The next thing that happens to him will happen entirely from God's side.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his people. He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Moses had grown up" — Stephen tells us he was forty (Acts 7:23). Forty years inside the palace, "instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22), with every door in the empire open to him.

"He went out to his people." He did not have to. Nothing compelled him but what his mother had taught him. And Hebrews calls this the great decision of his life: "By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt" (Heb 11:24-26). He weighed an empire against a slave gang and judged the slave gang the better investment. He was right.

"And looked on their burdens." Mark that verb. It is the very thing God will say of himself in two chapters: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people" (3:7). Moses is beginning to see what God sees. The compassion is real, and it is from God.

"He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian." There is the whole tragedy in one line. He looked this way and that — and never looked up. He checked for witnesses and forgot the Witness. "Seeing no one": there was Someone, and the sand hid nothing from him.

So: right about the injustice, right that Israel needs a deliverer, right that he is the man. Wrong about the method, wrong about the timing, wrong about who is in charge. Zeal without God's clock is just violence with a good motive. It will take forty years in a desert to teach him the difference, and God is not in a hurry.

verseByVerse.quote: When he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrews were struggling together. And he said to the man in the wrong, "Why do you strike your companion?" He answered, "Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid, and thought, "Surely the thing is known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes out again, and this time he uses a word rather than a fist: "Why do you strike your companion?" He is learning already. It makes no difference.

"Who made you a prince and a judge over us?" The question is perfectly right and perfectly wrong. Nobody had made him a prince and a judge — not yet. But God would. The man sneering the question has no idea that he is describing exactly what this man will be, and that he is forty years early.

Stephen sees what nobody else in Scripture stops to say: "He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand" (Acts 7:25). And then Stephen drives it home to the council that is about to stone him: "This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' — this man God sent as both ruler and redeemer" (Acts 7:35). The rejected one is the appointed one. That is the pattern of the whole Bible, and Stephen is preaching it with stones already in men's hands.

"He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him" (John 1:11). Moses is refused by his brothers before he can save them; so was Christ — and Christ was not refused for forty years but to the death. Moses is the shadow of it.

"Then Moses was afraid." There it is. The infant whose parents "were not afraid of the king's edict" is, at forty, afraid. The fear of man snares the strongest (Prov 29:25), and Moses will need a burning bush before he is free of it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day, and everything is gone. His position, his education, his standing, his plan for rescuing Israel — all of it, in the time it takes for a rumour to cross a courtyard. He is not a prince; he is a wanted man.

Midian lies east, out beyond the reach of Egypt — and it is family, distantly: the Midianites descend from Abraham through Keturah (Gen 25:2). The runaway flees, without knowing it, toward his own people.

"And he sat down by a well." It is a small sentence and any reader of Genesis feels it land. Wells are where covenant history turns: Abraham's servant finds Rebekah at a well (Gen 24); Jacob meets Rachel at a well (Gen 29). When a lone, emptied man sits down by a well in this book, God is about to give him a life. Moses thinks he is resting. He is arriving.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock. The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and saved them, and watered their flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third time in this chapter Moses sees someone strong pushing someone weak, and the third time he cannot walk past it. An Egyptian beating a Hebrew; a Hebrew striking a Hebrew; now shepherds bullying girls. This instinct is the making of the man, and it very nearly destroyed him.

But look what has changed. In Egypt he struck and hid a body in the sand. Here he "stood up and saved them" — and then stayed and watered their flock. No blood, no corpse, no glancing this way and that; just help, given and then followed through with hard, unglamorous work at a trough. The fire is the same. The hand is different.

The word for "saved" is yasha — the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus. God is teaching this man what saving actually looks like, and it looks less like a sword than a bucket.

And so the prince of Egypt becomes a shepherd for a foreigner. This is God's seminary, and the course lasts forty years. The man who will one day lead a vast, complaining flock through a waterless wilderness is learning, one trough at a time, how to keep sheep alive in a desert. Nothing God does with his servants in the wilderness is wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came home to their father Reuel, he said, "How is it that you have come home so soon today?" They said, "An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds and even drew water for us and watered the flock." He said to his daughters, "Then where is he? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How is it that you have come home so soon today?" A father's mild puzzlement at the supper hour. It is the kind of homely detail nobody invents, and it tells you this is remembered, not composed. It also tells you something grim in passing: being driven from the well was normal. The bullying happened every day.

"An Egyptian delivered us." Feel the weight of that word. The man who refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, who went out to his people and killed for them — is taken for an Egyptian by Midianite girls. His own brothers rejected him as an outsider; now foreigners identify him as the enemy he walked away from. He belongs nowhere on earth. God has him exactly where he can use him.

"Then where is he? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread." Reuel's reflex is hospitality — and a table is precisely what a homeless fugitive needs. God feeds his servant through the ordinary decency of a man who has no idea who is sitting down at his table.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah. She gave birth to a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Moses was content to dwell with the man." Read that slowly, because it is the saddest word in the chapter. The man who at forty threw away an empire to rescue his people is now content. Settled. A wife, a father-in-law, a flock, a routine. The fire has gone out. He has stopped trying to save anybody, and he will stay that way for forty years.

And the boy's name tells you what is really in him: Gershom — ger sham, "a sojourner there." "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land." He names his own son after his homelessness. Every time he calls the child in for supper he says out loud that he does not belong here.

He is more right than he knows. He is a sojourner in Midian — but he was a sojourner in Egypt too, and so is every Hebrew in those brickyards. So, come to that, are we: "strangers and exiles on the earth... seeking a homeland" (Heb 11:13-14). The ache Moses cannot name is the truest thing about him, and God is not going to cure it. God is going to use it. The man who feels he belongs nowhere is exactly the man to lead a people home.

So here is the bottom of the story: the deliverer is a shepherd with a foreign wife and a son named "I don't belong here," and nothing whatever happens for four decades. If you are in such a stretch, understand what it is. God was not idle and God was not late. He was making a man.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-25 — God Heard, Remembered, Saw, Knew
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 23: During those many days the king of Egypt died — the man Moses fled from is gone, and nothing improves — and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God.

Verses 24-25: Four verbs answer, and they are the hinge of the entire book: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. God saw the people of Israel — and God knew.
verseByVerse.theology:
Four Verbs, and the Silence Breaks

Heard, remembered, saw, knew. Not one of them describes a change in God; every one describes the moment his settled purpose begins to move. Remembered in Hebrew is never the opposite of having forgotten — it is the word for acting on a commitment. When God remembers Noah, the waters go down; when he remembers his covenant here, an empire is about to fall. And knew sits at the end with no object at all in the Hebrew, which is why the ESV prints it exactly like that: and God knew. The sentence simply stops. Whatever it is that God knows about these people is not spelled out, and the silence at the end of the verse is louder than an explanation would have been.

The Covenant Is the Reason

God does not act because Israel has improved, prayed correctly, or earned anything. The text says why he moves: he remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. The rescue is grounded in a promise made centuries earlier to men who were dead long before any of these slaves were born. That is the only security the people of God have ever had, and it has never yet failed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Notice what verse 23 does not say. It does not say Israel prayed, or repented, or turned back to the God of their fathers. It says they groaned and cried out — the inarticulate noise of people at the end of themselves, not addressed to anyone in particular. And that came up to God and was counted as prayer.

Now: This is the verse for anyone whose praying has stopped being praying and become noise. The cry that reached heaven and started the exodus was not eloquent, not theologically framed, and, so far as the text tells us, not even consciously directed at God. He heard it anyway. The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Rom. 8:26) — the same word, and the same God on the other end of it.

And a note on the timing, because it matters. The old king dies in verse 23 and the situation does not improve at all; a new Pharaoh simply inherits the policy. Israel had every reason to read that as the last door closing. It was, in fact, the moment the deliverance began — God was already at work, and the only evidence of it available to anyone in Egypt was that nothing had changed. What looked from the brickyards like the silence of heaven was the four verbs of verses 24-25 taking effect, and there was no way to see it from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: During those many days the king of Egypt died, and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"During those many days" — the narrator's way of covering forty years in four words. And then: "the king of Egypt died." The man who wanted Moses dead is dead himself, and it changes nothing at all. The bondage does not lift. Tyrants die and tyranny continues; that is the way of the world, and Israel has learned it the hard way.

Now notice exactly what the text says they did. It does not say they prayed. It does not say they repented, or believed, or called on the name of the LORD. It says they groaned. This is not eloquent intercession; it is the wordless noise people make when there is nothing left in them. And it "came up to God."

If that is all your faith can manage tonight — a groan with no words in it and no theology in it — take heart. "The Spirit helps us in our weakness... the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Rom 8:26). God is not deaf to inarticulate pain. He has never once required his people to suffer beautifully before he would listen.

verseByVerse.quote: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four verbs, and the whole book turns on them: God heard. God remembered. God saw. God knew. After two chapters in which God has not spoken a single word, the subject of every verb is suddenly God.

"Remembered" does not mean he had forgotten. Derek Kidner puts it exactly: God's remembering is not the waking of a forgetful deity but the activating of a sworn promise. "God remembered Noah," and the waters went down (Gen 8:1). When God remembers, God moves. Egypt is finished, and Egypt does not know it yet.

And look closely at what moves him. Not Israel's merit — the text does not offer any, and their behaviour in the wilderness will show there was none to offer. What moves God is "his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob" — a promise he made to three men who had been dead for four hundred years. The exodus does not rest on the worthiness of the slaves. It rests on the word of God, sworn to a man long buried. That is grace, and it is precisely why it cannot fail. Your salvation stands on the same footing.

"God saw the people of Israel — and God knew." And the Hebrew simply stops. There is no object. Knew what? Everything: their pain, their years, their names, the day of their going out, the blood on the doorposts, the sea standing up in walls, the glory coming down on a tent. The sentence breaks off because the answer will take forty chapters.

It is the silence before the storm of salvation. Turn the page: a bush is about to burn.

2.theology:
Providence. Every detail — a basket, a sister, a princess's compassion — is governed by an unseen hand bending Pharaoh's own household toward Israel's rescue.

The weakness of the flesh. Moses' premature, violent attempt at deliverance must fail so that God's deliverance may stand. Salvation is the LORD's, not the deliverer's.

Covenant remembrance. God hears, remembers, sees, and knows. His saving acts flow from his covenant faithfulness, not from Israel's worthiness.
2.examples:
Then: Under a death decree, God preserved a deliverer through the very waters of judgment, raised him in the enemy's house, then drove him into forty years of obscurity to prepare him.

Now: God still uses long, hidden seasons to empty us of self-confidence and fit us for his service. And he still hears the cry of his afflicted people — our groaning is never lost in the silence.

3.title: I AM WHO I AM
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.<sup>2</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed.<sup>3</sup>And Moses said, "I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned."<sup>4</sup>When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, "Moses, Moses!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>5</sup>Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."<sup>6</sup>And he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.<sup>7</sup>Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings,<sup>8</sup>and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>9</sup>And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.<sup>10</sup>Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt."<sup>11</sup>But Moses said to God, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?"<sup>12</sup>He said, "But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."<sup>13</sup>Then Moses said to God, "If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?"<sup>14</sup>God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"<sup>15</sup>God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.<sup>16</sup>Go and gather the elders of Israel together and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying, "I have observed you and what has been done to you in Egypt,<sup>17</sup>and I promise that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey."'<sup>18</sup>And they will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; and now, please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.'<sup>19</sup>But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.<sup>20</sup>So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go.<sup>21</sup>And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; and when you go, you shall not go empty,<sup>22</sup>but each woman shall ask of her neighbor, and any woman who lives in her house, for silver and gold jewelry, and for clothing. You shall put them on your sons and on your daughters. So you shall plunder the Egyptians."
3.overview:
Here is one of the holiest moments in all of Scripture. An eighty-year-old shepherd, long since written off, turns aside to see a bush that burns but is not consumed — and meets the living God. The fire that does not consume is a parable of God himself: blazing in holiness, yet not destroying; full of glory, yet stooping to speak with a fugitive on the back side of the desert.

God reveals his compassion before he reveals his name: "I have surely seen... I have heard... I have come down to deliver." The transcendent God of the bush is also the God who bends to the cries of slaves. Then comes the name above all names: "I AM WHO I AM" — the self-existent, eternal, unchanging God who depends on nothing and on whom all things depend. Sproul called this the most important text on the being of God in the Old Testament. The God of the burning bush is the God who simply IS.

When Jesus later says, "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), he claims this very name. The voice from the bush and the voice in Galilee are one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: Moses is keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian — another man's sheep, at the far end of the wilderness, forty years into obscurity — when he comes to Horeb, which the narrator already calls the mountain of God. There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush, and the bush burns without being consumed.

Verse 3: I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned. A man with a job to do stops.

Verses 4-5: Only then does the voice come — God called to him out of the bush, "Moses, Moses!" — and Moses answers with the servant's word, Here I am. The first instruction is not an errand but a boundary: Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.

Verse 6: God names himself by the men he made promises to — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob — the first word after four centuries of silence, and it is a word of continuity. And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Fire That Needs No Fuel

Every fire in human experience is consuming something; that is what fire is. This one is not, and the sign is the doctrine before the doctrine is spoken. Within a dozen verses God will give his name — I AM WHO I AM — and it means precisely what the bush is doing: existence that depends on nothing, is fed by nothing, and can be exhausted by nothing. Moses is shown God's self-existence in flame before he is told it in words.

Holiness Is a Presence, Not a Property

The sand where Moses stands is the same sand as the sand behind him. Nothing has happened to the ground. What makes it holy is that God is on it — which is why holiness in Scripture travels: to a tent, to a temple, to a body, to a people. Do not come near and Moses, Moses arrive in the same breath, and the whole of the rest of the Bible is the answer to how those two sentences can both be true.

The Tense of the Verb

God does not say he was the God of Abraham but that he is — and fifteen centuries later Jesus settles the question of the resurrection out of that single present tense: He is not God of the dead, but of the living (Matt. 22:32). Abraham had been buried for centuries when the bush burned, and the covenant was still in force. The grave did not end the relationship, because the God who made the promise did not.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The commission that would break an empire was handed to an eighty-year-old man who had spent half his life minding livestock he did not own. Nothing in the forty years in Midian looked like preparation. It was preparation. The Moses who tried to free Israel with his own hands at forty had to be unmade before the Moses who would free them with God's hand at eighty could exist.

Now: There is a particular comfort here for anyone who has quietly concluded that their useful years are behind them — that the long stretch of unremarkable work is what their life turned out to be instead of what it was for. God did not find Moses in a temple or on a pilgrimage. He found him at work, at the far end of nowhere, on an ordinary Tuesday with the sheep.

And note what God asks of him first. Not competence, not a plan, not courage — just that he take his sandals off. Before Moses is told anything about Egypt he is told whose ground he is standing on. Most of what goes wrong in a life of service goes wrong because that order gets reversed: the errand is taken up before the holiness is reckoned with. Moses hid his face, and he was right to. A man who has never been frightened of God has not yet met him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest commission in human history begins with a man minding someone else's sheep. Count what has already gone. Moses is eighty years old (Acts 7:30). Forty of those years were spent as a prince of Egypt, and forty more out here, and the second forty have produced precisely nothing that anyone would write down. He has no flock of his own; the text is careful to say so twice over — the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro. A man who once had the run of Pharaoh's household now owns no animal he is looking at.

Notice where he is. He led the flock to the west side of the wilderness — the far side, the back of beyond, the direction you go when the near grazing is finished. This is not a pilgrimage. Moses is not seeking a vision, not praying on a mountain, not waiting on God. He is working, and he is working at the far end of nowhere, and he has been doing it for four decades.

And then the narrator drops in a detail he has no business knowing yet: Moses came to Horeb, the mountain of God. It is not called that because of anything that has happened there. It is called that because of what is about to happen, and because of what will happen on that same rock when Moses comes back with a nation behind him. The storyteller is writing with the end in view. Moses walks up an ordinary hill; the reader is told it is the mountain of God.

There is a particular comfort here for anyone who has concluded that their useful years are behind them. The forty years in Midian were not a holding pattern God tolerated before the real work began. They were where a man who once tried to liberate Israel single-handed, and buried a body in the sand to cover it (2:12), was unmade. God was not wasting Moses in Midian. He was making the only kind of man who could be trusted with Israel — one who no longer believed he could do it. (cf. Acts 7:23-30)

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed. And Moses said, "I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire is the standard signature of God's presence in Scripture — the torch between the pieces in Genesis 15, the pillar that will lead this nation, the tongues at Pentecost.
