But look at what is actually strange here, because it is easy to miss under familiarity. Every fire you have ever seen is eating something. That is what fire is: a reaction that consumes its fuel. Wood becomes ash, wax becomes smoke, and when the fuel is gone the fire is gone with it. Fire is utterly dependent on what it burns.

This one is not. The bush is burning and the bush is not being used up. Moses is looking at a flame that needs nothing. And that is the point, because within a dozen verses God will tell him his name, and the name means exactly this: I AM WHO I AM — the one who depends on nothing and is consumed by nothing. Moses is given the doctrine as a picture before he is given it as a word. The sermon is preached in fire before it is preached in speech.

And consider the pulpit God chose. The Hebrew is seneh, a thornbush — desert scrub, the sort of thing you would burn precisely because it is worth nothing. Not a cedar of Lebanon, not an oak. Later Moses will bless Joseph with the favor of him who dwells in the bush (Deut. 33:16), and the phrase has stuck ever since, because it says something true about God's habits: he settles his glory on what the world would use for kindling.

Verse 3 records the decision the whole chapter hangs on. I will turn aside to see this great sight. Moses had a job to do and sheep to move, and he stopped. Be careful not to turn this into a lesson about spiritual attentiveness earning a revelation — God had already lit the bush, and God is the one who chose the hillside and the hour. But it is still true that a man on a schedule walks past a burning bush, and that God waited to speak until Moses came over.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, "Moses, Moses!" And he said, "Here I am." Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sequence is exact: When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him. The fire got his attention; the voice did the rest. And the voice does not begin with a doctrine or an errand. It begins with his name, twice — Moses, Moses! That doubling is not decoration. It is what God says when the matter is urgent and personal: Abraham, Abraham with the knife raised (Gen. 22:11); Samuel, Samuel in the dark; Saul, Saul on the Damascus road. A man is being summoned by name by someone who already knows it.

Moses answers with one word in Hebrew, hinneni — "Here I am." It is not a statement of location; God can see where he is standing. It is the word of a servant reporting for duty, the same word Abraham used, and Isaiah, and Samuel. Before Moses has heard a syllable of the assignment, he has made himself available to it.

Then, immediately: Do not come near. The invitation and the warning arrive in the same breath. God calls him by name and in the next sentence tells him to stop walking. Take the sandals off, because the ground is holy.

And here is the thing worth measuring. The sand under Moses' feet is the same sand as the sand a hundred yards behind him. Nothing has happened to the dirt. What makes that patch of desert holy is not a quality in the ground but a Presence on it — holiness here is not a property of places but of God, and it spreads to whatever he stands on. Which means the sandals are not a rule about footwear. A man took his sandals off to enter a house that was not his, and a slave went barefoot before his master. Moses is being told, before he is told anything else, whose ground this is. He came to graze sheep on that hill; he is standing in a throne room.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four hundred years of silence, and this is the first thing God says about himself: I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Not "I am the Almighty," not "I am the Creator" — both true, and neither is what a slave people need to hear first. He identifies himself by the men he made promises to. The message underneath the sentence is: nothing has lapsed. The God who spoke to Abraham about a land and a lineage has not changed his mind, changed his name, or changed his address. The silence was not absence.

Fifteen centuries later Jesus will stand in an argument with the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, and settle it out of this one verse — and he will do it on the tense of the verb. God did not say I was the God of Abraham. He said I am. And, Jesus says, "He is not God of the dead, but of the living" (Matt. 22:32). Abraham had been in his grave for centuries when the bush burned, and God was still, in the present tense, his God. Which means Abraham was not finished. The whole doctrine of the resurrection is drawn out of a verb that Moses probably heard as a simple introduction. (cf. Luke 20:37-38)

And Moses hid his face. Not out of etiquette but out of terror — he was afraid to look at God. Hold on to that, because it makes something later in this book almost unbearable to read. The man who covers his eyes at the bush will one day stand on this same mountain and say, "Please show me your glory" (33:18) — and be told no, because no one can see God's face and live (33:20). Moses will spend his life closer to God than any man of his age, and never get the one thing he asks for.

That request stayed unanswered for fifteen hundred years. It was answered on another mountain, where three men saw the glory of God in a human face and lived to describe it — and one of the three was Moses (Luke 9:30-31). The face he was not allowed to see in Exodus he saw at last in Christ, and had he asked at the bush what God's glory looked like, the honest answer would have been: like a Galilean carpenter, on a hill, talking with you about his exodus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-12 — I Have Come Down to Deliver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7-8: God piles up the verbs — I have surely seen the affliction of my people... have heard their cry... I know their sufferings — and then states the movement that governs everything he will ever do about human ruin: and I have come down to deliver them, out of Egypt and into a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, currently occupied by six named nations.

Verses 9-10: He says it a third time — the cry of the people of Israel has come to me — and then turns the whole thing on its hinge: Come, I will send you to Pharaoh. The God who comes down does so by sending a man.

Verse 11: Moses' objection is the most honest sentence he has spoken: Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?

Verse 12: God does not answer it. He answers a different question — But I will be with you — and attaches a sign that can only be checked at the far end: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Comes Down, and God Sends

Verse 8 says I have come down to deliver them; verse 10 says I will send you. Both are true and neither cancels the other. The rescue is entirely God's — his seeing, his hearing, his initiative, his mighty hand — and it arrives through a shepherd with a stick. This is the settled pattern: the deliverance does not become less divine because it has a man's footprints on it. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you (John 20:21).

The Descent

I have come down is two words in Hebrew and the shape of the whole gospel. He came down at Babel, he comes down here, and one day he came down so far that people who knew his mother's name could not believe it was him — the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), emptying himself and taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6-7). The distance from the throne to a burning bush is nothing beside the distance from the throne to a feeding trough, and he covered both in the same direction: downward, to get his people out.

The Cure for Inadequacy Is Not Self-Esteem

Moses asks who he is and God tells him who is going with him. There is no reassurance about Moses in verse 12 — no reminder of his palace education, no suggestion that he has gifts he has overlooked. Some of those things could truthfully have been said. God says none of them, because Moses' low estimate of himself is accurate and God simply declines to let it be decisive. If the qualification were the man, the man's opinion of himself would matter enormously. Since the qualification is God's presence, it does not matter at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel had been under the whip for generations, and chapter 2 ended with them groaning while heaven said nothing and forty more years went by. Anyone in those brickyards had every reason to conclude that God had not noticed. Verse 7 is the answer, and it is emphatic in the Hebrew: seeing I have seen. He had not merely observed the affliction; the word for know is the word for knowing a person. He had been inside it the whole time.

Now: The hardest form of suffering is not pain but pain that appears to be unwitnessed. Scripture gives part of an answer to the delay and withholds the rest: God had told Abraham the length of it in advance, and why, for reasons involving nations Israel had never heard of (Gen. 15:13-16). That tells a suffering people their pain sits inside a purpose. It should be said plainly that this is an explanation and not an anaesthetic — it does not make four hundred years feel shorter, and the text never pretends it does.

There is a second thing here for anyone who has prayed hard about something wrong in the world. Israel cried out; God heard; and God's response was to walk up to a man on a hillside and say Come, I will send you. It is a real possibility that the answer to a prayer is the person praying it. And when that lands on someone who feels wholly unequal to it, the reply on offer is not a better opinion of themselves. It is a promise, and the promise has not been withdrawn: Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt. 28:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pile up the verbs, because God does: I have surely seen... have heard their cry... I know their sufferings... I have come down. Four movements, and every one of them is a rebuttal of what Israel has surely concluded by now. "Surely seen" is emphatic in Hebrew — ra'oh ra'iti, literally "seeing I have seen," the construction you use when you mean it beyond any doubt. And I know is yada', which is never cold information; it is the word for knowing a person, knowing by acquaintance. God is not reporting that he has received intelligence about Israel's condition. He is saying he has been inside it.

Now put that against the arithmetic. Israel has been in Egypt four hundred years and under the whip for a long stretch of it. Chapter 2 ended with the people groaning and God hearing — and then the curtain came down and forty more years passed while Moses kept sheep. Anyone in those brickyards had every reason to believe that heaven had either not noticed or not cared. The honest question is not whether God saw. It is why, having seen, he waited so long.

Scripture gives part of an answer and withholds the rest. God had told Abraham this would happen, and how long it would run, and why: four hundred years, and then the fourth generation would come back, "for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" (Gen. 15:13-16). The delay was not indifference; it was a clock God was keeping for reasons that involved nations Israel had never heard of. But it should be said plainly that this is an explanation, not an anaesthetic. It tells a suffering people that their pain is inside a purpose. It does not make four hundred years feel shorter.

Then: I have come down. Two words in Hebrew, and they set the pattern for everything God will ever do about human ruin. He does not shout instructions from a height or send terms for negotiation. He comes down. He came down at Babel, he comes down here, and one day he will come down so far that people who knew his mother's name would not believe it was him. The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us (John 1:14); he did not count equality with God a thing to be clutched, but emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6-7). The distance from the throne to the burning bush is nothing beside the distance from the throne to the feeding trough — and he covered both in the same direction, downward, to get his people out.

And the destination is described in a phrase worth slowing over: a land flowing with milk and honey. Not a poetic way of saying "nice." Milk means there is grazing enough to keep flocks in permanent milk; honey means wildflowers in quantity enough to keep bees. It is a picture of a country that produces without being flogged for it — the exact opposite of the Nile mud these people are treading into bricks. God is not offering them a better version of Egypt. He is offering them the end of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them. Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says it again, and the repetition is not padding: the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression. He has now stated three times in four verses that he has heard. Then comes the sentence that changes everything, and it is not the one anybody would predict.

In verse 8 God said, "I have come down to deliver them." In verse 10 he says, Come, I will send you. Read those two together, because the whole doctrine of how God works in the world sits in the join. God's coming down does not bypass a human being; it takes the form of one. The deliverance is entirely his — his seeing, his hearing, his initiative, his mighty hand — and it arrives through an eighty-year-old shepherd with a stick.

This answers a question people genuinely ask, usually in frustration: if God cares about this situation, why does he not simply fix it? Verse 8 says he will. Verse 10 says how. The God who comes down is the God who sends, and the two are not alternatives. The rescue does not become less divine because it has a man's footprints on it.

There is a sharp edge here for anyone who has prayed hard about something wrong in the world. Israel cried out; God heard; and God's response was to walk up to a man on a hillside and say, "Come, I will send you." It is a real possibility that the answer to a prayer is the person praying it. That is not a burden laid on the inadequate — the next two verses deal with exactly that fear — but it is a pattern, and it runs right through to the end of the book: "As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you" (John 20:21).

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to God, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh? It is the most honest sentence Moses has ever spoken, and it is right. He is nobody. He is a fugitive with a price on his head in the country he is being sent to, a man whose last attempt at rescuing Israel produced one dead Egyptian, a hidden corpse, and a forty-year exile. If anyone in Scripture has earned the right to ask that question, it is this man.

And the answer God gives — this is the hinge of the entire chapter — is to ignore the question.

Read verse 12 again and see what is not in it. There is no reassurance about Moses. God does not tell him he has leadership gifts he has not noticed, or that eighty is the new fifty, or that his years at Pharaoh's court were providential training. Every one of those things could have been said, and one or two of them are even true. God says none of them. Moses asks "Who am I?" and God answers a completely different question: I will be with you. Who you are is not the issue. Who is going with you is the issue.

Get this right, because it is where a great deal of well-meant encouragement goes wrong. When someone says they are not up to what has been asked of them, the instinct is to talk them up — to argue them out of their low view of themselves. God does not do that here, and the reason is that Moses' low view of himself is accurate. He really cannot do this. Forty years earlier he thought he could, and he was wrong then in a way that cost a man his life. His self-assessment has finally caught up with reality, and God does not overturn it. He simply declines to let it be decisive.

Which is oddly freeing. If the qualification for the errand were Moses, then Moses' opinion of Moses would matter enormously. Since the qualification is God's presence, it does not matter at all. The question is never whether the instrument is adequate to the work. It is whose hand is on it.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things are given here, and the first one is a word Moses will not fully understand until two verses later. God says ehyeh immak — "I will be with you." Fix that verb in mind: ehyeh, "I will be." Because when Moses asks for God's name in verse 13, the answer will come back ehyeh asher ehyeh, built out of the very same word. The name has already been given, quietly, as a promise, before it is ever given as a name. What God calls himself and what God pledges to Moses are the same syllables. His identity is his commitment to be there.

The second thing is stranger, and readers usually slide past it. Moses is offered a sign — and the sign is set after the mission: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain. That is a guarantee that can only be checked at the far end. It proves nothing today. Moses is being asked to walk into Pharaoh's throne room on the strength of a confirmation he will not receive until the throne room is a long way behind him.

Measure that against how we would prefer these things to run. We want the evidence first and the obedience afterwards — show me it will work and I will go. God reverses the order. He gives a promise now and the proof later, and the interval between them is called faith. Notice too what the sign actually is: not a miracle to reassure Moses about his own safety, but a scene of the whole nation worshipping on this rock. The sign that Moses was truly sent is Israel at the foot of Sinai with God in the fire again.

And the promise itself has never been withdrawn. It is what was said to Joshua at the river, to Jeremiah at his commissioning, to a frightened church at the end of Matthew by a voice that had every right to use these words: "Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age" (Matt. 28:20). The same assurance, from the same person, on the same terms. It was enough for a shepherd facing an empire, and the arithmetic has not changed since.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13: Moses asks the question a people surrounded by Egypt's named gods would certainly ask — What is his name?

Verse 14: I AM WHO I AM — ehyeh asher ehyeh — and the shorter form to carry to Israel: I AM has sent me to you.

Verse 15: The name in the form Israel will use, YHWH, tied at once to three men with biographies, and given as something to be spoken: This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.

Verses 16-17: Moses is given his words for the elders — I have observed you and what has been done to you in Egypt — and the promise of the land is repeated in the same terms as verse 8.

Verses 18-20: The elders will listen; Pharaoh will not. The request is modest — a three days' journey into the wilderness — and God says in advance that even this will be refused: I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand. The plagues are announced before one has fallen.

Verses 21-22: Israel will not leave empty. I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, and they will go out carrying silver, gold and clothing: So you shall plunder the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.theology:
Aseity, in Plain Words

Everything that exists has its explanation somewhere else — you because of your parents, they because of theirs, the sun because of the hydrogen in it. Every single thing that can be named is a borrowed existence, held up by something underneath it. Follow that chain far enough and you arrive at the one being whose existence is explained by nothing outside himself, because there is nothing outside himself. He has no cause and no beginning. He is not the largest item in the universe; he is the reason there is a universe for anything to be large in.

The grammar of ehyeh asher ehyeh will honestly carry more than one rendering — "I am who I am," "I will be who I will be," "I will be what I will be" — and Hebrew tenses do not map neatly onto English. But the renderings point one way: a God defined by nothing outside himself, and available to be nothing other than what he is.

The Name Is a Promise Before It Is a Definition

In verse 12 God had already said ehyeh immak, "I will be with you" — the same verb. The name has been given quietly as a pledge before it is ever given as a name. Which means this is not metaphysics handed to a man about to walk into Egypt; it is the hardest possible guarantee. A God who depends on nothing cannot be starved out by Pharaoh, worn down by four centuries, or bargained with by anybody. And it is refused as a lever in the same breath as it is given as a comfort: he will be who he will be, and no ritual will make him otherwise.

The Name Made Flesh

A man stood in the temple courts and said before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), and the men listening reached for stones, because they understood the grammar perfectly. He had not claimed to be old. He had taken the name out of the bush and put it on himself. The voice that spoke from the fire on Horeb and the voice that wept outside a tomb in Bethany belong to one person — and the I AM who could not be consumed walked to a hill outside Jerusalem and let himself be.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Wherever an English Bible prints LORD in small capitals, the Hebrew underneath is not the word "lord" at all but this name, the four consonants YHWH — so revered that Jewish readers eventually stopped pronouncing it and said Adonai instead. Once seen, it is visible everywhere, standing thousands of times in the Old Testament behind a typographical convention almost no reader has had explained.

Now: Two questions in this section stop honest readers, and both deserve a straight answer rather than a quick pass.

The first is the three days' journey. God's declared intention is to bring Israel out permanently, so is Moses told to put a misleading proposal to Pharaoh? What he carries is an opening demand rather than a full statement of terms, and nothing false is said — Israel does want to sacrifice, and in due course they will do exactly that at this very mountain, which is the sign of verse 12. The modest size of the request is its whole design: Pharaoh is not asked to surrender his workforce, only to grant three days, and when he refuses even that his refusal is exposed for what it is. It remains fair to feel the discomfort; Scripture does not tidy Pharaoh's downfall into something comfortable.

The second is the plunder. The verb is sha'al, to ask — the old rendering "borrow" created centuries of a problem the text does not have. Israel asks and the Egyptians give, because of something God does to the givers, not something Israel does to them. And what changes hands is four hundred years of unpaid wages: when Israel later writes its own law on freeing a slave it will require precisely this — you shall not let him go empty-handed; you shall furnish him liberally (Deut. 15:13-14). It is also a promise kept to the letter, made to a childless old man in a tent centuries earlier (Gen. 15:14).

One sober note, because the storyteller is playing a long game: this same Egyptian gold is what gets melted into the calf in chapter 32. The gift was never the problem. What the gold became depended entirely on what the heart holding it wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to God, "If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses' second objection sounds like a technicality and is not. What is his name? — why would that be the question Israel asks?

Because these people have spent four centuries in the most religious country on earth. Egypt had gods for the river, the sun, the sky, childbirth, the harvest, the dead — every one of them named, imaged, and housed in stone. In that world a name was not a label; it was a god's character and jurisdiction and the handle by which he could be approached. To arrive in the brickyards announcing that "the God of your fathers" has sent you is, to that audience, an incomplete sentence. Which God? Whose? With what power, against a Pharaoh who is himself worshipped as divine?

And there is a second thing in the question, closer to home. A name in the ancient world was also a lever. Knowing a god's name was thought to give you some purchase on him — the right syllable in the right ritual, and the god was obliged. Moses is asking for credentials. He may also, without meaning to, be asking for a handle.

What he gets in the next verse answers the first request magnificently and refuses the second absolutely.

verseByVerse.quote: God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I AM WHO I AM. In Hebrew, ehyeh asher ehyeh — three words, and the most consequential self-disclosure in the Old Testament. The verb is the ordinary verb "to be," and the grammar will carry more than one rendering honestly: "I am who I am," "I will be who I will be," "I will be what I will be." Translators have argued about it for centuries and the argument is not manufactured; Hebrew tenses do not map neatly onto English ones. But the several renderings point the same direction. This is a God defined by nothing outside himself, and available to be nothing other than what he is.

Take the plainest sense first. Everything else that exists has an explanation somewhere else. You exist because of your parents; they existed because of theirs; the sun burns because of the hydrogen in it; the hydrogen is there because of something before that. Every single thing you can name, including yourself, is a borrowed existence — handed on, caused, held up by something underneath it. Trace any of it far enough back and you arrive at the one being whose existence is not explained by anything else, because there is nothing else. He does not have a cause. He does not have a beginning. He is not the biggest thing in the universe; he is the reason there is a universe to be big in. That is what the burning bush was saying in flame before God said it in words: a fire that needs no fuel.

Here is a test that will settle it faster than an argument. Name one thing you have that you did not receive — one capacity, one breath, one hour of the life you are living. There is nothing on the list. Everything about you is on loan, including the next heartbeat. Now ask what God received, and from whom. The list is empty, and the emptiness is the doctrine.

But it must not be left as metaphysics, because that is not what it is doing here. This name is given to a man about to walk into Egypt, on behalf of slaves, and its force in context is not "I am the ground of being" but "I will be there." A God who depends on nothing is a God whom nothing can deflect, exhaust, outlast or bargain with. Pharaoh cannot starve him out. Four hundred years cannot wear him down. The name is not cold; it is the hardest possible guarantee that the promise of verse 12 will hold.

And it is refused as a lever even while it is given as a comfort. Moses asked for a name and received a sentence that cannot be used to manipulate: God will be who he will be, and no ritual will make him otherwise.

Fifteen hundred years later a man stood in the temple courts and said, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58) — and the men listening picked up stones, because they understood the grammar perfectly. He had not claimed to be old. He had taken the name out of the bush and put it on himself. The voice that spoke from the fire on Horeb and the voice that wept outside a tomb in Bethany belong to one person; and the I AM who could not be consumed walked to a hill outside Jerusalem and let himself be.

verseByVerse.quote: God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the name is given in the form Israel will actually use. The Hebrew is four consonants, YHWH, formed from that same verb "to be" — the name so revered that Jewish readers eventually stopped pronouncing it altogether, saying Adonai, "Lord," whenever they reached it. That reverence is the reason for a convention every English Bible follows and almost no reader has had explained: wherever the printed page reads LORD in small capitals, the Hebrew underneath is not the word "lord" at all. It is this name. Once seen, it is visible everywhere — the personal name of God, standing in the text thousands of times, hiding in plain sight behind a typographical convention.

And look what he ties it to. Having just declared himself the self-existent one, God attaches the name immediately to three men with biographies: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Abraham, who lied about his wife twice. Isaac, who repeated the trick. Jacob, who cheated his brother and wrestled God to a draw and limped away. Eternal, underived being — and it insists on being introduced by the names of three flawed men it made promises to.

Then: this is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations. The word behind "remembered" is zeker, which carries the sense of a name being invoked, spoken aloud, called upon. This is the point at which the doctrine becomes usable. God has not handed Moses a definition to be filed. He has given his people something to say when they have nothing else — a name to call in the dark, guaranteed to be answered, and guaranteed for every generation that comes after, including the ones sitting in brickyards who have never heard it yet.

The God who needs nothing from anyone gives his personal name to slaves and tells them to use it. Nothing obliged him to be known. He could have remained the unnamed power behind the world and been no less God for it. Instead he spells himself out on a hillside so that a nation of brickmakers can address him by name — and then, when the generations had run their course, he gave that name a face and let it be nailed up under a placard so that anyone at all could call on the name of the Lord and be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: Go and gather the elders of Israel together and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying, "I have observed you and what has been done to you in Egypt, and I promise that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is not sent out to improvise. God writes the speech: go to the elders, and here is what you will say. And the message opens where the chapter opened, with the fathers — Abraham, Isaac, Jacob — because these people need to hear that what is about to happen is not a new departure but an old promise coming due.

The verb in I have observed you is paqad, a word with more muscle than English "observe" suggests. It means to attend to, to visit with intent, to come and take an interest that changes things. It is used of a shepherd counting his flock and of a king reviewing his troops. It is not the language of a spectator. And it is the very word Joseph used on his deathbed, generations back: "God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land" (Gen. 50:24). Joseph's bones are still in Egypt waiting on that sentence. Israel has been sitting on a promise with a specific verb in it, and God now sends Moses to tell them the verb has been activated.

Then the land again, with the same six nations listed and the same milk and honey. God has now said it twice in eleven verses. He is not being repetitive for the sake of it; he is doing what he consistently does with a people who will find the promise hard to believe — saying it again, in the same words, so that it can be quoted back to him later when the wilderness gets long. And they will need to. Within two chapters these same elders will have their hopes flattened when Pharaoh doubles the workload, and the only thing standing between them and despair will be a sentence God took care to say twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; and now, please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.' But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand. So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things in this passage stop honest readers, and both deserve a straight answer rather than a quick pass.

The first is the request itself: let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God. God's declared intention is to bring Israel out of Egypt permanently. So is Moses being told to put a misleading proposal to Pharaoh? The question is fair and should not be waved away.

Several things bear on it. What Moses is told to deliver is an opening demand, not a full statement of intent — and there is a difference between withholding your final terms from a hostile power and telling him a lie. Nothing false is said: Israel does want to sacrifice, and in due course they will go into that wilderness and do exactly that at this very mountain, which is precisely the sign promised in verse 12. More to the point, the modest size of the request is the whole design of it. Pharaoh is not being asked to release his workforce; he is being asked for three days. When he refuses even that, his refusal is exposed for what it is. God says so in advance in verse 19 — I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go — so the small request functions as a test that reveals a heart rather than a trick that steals a nation. It is still fair to feel the discomfort of it; Scripture does not tidy Pharaoh's downfall into something comfortable.

The second is verse 19 itself, and it is the larger of the two. Before a single plague has fallen, before Moses has walked out of Midian, God states the outcome: Pharaoh will refuse, and will only yield to a mighty hand, and then I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go. The entire contest is described in advance, including its ending. Nothing that happens in chapters 5 to 14 will surprise God, and nothing in them is a recovery from a setback. When Pharaoh hardens, when the people's workload doubles, when Moses complains that things have got worse rather than better (5:22-23) — all of it is inside a plan already spoken aloud on this hillside.

Which changes how the reader should carry the next eleven chapters. The delays are not God losing ground. He is not improvising against an opponent who keeps surprising him. The most powerful man on earth is about to spend ten rounds discovering that he is a character in someone else's account, and the ending was told to a shepherd, in the desert, before the story started.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; and when you go, you shall not go empty, but each woman shall ask of her neighbor, and any woman who lives in her house, for silver and gold jewelry, and for clothing. You shall put them on your sons and on your daughters. So you shall plunder the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a promise that has troubled readers for a long time: Israel will walk out of Egypt carrying Egyptian silver, Egyptian gold and Egyptian clothing. So you shall plunder the Egyptians. Is God arranging a robbery?

Start with the verb, because an old translation caused most of the trouble. The Hebrew is sha'al, to ask or request — the King James "borrow" is misleading, and it created centuries of a problem the text does not have. Israel asks; the Egyptians hand it over. And they hand it over because of something God says he will do to them, not something Israel will do to them: I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. The transfer happens because God turns the hearts of the givers.

Then consider what is actually being transferred. These are people who have built cities for generations and been paid in nothing but survival. When Israel later writes its own law about setting a slave free, it will require precisely this: "you shall not let him go empty-handed; you shall furnish him liberally" (Deut. 15:13-14). What Egypt gives at the exodus is what God will one day require of every Israelite master — a leaving gift for the person whose unpaid labour built your prosperity. This is not theft. It is four hundred years of back wages, paid late, by a nation that could afford it.

And it is a promise being kept to the letter. God told Abraham this, in these terms, before Israel existed: "they shall come out with great possessions" (Gen. 15:14). The gold in those saddlebags is a receipt on a promise made four centuries earlier to a childless old man in a tent.

One sober note, because the storyteller is playing a long game. Hold on to where this gold came from, because it is going to matter. In chapter 32, while Moses is up the mountain receiving the law, this same Egyptian gold will be melted down into a calf, and Israel will bow to it and say, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (32:4). The very treasure God gave them as evidence that he keeps his promises becomes the material of their worst betrayal of him. The gift was not the problem. It never is. What the gold became depended entirely on what the heart holding it wanted, and this is the last quiet word of a chapter that has spent twenty-two verses establishing who God is: he can be trusted with a nation's rescue, and the danger was never going to come from his side.

3.theology:
The holiness of God. The fire, the holy ground, the hidden face — all proclaim that God is set apart, unapproachable except on his own terms.

The aseity and eternity of God. "I AM WHO I AM" reveals a God who simply is — self-existent, unchanging, the source of all being.

The compassion of God. The transcendent I AM is also the God who has seen, heard, and come down. Holiness and mercy meet in the bush as they will meet at the cross.
3.examples:
Then: A discarded fugitive met the eternal God in a desert and was commissioned to confront an empire — armed with nothing but a name and a promise: "I will be with you."

Now: The same I AM meets us in Christ. When we feel inadequate to our calling — "Who am I?" — the answer is not our resume but his presence. The God who is enough has promised to be with us.

4.title: The Sufficiency of God in Our Weakness
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses answered, "But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'"<sup>2</sup>The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" He said, "A staff."<sup>3</sup>And he said, "Throw it on the ground." So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it.<sup>4</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Put out your hand and catch it by the tail"—so he put out his hand and caught it, and it became a staff in his hand—<sup>5</sup>"that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."<sup>6</sup>Again, the LORD said to him, "Put your hand inside your cloak." And he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous like snow.<sup>7</sup>Then God said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." So he put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, it was restored like the rest of his flesh.<sup>8</sup>"If they will not believe you," God said, "or listen to the first sign, they may believe the latter sign.<sup>9</sup>If they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, you shall take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water that you shall take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground."<sup>10</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue."<sup>11</sup>Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?<sup>12</sup>Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak."<sup>13</sup>But he said, "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else."<sup>14</sup>Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Behold, he is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.<sup>15</sup>You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you both what to do.<sup>16</sup>He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him.<sup>17</sup>And take in your hand this staff, with which you shall do the signs."<sup>18</sup>Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, "Please let me go back to my brothers in Egypt to see whether they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace."<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead."<sup>20</sup>So Moses took his wife and his sons and had them ride on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the miracles that I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go.<sup>22</sup>Then you shall say to Pharaoh, 'Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son,<sup>23</sup>and I say to you, "Let my son go that he may serve me." If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'"<sup>24</sup>At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.<sup>25</sup>Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!"<sup>26</sup>So he let him alone. It was then that she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.<sup>27</sup>The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him.<sup>28</sup>And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do.<sup>29</sup>Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the people of Israel.<sup>30</sup>Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses and did the signs in the sight of the people.<sup>31</sup>And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
4.overview:
Moses meets the call of God with a string of excuses: they won't believe me; I'm not eloquent; please send someone else. To each objection God answers not by flattering Moses but by revealing more of himself — his power over signs, his lordship over the human mouth, his promise to be present. The lesson is bracing: God's calling rests on God's sufficiency, not ours. As Begg often says, God does not call the equipped; he equips the called.

God gives Moses three signs — the staff that becomes a serpent, the leprous hand, the water turned to blood — visible proofs that the I AM has sent him. When Moses still pleads inadequacy, God's anger is kindled, yet even his displeasure bends toward grace: he gives Aaron as a mouthpiece. God will accomplish his purpose, with or without our willing cooperation, but he delights to use surrendered servants.

The chapter introduces a staggering phrase: "Israel is my firstborn son." The exodus is not merely a slave rebellion; it is a Father reclaiming his child. And the demand — "let my son go that he may serve me" — sets the true purpose of redemption: not merely freedom from, but freedom for the worship of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — Three Signs for a Doubting Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: Moses' third objection — But behold, they will not believe me — is a prediction God has already contradicted. God answers with a question: What is that in your hand? A shepherd's staff.

Verses 3-5: Thrown down it becomes a serpent and Moses runs; he is told to take it by the tail, the dangerous end. The purpose is stated: that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers... has appeared to you.

Verses 6-7: The second sign is worked on Moses' own body — a hand leprous like snow, then restored.

Verses 8-9: And a third held in reserve: water from the Nile poured on dry ground will become blood.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Begins With What Is Already in the Hand

The staff is the least impressive object in the story and the only thing Moses owns — a stick worn smooth by forty years of pushing sheep about. God does not send him back for equipment or ask him to wait until he is better supplied. By verse 20 the same stick is called the staff of God. Nothing was added to the wood; what changed was whose hand it was answering to.

The Serpent Taken by the Tail

Of every creature available, God chose the one Egypt wore on its crown — the uraeus, the reared cobra that was the emblem of Pharaoh's sovereignty. The power Egypt displays on its forehead is a thing the God of the Hebrews can pick up by the tail. And behind that stands the older promise about the woman's offspring bruising the serpent's head (Gen. 3:15), which comes to its end at a cross where Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Col. 2:15).

The Signs Are Previews

A serpent, a disease, a river turned to blood — all three return at full scale when the plagues begin. These are not tricks to impress a crowd; they are the three fronts on which Egypt is about to be dismantled, shown in miniature and in advance: its power, its flesh, and its river.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses raised an objection God had already answered, and God's response was not a rebuke but a third sign in case the first two were not enough. Heaven is not stingy with a man who is struggling to believe; the signs escalate in proportion to the doubt.

Now: Notice that the second sign is worked on Moses in private, on a hillside, before any audience exists. Before he demonstrates to anyone that God has power over disease, he has felt it in his own arm — the horror of looking down at a hand that is no longer his hand, and then the relief. God tends to teach his servants on their own bodies before he sends them out to speak about it.

And there is a direction in that sign worth holding. The hand goes in clean and comes out diseased; goes in diseased and comes out clean. When a leper knelt in front of Jesus and said If you will, you can make me clean, the astonishing thing was what happened next: he stretched out his hand and touched him (Mark 1:41). Under the law that touch should have carried uncleanness up the arm. It ran the other way. He is the only man who ever touched defilement and left it clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses answered, "But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'" The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" He said, "A staff."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses has run out of theological questions and reaches for a practical one: But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, "The LORD did not appear to you." It sounds reasonable. It is also, strictly, a slander — God has said nothing of the kind. What God actually said was they will listen to your voice (3:18), and at the end of this chapter they do. Moses is arguing against a promise by predicting a failure.

And God does not scold him for it. He asks a question instead, and it is one of the gentlest in Scripture: What is that in your hand?

Consider what was actually in it. A shepherd's staff — a stick cut from a tree somewhere in Midian, worn smooth at the grip by forty years of holding, used for pushing sheep off ledges and leaning on at the end of a long day. It is the least impressive object in the story. It is also the only thing Moses owns. God does not ask him to fetch something holy, or to go back for equipment, or to wait until he is better supplied. He asks what is already in the hand.

By verse 20 that stick has a new name. It is called the staff of God, and it will divide a sea, strike a rock until water runs out of it, and be lifted over a battlefield while a nation watches. Nothing was added to the wood. What changed was whose hand it was answering to.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Throw it on the ground." So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it. But the LORD said to Moses, "Put out your hand and catch it by the tail"—so he put out his hand and caught it, and it became a staff in his hand— "that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Throw it on the ground. He does, and it becomes a serpent, and Moses — a man who has handled livestock in snake country for four decades and knows exactly what he is looking at — runs.

Then the instruction that must have taken more nerve than anything else in the chapter: Put out your hand and catch it by the tail. Anyone who has ever handled a snake knows you take it behind the head, because the tail end is the end that can still reach you. God deliberately tells Moses to pick it up the wrong way round, the dangerous way, the way that only works if the God who turned the staff into a snake is also holding the snake.

And of all the creatures God could have chosen, he chose this one. The cobra reared on Pharaoh's crown was the uraeus, the royal serpent, the emblem of Egypt's sovereignty and the goddess said to spit fire at the king's enemies. Moses is being shown, in his own hand, what the whole contest is going to be: the power Egypt wears on its forehead is a thing the God of the Hebrews can pick up by the tail.

Behind that lies an older promise still. Ever since a garden and a sentence about the woman's offspring bruising the serpent's head (Gen. 3:15), Scripture has been moving toward a moment when the serpent is not negotiated with but crushed. Moses grasping a snake by the tail on a hillside in Midian is a small rehearsal. The full performance is a cross, where the one who had no staff but a borrowed beam disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col. 2:15). The head of the serpent has already been stepped on. Everything since has been the long business of the last coils going still.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the LORD said to him, "Put your hand inside your cloak." And he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous like snow. Then God said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." So he put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, it was restored like the rest of his flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second sign is done not on a stick but on Moses' own body. Put your hand inside your cloak — and it comes out leprous like snow. Whatever the precise condition, the word covers the skin diseases that in Israel meant exclusion: out of the camp, out of the worship, out of every human touch, calling Unclean at anyone who came near.

Put it back, and it comes out whole.

Notice that God does not ask Moses to perform this one on someone else first. The sign is worked on the man himself, in private, on a hillside, before any audience exists. Before Moses demonstrates to anybody that God has power over disease, he has felt it in his own arm — the horror of looking down at a hand that is not his hand any more, and then the relief. God tends to teach his servants on their own bodies before he sends them to speak about it.

And there is a direction to this sign worth sitting with. The hand goes in clean and comes out diseased; goes in diseased and comes out clean. Fifteen centuries later a leper knelt in front of Jesus and said, If you will, you can make me clean — and the astonishing thing, the thing no rabbi would have done, is what happened next: Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him (Mark 1:41). Under the law that touch should have run one way, and uncleanness should have travelled up the arm. It ran the other way. He is the only man who ever touched defilement and left it clean, and he did it at last on a scale that took him outside the camp himself, where the unclean are put, so that the unclean could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: "If they will not believe you," God said, "or listen to the first sign, they may believe the latter sign. If they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, you shall take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water that you shall take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a third sign, held in reserve: if they will not believe even these two signs, take water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and it will become blood.

Two things are worth seeing here, and the first is simply the patience. Moses has raised an objection God never conceded, and God's response is not a rebuke but a third sign in case the first two are not enough. Heaven is not stingy with a man who is struggling to believe. The signs escalate precisely in proportion to the doubt.

The second is where the water comes from. Not from a well or a spring — from the Nile, named. That river was Egypt's economy, its calendar and its god, worshipped as Hapi, the reason anything grew in a country with no rain. Pharaoh had thrown Hebrew infants into it (1:22). And the sign says: this water becomes blood in the hand of the God of the Hebrews.

All three signs are previews. A serpent, a disease, a river turned to blood — and every one of them will return at full scale when the plagues begin. Moses is not being given magic tricks to impress a crowd. He is being shown, in miniature and in advance, the three fronts on which Egypt is about to be dismantled: its power, its flesh, and its river.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 10: Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent... but I am slow of speech and of tongue. Probably a plain description rather than an excuse — Stephen says Moses had once been mighty in his words (Acts 7:22), and Midian took that too.

Verses 11-12: Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? — and then the commission: I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.

Verses 13-14: The mask comes off — Oh, my Lord, please send someone else — and for the only time in the chapter the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses. The anger produces a brother: Behold, he is coming out to meet you.

Verses 15-17: Aaron will be Moses' mouth and Moses will be as God to him; and Moses is to take the staff.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hardest Sentence, Left Hard

God does not say that muteness and blindness happen in a world he permits at arm's length; he puts himself in the sentence. It should not be softened, because softening it empties the comfort out of it. The alternative to verse 11 is not a kinder God but an absent or overruled one, and that is a colder universe than the one Moses is standing in. Scripture never offers the comfort of a God who was not there. When Jesus was asked whose sin had caused a man to be born blind he refused both offered answers and gave a third — that the works of God might be displayed in him (John 9:3).

Grace That Left Before It Was Asked For

Aaron is already on the road when God says so. He set out before Moses spoke the words that made God angry. The provision for the refusal was travelling toward Moses while the refusal was still in his mouth — God had made arrangements for a failure that had not yet happened, in a man he had every right to abandon.

The Chain of Mediation, and Its End

He shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him is the prophetic office in one sentence: a word originates with God, is given to a man, and is carried by someone who adds nothing of his own. Every link in that chain existed because of a gap. Long ago... God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb. 1:1-2). Christ does not receive the word and pass it on; he is the Word. Moses needed Aaron. The Son needs no one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every earlier objection had a shape and God answered each one completely. Please send someone else has no argument in it at all — it is a refusal with a courtesy attached, and it reveals that the other four were packaging. Moses never had an adequacy problem. He had an unwillingness problem.

Now: Verse 11 will be read by people living inside it — someone who cannot hear, or a parent who has sat in a consulting room and been handed a word they did not want. To them it is not an abstraction to be balanced against other verses, and it should be allowed to say what it says: a disability is not evidence that God has looked away. He was there, he has not explained himself, and he can be trusted with what he has not explained.

And the verse is not finally about disability at all. It is about who is doing the sending: I will be with your mouth. That promise was handed down the whole line of people who have had to speak for God without feeling able to — the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:12). The one who framed the human mouth out of dust took a mouth of his own and used it to call Lazarus out of a tomb, to still a sea, to say Father, forgive them, and at the last It is finished.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue.

Take it at face value, because it probably is. Whatever the precise difficulty — a stammer, a lost fluency in Egyptian after forty years of speaking Midianite among sheep, a genuine speech impediment — Moses is not inventing a disability to get out of an errand. He is describing what happens when he opens his mouth in front of people.

And there is a poignancy in it that Stephen's sermon supplies. Moses was mighty in his words and deeds (Acts 7:22) — in Egypt, at forty, with a palace education and every door open. That man could speak. Forty years in Midian took the fluency along with everything else. The wilderness did not merely humble Moses; it appears to have cost him the one gift a leader most obviously needs.

Which sets up the honest shape of this objection. It is not that Moses has a poor opinion of himself. It is that he is right, and he is being asked to go and speak anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?

This is one of the hardest sentences in the book, and it should not be softened, because softening it would empty the comfort out of it. God does not say that muteness and blindness happen in a world he permits at arm's length. He puts himself in the sentence. He claims the making of the mouth that works and the mouth that does not.

It needs saying carefully, because this verse will be read by people who are living inside it — someone who cannot hear, or a parent who has sat in a consulting room and been given a word they did not want. To such a reader the verse is not an abstraction to be balanced against other verses. So let it say the two things it actually says.

The first is that a disability is not evidence that God has looked away. The alternative to this verse is not a kinder God; it is a God who was absent or overruled when it happened, and that is a colder universe than the one Moses is standing in. Scripture never offers the comfort of a God who was not there. It offers the harder and better comfort of a God who was, and who has not explained himself, and who can be trusted with what he has not explained. When Jesus was asked whose sin had caused a man to be born blind, he refused both offered answers and gave a third: that the works of God might be displayed in him (John 9:3).

The second is what God says next, because the verse is not making a point about disability at all. It is making a point about who is sending Moses: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak. The Maker of the mouth is undertaking to supply its contents. That promise was handed down the whole line of people who have had to speak for God when they did not feel able — do not be anxious how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say (Luke 12:11-12).

The one who framed the human mouth out of dust took a mouth of his own, and used it to call Lazarus out of a tomb, to still a sea, to say Father, forgive them, and at the last to say It is finished. He never once needed an interpreter, and he made the deaf hear and the mute speak wherever he went — not to prove the doctrine of verse 11 but to show what it is finally for.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else." Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Behold, he is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the mask comes off. Oh, my Lord, please send someone else.

There is no argument left in it. Every previous objection had a shape — who am I, what is your name, they will not believe me, I cannot speak — and God had answered every one, comprehensively, one after another. This last one is not a question. It is a refusal with a courtesy attached, and it reveals what was underneath the other four. Moses did not have an adequacy problem. He had an unwillingness problem, and the reasons were the packaging.

So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses — the only time in the chapter, and it should not be hurried past. God had been extraordinarily patient through four objections and a third sign given in case two were not enough. Patience is not indifference. There comes a point at which continued refusal in the face of an answered objection stops being humility and becomes something else, and God names it by being angry about it.

And then look what the anger produces. Not a thunderbolt, not a withdrawal of the call, not a replacement candidate — a brother. Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Behold, he is coming out to meet you.

Read that last clause again and notice the tense. Aaron is already on the road. He set out before Moses said the words that made God angry. The provision for the refusal was travelling toward Moses while the refusal was still in his mouth — which means God had made arrangements for a failure that had not yet happened, in a man he had every right to give up on. That is not God tolerating Moses. That is grace arriving early, as it always does, having left before it was asked for.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you both what to do. He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him. And take in your hand this staff, with which you shall do the signs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The arrangement God sets up is precise, and it establishes something that will run through the rest of the Old Testament. You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth... He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him.

That is the prophetic office in one sentence. A word originates with God, is given to a man, and is carried to the people by someone who adds nothing of his own. The prophet is not a commentator. He is a mouth. Everything from Isaiah to Malachi runs on this arrangement, and every one of those books is a link in a chain that has God at one end and a congregation at the other, with a man in the middle who did not invent the message.

But this is plainly a second-best, and the text does not hide it. Moses was offered God with his mouth and asked for a brother instead, and God gave him what he asked for. There is a cost to it that the book will collect later: Aaron, the man appointed here because he can speak well, is the man who will stand in front of a gold calf and speak well about it (32:22-24). A concession granted to unbelief is still a concession.

And the chain of mediation, once you see it, is what makes the New Testament's opening claim land. Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb. 1:1-2). Every link in that chain existed because of a gap — God here, people there, and a man required in between to carry the words across. In Christ the gap closes. He does not receive the word and pass it on; he is the Word, and when he speaks there is no one standing between the voice and the ear. Moses needed Aaron. The Son needs no one, and he came so that no one would ever need an Aaron again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-31 — Return to Egypt and the Firstborn Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 18-20: Jethro says Go in peace; God adds that all the men who were seeking your life are dead; and Moses sets out with his family and the staff of God in his hand.

Verses 21-23: The outcome is announced in advance — I will harden his heart — together with the claim that changes the temperature of the book: Israel is my firstborn son... Let my son go that he may serve me, and if not, I will kill your firstborn son.

Verses 24-26: At a lodging place the LORD met him and sought to put him to death, until Zipporah circumcises their son and touches Moses with the blood. So he let him alone.

Verses 27-28: Aaron meets Moses at the mountain of God and kisses him, and Moses tells him everything.

Verses 29-31: The elders are gathered, the signs are done, and the people believed; hearing that the LORD had visited them, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
verseByVerse.theology:
Hardening, Said Two Ways

Scripture states this from both sides and declines to resolve it for us: Pharaoh hardens his own heart, repeatedly and deliberately, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart, and both stand in the same narrative without embarrassment. Paul takes up this very case — he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills (Rom. 9:18) — and pointedly does not excuse Pharaoh on the strength of it. What can be said confidently is that God is not bending a heart that wanted to obey; he is confirming a man in the direction he has already chosen. Anyone who claims to have this fully mapped has stopped reading the text and started tidying it.

A Son for a Son

Up to now Israel has been a family, a people, a labour force. Israel is my firstborn son is a claim of paternity, and it makes the demand something other than a labour negotiation: this is a Father coming for his child. Egypt has been drowning Hebrew boys for a generation, and the account will be settled in the same currency.

Hosea looked back at this exodus and wrote out of Egypt I called my son, and Matthew laid the sentence over a refugee child (Matt. 2:15). Israel is the firstborn son by adoption; there is a firstborn Son by nature. And at the true exodus the pattern did not repeat, it inverted: here God said let my son go, Pharaoh refused, and Egypt's firstborn died. There, no one refused and no substitute was found, and he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The three verses at the lodging place are among the strangest in Scripture, and much in them is genuinely obscure — the Hebrew pronouns are ambiguous. But the centre is not obscure, because Zipporah's action identifies the problem exactly: the covenant sign had been neglected. Moses is walking to Egypt to say let my son go while his own son does not carry the mark that says he belongs to God. Judgement begins at the household of God, and it begins at this one first.

Now: Notice the shape of that rescue, because it is the shape of everything coming. A household under sentence of death; blood applied; the LORD let him alone. That is Passover, eight chapters early and in miniature — the destroyer at the door, the blood on the household, the passing over. A Midianite woman with a piece of flint performs the first Passover in Exodus without knowing that is what it is.

And the chapter ends where the whole book is heading. Nothing has yet been delivered. Not a plague has fallen, no chain has been struck off; tomorrow they will still make bricks, and within a chapter the workload will double and they will curse Moses for it. All they have is a report that God has seen — and on the strength of that alone they go down on their faces. Egypt was never the point. He was.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, "Please let me go back to my brothers in Egypt to see whether they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace." And the LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead." So Moses took his wife and his sons and had them ride on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses goes back to Jethro and asks leave to return to Egypt — and does not mention the burning bush. He says only that he wants to see whether his brothers are still alive. Whatever the reason for the reticence, Jethro's answer is four words that anyone who has ever been sent anywhere would want to hear: Go in peace.

Then the LORD adds a mercy Moses had not asked for: Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead. The manhunt that drove him out at forty has outlived its hunters. Moses has spent four decades as a wanted man, and somewhere in those years the warrant quietly expired and nobody sent word.

That sentence has a long echo. Fifteen centuries later an angel spoke to a carpenter in Egypt about another child whose life had been sought by another king: Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead (Matt. 2:20). Matthew is not being accidental. He has already told us out of Egypt I called my son (Matt. 2:15), and he is deliberately laying the infant Christ over the outline of Moses — the decree against the baby boys, the child preserved, the exile, the return, the same words about dead pursuers. Moses is the sketch. The Gospel is the painting.

So Moses sets his wife and sons on a donkey and turns back toward the country he fled, and the narrator adds one detail: And Moses took the staff of God in his hand. It is the same stick he was leaning on in verse 2. It has a different name now.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the miracles that I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go. Then you shall say to Pharaoh, 'Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son, and I say to you, "Let my son go that he may serve me." If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Moses reaches Egypt he is told how it will go, and the telling contains the hardest theological sentence in the chapter: but I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go.

The honest thing is to say that Scripture puts this two ways and does not resolve them for us. Across the plague narratives Pharaoh hardens his own heart, repeatedly and deliberately, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart, and both statements stand in the same account without embarrassment. Paul takes up this exact case and does not soften it either — he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills (Rom. 9:18) — and then, importantly, he does not excuse Pharaoh on the strength of it. What can be said with confidence is this: God is not reaching into a heart that wanted to obey and bending it toward evil. He is confirming a man in the direction he has already chosen, and he remains sovereign over the outcome. Anyone who claims to have this fully mapped has stopped reading the text and started tidying it.

Then comes something the Old Testament has not said before, and it changes the whole temperature of the book: Israel is my firstborn son.

Up to this point Israel has been a family, a people, a labour force. Now God calls them a child, and not just any child — the firstborn, the heir, the one with the birthright. That is not a description of what Israel is like. It is a claim of paternity. And the demand that follows is therefore not a labour negotiation: Let my son go that he may serve me. This is a Father coming for his child.

And the warning attached is exact: if you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son. A son for a son. Egypt has been drowning Hebrew boys for a generation and the account is going to be settled in the same currency.

Hold both halves of that together, because the New Testament will pick them up as one. Hosea looked back at this exodus and wrote out of Egypt I called my son, and Matthew took the sentence and put it over a refugee child in Egypt (Matt. 2:15). Israel is the firstborn son by adoption; there is a firstborn Son by nature. And when the true exodus came, the pattern did not repeat — it inverted. At the first exodus God said let my son go, Pharaoh refused, and Egypt's firstborn died. At the last, no one refused and no substitute was found, and the Father did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32). The firstborn who died so that the enslaved could go free was his own.

verseByVerse.quote: At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!" So he let him alone. It was then that she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verses, and they are among the strangest in Scripture. At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death. The man God has just spent two chapters commissioning is nearly killed by God on the journey out.

It is right to admit at once that much here is obscure — the pronouns are ambiguous in Hebrew, and honest commentators differ over whether it is Moses or the son who is in danger. But the centre of it is not obscure at all, because Zipporah's action identifies the problem exactly. She takes a flint, circumcises her son, and touches Moses with the foreskin. The issue is the covenant sign, and it had been neglected.

Set that against the errand. Moses is walking to Egypt to say Israel is my firstborn son; let my son go — and his own son does not carry the mark that says he belongs to the God who gave it. God had told Abraham that an uncircumcised male shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant (Gen. 17:14). The deliverer cannot demand that Pharaoh honour God's claim on his children while ignoring God's claim on his own. Judgement begins at the household of God, and it begins at this one first.

And notice the shape of the rescue, because it is the shape of everything that is coming. A household is under sentence of death. Blood is applied. The LORD let him alone. That is Passover, three chapters early and in miniature — the destroyer at the door, the blood on the household, the passing over. The book will do this again at full scale with a lamb and a doorpost, and the whole Bible will do it once more with a cross. Zipporah, a Midianite woman with a piece of flint in her hand, performs the first Passover in Exodus without knowing that is what it is.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him. And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two brothers who have not seen each other for forty years meet in a desert, and the place is named: the mountain of God. It is Horeb. The bush burned on that hillside a few verses ago, and the law will be given on it a few chapters from now, and Moses will hide in a cleft of its rock and see the back of the glory of God. Everything important in this part of the book keeps happening on the same hill.
