God had told Moses that Aaron was already coming (v.14), and here he is, and he kissed him. It is a small, warm, entirely human detail in a chapter full of signs and warnings, and it is the only reunion in Exodus. Whatever had passed between them in four decades of separation, whatever Aaron thought of a brother who fled and never came back, the text records a kiss.

Then: And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do. All of them. The first thing the mouth of God's prophet does is listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the people of Israel. Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses and did the signs in the sight of the people. And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They go together, gather the elders, Aaron speaks the words and Moses does the signs — and then the sentence that answers verse 1 of this chapter: And the people believed.

Moses had said they would not. He had said it as though it were the obvious outcome, and God had told him otherwise, and Moses had gone on arguing until God grew angry. He was wrong. The objection that felt most realistic to him, the one built on knowing his own people, was simply mistaken. How often the thing we are most certain will fail turns out to be the very thing God has already promised will not.

And what convinced them is stated precisely: when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction. The verb is paqad, the same word Joseph used on his deathbed four centuries earlier when he told his brothers that God would surely visit them and bring them up out of this land (Gen. 50:24). Joseph's bones are still in Egypt, still waiting on that verb, and a promise the last man who remembered it had been dead for four hundred years turns out to have been keeping time all along.

Then the last clause of the chapter: and they bowed their heads and worshiped.

Nothing has been delivered yet. Not a plague has fallen, not a chain has been struck off; they are still slaves, and tomorrow they will still make bricks, and within one chapter the workload will be doubled and they will curse Moses for it. All they have is a report that God has seen. And on the strength of that alone they go down on their faces. This is what God has been after since the bush, and he said so plainly — let my people go that they may serve me — because the end of the exodus was never a change of address but a people on their knees in front of the God who came down for them. Egypt was never the point. He was.

4.theology:
The sufficiency of God in human weakness. God's call rests on his power, not the servant's gifts. "Who made man's mouth?" silences every excuse.

Divine sovereignty. God claims authority over speech, disability, Pharaoh's heart, and the outcome of history. Nothing lies outside his rule.

Redemption unto worship. "Let my son go that he may serve me." Salvation's goal is not mere liberation but the worship of God.
4.examples:
Then: A reluctant shepherd, full of excuses, was sent to confront a superpower, assured only that the God who made his mouth would go with him.

Now: When God calls us beyond our competence, the question is never "Am I able?" but "Is God able?" Our weakness is the stage for his strength. And we are redeemed not for ourselves but to serve and worship our Redeemer.

5.title: When Obedience Makes Things Worse
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'"<sup>2</sup>But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."<sup>3</sup>Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword."<sup>4</sup>But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens."<sup>5</sup>And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"<sup>6</sup>The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen,<sup>7</sup>"You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves.<sup>8</sup>But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.'<sup>9</sup>Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."<sup>10</sup>So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw.<sup>11</sup>Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'"<sup>12</sup>So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.<sup>13</sup>The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw."<sup>14</sup>And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"<sup>15</sup>Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this?<sup>16</sup>No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."<sup>17</sup>But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'<sup>18</sup>Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks."<sup>19</sup>The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."<sup>20</sup>They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh;<sup>21</sup>and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."<sup>22</sup>Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?<sup>23</sup>For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
5.overview:
The first confrontation goes badly. Moses and Aaron deliver God's word — "Let my people go" — and Pharaoh responds with the defiant question that defines all human rebellion: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" Pharaoh, worshiped as a god in Egypt, will not bow to the God of slaves. So he doubles the burden: the Israelites must now gather their own straw while meeting the same quota of bricks.

The result is that obedience to God makes things, for the moment, far worse. The Israelite foremen turn on Moses; Moses turns on God: "Why did you ever send me?" This is the dark valley every believer eventually walks — when doing the right thing brings not relief but trouble, and faith is stretched to its breaking point. Ferguson reminds us that God's deliverances often deepen before they dawn; the darkest hour is just before the outstretched arm.

The chapter teaches us that God's timetable is not ours, and that the lowest point of our circumstances may be precisely the threshold of his greatest work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: The first Thus says the LORD in Scripture, and the demand is for a festival: Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness. Pharaoh answers with the question the whole book exists to settle — Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?... I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.

Verses 3-5: The demand softens to a request for a three days' journey. Pharaoh does not argue theology; he issues a work order — Get back to your burdens — and complains that Moses would make them rest from their work.

Verses 6-9: Straw is withdrawn and the quota kept. His diagnosis: They are idle; therefore they cry, "Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God." And his instruction: let them not pay regard to lying words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Question the Book Answers

Who is the LORD? is asked dismissively and answered exhaustively. By 9:27 Pharaoh says The LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong; by 12:31 he is out of bed in the night begging Israel to leave; by 14:25 his own army is shouting the LORD fights for them. Every man who has asked that question dismissively has been answered eventually. The only variable is whether the answer arrives as mercy or as ruin.

And the verb in I do not know the LORD is yada — the same word used of the king who did not know Joseph (1:8). Not a gap in his information but a refusal of any claim on him. Ingratitude and unbelief turn out to be one reflex applied to two objects.

Pharaoh Objects to Rest

You make them rest from their work uses shabath. The first sabbath language in Exodus is on a slave-master's lips, as an accusation — his complaint against God is precisely that God gives people rest. The book answers it directly: God will command a sabbath and give the reason, you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt (Deut. 5:15). Slavery has no day off; that is what makes it slavery. Every kingdom that has owned people has said get back to your burdens. One master says my burden is light (Matt. 11:28-30).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Something quietly discouraging happens between verse 1 and verse 3. The first demand was an imperative from God; the second is please, with a reason attached. Moses and Aaron have been in the room for one verse and are already negotiating downward. Anyone who has had to say something difficult on God's behalf will recognise it.

Now: Pharaoh looks at a people asking for a festival and concludes they have too much spare time. It is the oldest sneer available and it has never gone out of use — that devotion is a hobby for those with insufficient responsibilities, and the cure is a heavier schedule. Note too that he does not call the message false because he misunderstood it. He understood it exactly, and named it lying words, because a lie can be legislated against and a word from God cannot.

Why did God permit this, having warned Moses it was coming? Because had Pharaoh released Israel at the first request, they would have walked out grateful to a reasonable king and the story would have been a successful negotiation. Every avenue of human explanation is being closed off in advance, so that when Israel finally walks out there is no one left to thank but God.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'" But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel..." Three words there are about to be spoken ten thousand times in the Old Testament, and this is the first of them. Thus says the LORD. Every prophet from here to Malachi will open his mouth with that formula, and it begins in a throne room in Egypt, in front of a man who is about to say he has never heard of the speaker.

And notice what is actually demanded. Not freedom, not land, not wages, not an end to the beatings — that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness. The word is chag, a festival, the sort of thing Israel will keep three times a year for the rest of its history. God is not asking Pharaoh to be more humane. He is asking him to release a congregation.

Pharaoh's reply is the most naked sentence in the book: Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.

Take the verb. I do not know — yada, the same word used of the king in 1:8 who did not know Joseph. It is not a gap in his information; it is a refusal of relationship and of any claim on him. He did not acknowledge the Hebrew who saved Egypt, and he does not acknowledge the Hebrew's God. Ingratitude and atheism turn out to be the same reflex applied to different objects.

But the question is a real one, and it is the question this entire book exists to answer. Who is the LORD? Watch what happens to the man who asked it. By 9:27 he will say The LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. By 10:16 he is asking for forgiveness. By 12:31 he is out of bed in the middle of the night begging them to leave. And by 14:25 his own army is shouting Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them. Pharaoh asked who the LORD was, and he received a full and unhurried answer over eighteen chapters. Every man who has ever asked that question dismissively has been answered eventually. The only variable is whether the answer arrives as mercy or as ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword." But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens." And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something quietly discouraging happens between verse 1 and verse 3. The first demand was Thus says the LORD... Let my people go. The second is please let us go a three days' journey, with a reason attached and a note of self-protection: lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword. The imperative has become a request. Moses and Aaron have been in the room for one verse and they are already softening.

It is very human, and most people who have ever had to say something difficult on God's behalf will recognise it — the message that was clear in the preparation and gets negotiated downward in the delivery.

Pharaoh does not engage with any of it. Why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens. He does not argue theology; he issues a work order. That is how the world most often deals with the claims of God — not by refuting them but by pointing at the schedule.

Then his last sentence, and it contains a word nobody expects here: you make them rest from their work. The Hebrew is shabath. The first appearance of sabbath language in Exodus is on the lips of a slave-master, using it as an accusation. Pharaoh's complaint against God is precisely that God gives people rest.

Hold that, because the book is going to answer it directly. On a mountain not many chapters from here God will command a sabbath and give as the reason: You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt (Deut. 5:15). Slavery has no day off; that is what makes it slavery. The God who redeems builds rest into the week and writes it into stone. And the one who came to finish the exodus said the thing Pharaoh could never have said — Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). Every kingdom that has ever owned people has said get back to your burdens. He is the only master who says my burden is light.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen, "You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves. But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.' Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh's counter-measure is precise and vicious. They will still make the same number of bricks; they will simply no longer be given the straw. Straw is not optional in Nile-mud brick — the fibres bind the clay and stop it crumbling as it dries. So the quota stays and the raw material is withdrawn, and the labour of gathering it is added on top of a day that was already full.

And listen to his diagnosis: They are idle; therefore they cry, "Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God." He has looked at a people asking for a festival and concluded they have too much spare time. Worship, to Pharaoh, is what happens when the workforce is under-employed. It is the oldest sneer there is, and it has never gone out of use — that devotion is a hobby for people with insufficient responsibilities, and the cure is a heavier schedule.

Then: let them not pay regard to lying words. The word of God, delivered by his appointed messenger with signs to authenticate it, is called a lie by the man it was addressed to. He is not confused. He has understood exactly what was said and has decided to name it falsehood, because a lie can be legislated against and a word from God cannot.

Why did God let this happen, having told Moses in advance that it would? Had Pharaoh released Israel at the first request, they would have walked out of Egypt grateful to a reasonable king, and the story would have been about a successful negotiation. God is going to make that reading impossible. Every avenue of human explanation is being closed off in advance, so that when Israel finally walks out there will be no one left to thank but God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 10-12: The order travels down the chain in the same form Moses used — Thus says Pharaoh — and Israel is scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.

Verses 13-14: The quota is unchanged and impossible, and it is the Israelite foremen, not the Egyptian taskmasters, who were beaten for the shortfall.

Verses 15-16: Those foremen appeal over their heads to Pharaoh himself: Why do you treat your servants like this?... the fault is in your own people.

Verses 17-19: You are idle, you are idle — the sneer repeated to their faces — and the appeal fails. The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble.

Verses 20-21: They come out and find Moses and Aaron waiting: The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh... and have put a sword in their hand to kill us.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Machine Built to Turn a People Against Its Deliverer

The foremen are Hebrews. Egypt appoints men from among the slaves to drive the slaves, holds them responsible for an arithmetic that cannot work, and flogs them when it fails. It is one of the cruellest arrangements oppression has devised and it is still in use: put some of the oppressed in charge of the rest, and the resentment of the many falls on the few instead of on the throne. By verse 21 those beaten men are cursing Moses. Pharaoh does not have to lift a finger.

Appealing to the Wrong Throne

There is nothing dishonourable in the foremen's petition — it is what any sensible person would try, respectfully made and factually unanswerable, and God does not condemn them for it. But the man they are petitioning is the man who wrote the order. The only relief available inside Egypt comes from a king who has already answered Who is the LORD? with I will not. They are asking the disease for a cure.

The Rejected Deliverer

This is the second time Israel has turned on Moses — the first was Who made you a prince and a judge over us? (2:14) — and he will hear it at the sea, over water, over food, and over a report about giants. It is the pattern of the greater Deliverer drawn small: He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). The crowd that spread cloaks on the road on Sunday was calling for his execution by Friday, on much the same charge sheet — he had made things worse, he had provoked Rome, it was better that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Straw is not decorative in Nile-mud brick; the fibres bind the clay and stop it crumbling as it dries. Withdraw it, keep the quota, and add the gathering to a day that was already full — and not even straw, but stubble, the stumps left after harvest, the scrapings. A nation is put on its knees in other people's fields picking up chaff to make the same number of bricks it made yesterday.

Now: Scripture does not hurry verse 19. It could have moved straight from Pharaoh's refusal to God's answer in chapter 6, and instead it stops to record what it is like to try everything available and watch it fail. There are stretches of the Christian life that look exactly like that verse, and it matters that the Bible has one for them.

And the curse in verse 21 is not petulance — it is reasonable. Before Moses came they were slaves; now they are slaves being flogged for an impossible quota, and the only thing that has changed since they bowed and worshipped in 4:31 is that life is measurably worse. From where the foremen stand, Moses is not the deliverer. He is the cause.

verseByVerse.quote: So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw. Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'" So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The policy is passed down the chain, and how it travels repays attention. The taskmasters and the foremen go out and repeat it almost word for word: Thus says Pharaoh, "I will not give you straw. Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least."

Thus says Pharaoh. The same formula Moses used in verse 1, now on the other side. Two words are loose in Egypt — one from the throne of God and one from the throne of Egypt — and for the moment the second is the one with the whips behind it.

So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw. Not even straw: stubble — the stumps left in a field after harvest, the scrapings, what remains when everything usable has already been taken. A nation is put on its knees in the dirt of other people's fields, picking up chaff, to make the same number of bricks it made yesterday.

The word for scattered is the word used of dispersing an army. Israel, which has just begun to be addressed by God as a single son, is broken up across the whole country, each family scrabbling alone. It is hard to organise a people who are spread that thin, and Pharaoh knows it.

verseByVerse.quote: The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw." And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw." The arithmetic is impossible and everybody involved knows it is impossible. That is not a flaw in the policy; it is the policy. A quota that cannot be met turns every day into a failure and every worker into a debtor.

And then the detail that makes this chapter hurt: the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten. The foremen are Hebrews. Egypt has appointed men from among the slaves to drive the slaves, and when the quota fails it is not the Egyptian taskmasters who are flogged but the Israelite middle-men.

It is one of the cruellest arrangements oppression has ever devised, and it is still in use: put some of the oppressed in charge of the rest, make them responsible for the impossible, and let the resentment of the many fall on the few instead of on the throne. By verse 21 those beaten men will be blaming Moses. Pharaoh will not have to lift a finger to turn Israel against its deliverer. He has built a machine that does it for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foremen do something brave. They go over the taskmasters' heads and appeal directly to Pharaoh — bruised men walking into the presence of the king who ordered the bruising — and they put their case well: Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, "Make bricks!" And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people.

It is a good argument, respectfully made, and factually unanswerable. They are not asking for freedom. They are not mentioning Moses, or the LORD, or the feast in the wilderness. They are asking a reasonable man to look at an unreasonable arrangement and correct it.

And here is the thing to notice, because it explains the whole chapter. They have appealed to the wrong throne. There is nothing dishonourable in what they have done — it is what any sensible person would try, and God is not condemning them for it. But the man they are petitioning is the man who wrote the order, and the only relief available in Egypt is from a king who has already answered Who is the LORD? with I will not. They are asking the disease for a cure.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.' Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks." The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'" He says it twice. The sneer of verse 8 is now delivered to the faces of men whose backs are bleeding from a quota they could not meet. There is no argument here and no engagement; there is a phrase repeated because repeating it is easier than thinking.

Then Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks. The appeal is over. The policy stands.

And the narrator gives us the moment it lands: The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble. That is the sentence, flat and without comment. They had one card and they played it, and it did not work, and now they have to walk back out and tell their people that nothing is going to change.

Scripture does not rush this. It could have moved straight from Pharaoh's refusal to God's answer in chapter 6, and instead it stops to record what it is like to try everything available and watch it fail. There are stretches of the Christian life that look exactly like verse 19, and the Bible has a verse for them.

verseByVerse.quote: They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh; and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come out of the palace and Moses and Aaron are standing there waiting to hear how it went.

The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us.

That is not grumbling. That is a curse, invoking God against the men God sent. And the terrible thing is how reasonable it is. Before Moses came they were slaves; now they are slaves being flogged for an impossible quota, and the only thing that has changed since the signs were performed and the people bowed their heads and worshipped (4:31) is that life has become measurably worse. From where the foremen are standing, Moses is not a deliverer. He is the cause.

This is the second time Israel has turned on him. The first was forty years ago — Who made you a prince and a judge over us? (2:14) — and it drove him into the desert. He will hear it again at the sea, and over water, and over food, and over a report about giants, until at the end of his life he is still absorbing it.

And it is the pattern of the greater Deliverer, drawn small. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). The crowd that spread cloaks on the road for him on Sunday was calling for his execution by Friday, and the charge sheet was much the same: he had made things worse, he had provoked Rome, it was better that one man should die for the people. Moses was blamed for a beating. Christ was blamed for everything, and did not defend himself, and went on delivering the people who were shouting.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-23: Moses takes it straight to God, and it is an accusation rather than a question: O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Does Not Rebuke the Complaint

Moses tells God that God has done evil and has not delivered his people at all — the bluntest speech in Exodus so far, made by the man God chose — and there is no correction, no reminder of who is addressing whom. The next verse simply begins Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh. An answer, not a reprimand.

Scripture is full of this and never treats it as a failure of faith: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps. 13:1); O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (Hab. 1:2); Jeremiah telling God outright that he has been deceived (Jer. 20:7). The alternative to Moses' prayer is not a more reverent prayer; it is silence, or walking away. Note the direction — Moses turned to the LORD. Where the protest is taken is the evidence of the faith. A man who has stopped believing does not bother to argue.

The Why That Was Not Answered

There is one prayer of exactly this shape that received no reply. In a garden and then on a cross the true Deliverer asked My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? — and no voice came, and no rescue arrived, and the darkness held for three hours. Moses said you have not delivered your people at all and was told to watch. The Son was not answered, because the deliverance being worked that afternoon required him to stay where he was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses obeyed exactly. He went where he was sent, said what he was given to say, performed the signs — and the measurable result was that a suffering people suffered more and began cursing him for it.

Now: Obedience made things worse. Scripture says so plainly and does not apologise for it, and it is important to see what God does not say in reply. He does not tell Moses he must have misheard the call. He does not suggest the difficulty proves a wrong turn, or that more faith would have produced a smoother result. He tells him to wait one verse.

That is the word for anyone who did the obedient thing and watched it cost them — who spoke the true word and lost the friendship, took the harder road and found it harder than advertised. The chapter ends with nothing fixed and no explanation given, and the man who prayed it was not wrong about any of his facts. He was only early.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."

Read that again and notice that it is an accusation. Not a request for understanding, not a carefully hedged question — Moses tells God that God has done evil to these people and has not delivered them at all. It is the bluntest thing anyone has said to God so far in Exodus, and it is said by the man God chose.

And God does not rebuke him for it. There is no correction, no reminder of who is speaking to whom. The very next verse begins But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh" — an answer, not a reprimand.

That should reframe how a great many people pray. Scripture is full of this kind of speech and it is never treated as a failure of faith: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps. 13:1); O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (Hab. 1:2); Jeremiah telling God outright that he has been deceived (Jer. 20:7). The alternative to Moses' prayer is not a more reverent prayer. It is silence, or leaving. He does neither. Note where he goes with the complaint — Moses turned to the LORD. The direction of the protest is the evidence of the faith. A man who has stopped believing does not bother to argue.

Here is the situation in full, because it is one many readers are living in. Moses obeyed exactly. He went where he was sent, said what he was given to say, performed the signs, and the measurable result of his obedience was that a suffering people suffered more and started cursing him for it. Obedience made things worse. Scripture says so plainly and does not apologise for it, and it does not tell Moses that he must have misheard the call. It tells him to wait one more verse.

And there is one prayer of this shape that was not answered. In a garden and then on a cross, the true Deliverer asked why — My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? — and no voice came back, and no rescue arrived, and the darkness held for three hours. Moses said you have not delivered your people at all and was told to watch. The Son said why have you forsaken me and was not answered, because the deliverance being worked that afternoon required him to stay where he was. Every unanswered why since has been prayed by people whose why was answered at Golgotha, by someone whose was not.

5.theology:
The defiance of unbelief. "Who is the LORD?" exposes the heart of rebellion — a refusal to acknowledge God's right to rule.

The cost of obedience. Following God's word can bring immediate hardship. God's deliverances often deepen the darkness before the dawn.

Honest lament. Moses brings his bewilderment to God himself. Faith may wrestle in the dark, so long as it wrestles with God.
5.examples:
Then: The first obedience to God's command brought heavier chains, not freedom, and the deliverer was blamed by the very people he came to save.

Now: When obedience seems to make life harder and prayers seem to go unanswered, we are exactly where Moses stood. The lowest point is often the threshold of God's mightiest work. Bring your "why" to the LORD.

6.title: I Will Redeem You with an Outstretched Arm
6.text: <sup>6</sup>"Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment. <sup>7</sup>I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God... <sup>8</sup>I will bring you into the land... I am the LORD.'"
6.overview:
In answer to Moses' despair, God responds not with a new plan but with a renewed revelation of himself. "I am the LORD" frames the passage like a refrain. God recalls his covenant with the patriarchs and then unfurls a magnificent chain of "I will" promises — the so-called seven "I wills" of redemption: I will bring you out, I will deliver you, I will redeem you, I will take you, I will be your God, I will bring you in, I will give you the land. Salvation is spelled out entirely in the first person of God. Every verb belongs to him.

Here the great word redeem enters in force: "I will redeem you with an outstretched arm." To redeem is to buy back, to free at cost, to claim as one's own. The outstretched arm — a recurring image of God's saving power — will reach its fullest stretch on a Roman cross, where the Redeemer's arms are stretched out to purchase a people at the cost of his blood.

Yet the chapter ends realistically: the people, broken in spirit by their slavery, do not listen. God's promises are not finally validated by the faith of his people but by the faithfulness of God himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God reassures Moses, recalling that he revealed himself to the patriarchs as God Almighty but now makes known his covenant name, the LORD, and has remembered his covenant in hearing Israel's groaning.
verseByVerse.theology: God's saving acts are grounded in his prior covenant promises. He acts to keep his sworn word, and the unveiling of his name marks a new stage of revelation.
verseByVerse.examples: Redemption is rooted in covenant. God binds himself to a people and then moves heaven and earth to keep faith with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary: Again that great word: God "remembered." His remembering is covenant in motion. The groaning that rose in chapter 2 has not been forgotten; it is the trigger of the outstretched arm.

verseByVerse.quote: God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter is bracketed by "I am the LORD." Before any promise, God names himself. The ground of every "I will" is the unchanging "I am." Our hope rests not first on what God will do but on who God is.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: A new depth of revelation dawns. The patriarchs knew God as El Shaddai; now the covenant name YHWH is unveiled in saving power. God reveals himself progressively, each generation receiving more of his glory — until the fullness shines in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God lays out the chain of redemption: I will bring out, deliver, redeem, take you as my people, be your God, bring you in, and give the land. Every promise is bracketed by "I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation is monergistic — the work of God alone. Each verb belongs to God; Israel's role is to be brought, delivered, and taken. So too our redemption is God's doing from first to last.
verseByVerse.examples: These promises form the covenant heart of the gospel: "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" — echoed in Jeremiah's new covenant and fulfilled in Revelation 21:3.

verseByVerse.quote: Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary: The word "redeem" (ga'al) means to buy back as a kinsman-redeemer. God acts as Israel's near kinsman. The "outstretched arm" becomes the signature of his saving power — fully extended at Calvary, where Christ our Redeemer is stretched out for us.

verseByVerse.quote: I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant formula in its purest form. The goal of redemption is relationship: "my people" and "your God." Keller notes this is the deepest human longing — to belong wholly to God and have God belong wholly to us — and it is the very thing redemption secures.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise reaches its goal: the land, sworn to the fathers. Redemption is never merely rescue from; it is always rescue into — into a possession, an inheritance, a home. So our redemption in Christ secures an inheritance kept in heaven for us (1 Pet. 1:4).

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, one of uncircumcised lips?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Even after the magnificent "I wills," Moses returns to his weakness. Carson notes that the persistence of human frailty only magnifies the sufficiency of God, who accomplishes his purpose through unwilling and faltering servants.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-30 — Unbelief, Genealogy, and a Reluctant Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people do not listen because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery. A genealogy establishes the lineage of Moses and Aaron, and Moses again protests his "uncircumcised lips."
verseByVerse.theology: God's promises stand even when his people cannot believe them. The genealogy roots redemption in real history and real, flawed people whom God nonetheless uses.
verseByVerse.examples: Even great mediators are weak vessels. Moses' faltering points us to the one Mediator whose lips never faltered and whose obedience never failed.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary: Sometimes suffering so crushes the spirit that even good news cannot penetrate. God's promise does not depend on their reception of it. He will deliver a people too beaten to believe — grace that runs ahead of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary: The "outstretched arm" recurs as the signature of God's saving might. Isaiah will ask, "To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?" (Isa. 53:1) — and answer with the Suffering Servant. The arm fully outstretched is Christ crucified, redeeming us at the cost of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's answer to Moses' lament is not explanation but promise — and not just any promise, but the covenant name. I am the LORD. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them. The patriarchs knew God as El Shaddai — the God who is enough, the God of sustaining provision. Now God reveals himself as YHWH — the God who acts in history, who keeps his covenant through time, who has not forgotten what he swore. The difference is not a new God but a new depth of knowing the same God. Every generation learns more of who God is by seeing him act.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary: The people cannot hear the promise because the suffering is too loud. Broken spirit — literally shortness of breath. Slavery has stolen their capacity to hope. This is one of the most compassionate verses in Exodus: God does not condemn the people for their failure to believe. He notes the cause. Kidner observes that there is a kind of suffering that temporarily disables faith — not through sin but through sheer exhaustion. The God who gave the promise will have to create the conditions for the promise to be heard. He is patient enough to do that.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses... These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their companies.
verseByVerse.commentary: The genealogy interrupts the narrative to establish the pedigree of Moses and Aaron — Levi, Kohath, Amram, Aaron and Moses. The names anchor the story in covenant history. This is not a random deliverer appearing from nowhere; this is the son of Amram and Jochebed, from the tribe of Levi, from the family of Kohath. The redemption of Israel will be accomplished through specific people, in specific families, descended from specific ancestors. God works in history, through lineage, through flesh and blood. The Word will become flesh — and that flesh will have a genealogy too.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt, the LORD said to Moses, I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you. But Moses said to the LORD, Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses' objection — uncircumcised lips — is the same objection of inadequacy he raised at the burning bush. The repetition is not carelessness; it frames the entire section between the two commissions and signals that God's answer will be the same: I will be with you, and my word will be in your mouth. The great acts of God in Exodus are accomplished through a man who is convinced he cannot do them. This is by design. If a great orator had led the Exodus, the glory might have been shared with human eloquence. God chooses a stammerer so the glory stays with God.

6.theology:
Redemption is God's work. The seven "I wills" make every verb of salvation God's own. We are brought, delivered, redeemed, and taken — monergism written into the exodus.

The covenant relationship. "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" is the goal of redemption — not just rescue from bondage but belonging to God.

God's faithfulness over our unbelief. The people cannot believe, yet God will save. His promises rest on his character, not our capacity to receive them.
6.examples:
Then: To a people too broken by slavery to listen, God spoke seven sovereign "I wills," pledging to redeem them with an outstretched arm purely on the basis of his covenant.

Now: When our spirits are too crushed to believe the gospel, the ground of our hope is not the strength of our faith but the faithfulness of our Redeemer. His outstretched arm — Christ on the cross — has already secured the "I wills" of our salvation.

7.title: The Battle of the Gods Begins
7.text: <sup>5</sup>"The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them." <sup>10</sup>...Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent. <sup>13</sup>Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said. <sup>20</sup>...all the water in the Nile turned into blood.
7.overview:
The plagues begin, and we must understand what they truly are: not random disasters but a systematic dismantling of the gods of Egypt. "On all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments," God says (12:12). Each plague topples a deity — the Nile that Egypt worshiped, the sun, the livestock, life itself. This is cosmic warfare: YHWH versus the entire pantheon of the world's greatest superpower, and it is no contest.

The chapter sets the terms. Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs — a sign that God's power consumes all counterfeits. Then the Nile, the very lifeblood of Egypt and an object of worship, turns to blood. The river that ran red with Hebrew infants' blood (1:22) now runs red in judgment. God repays in kind.

Threaded through it all is the refrain of Pharaoh's hardening and the divine purpose: "that the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." The plagues are not merely punitive; they are revelatory. Even in judgment, God is making himself known.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Moses as God to Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commissions Moses again, making him "like God to Pharaoh" with Aaron as prophet. He forewarns that he will harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply signs, that Egypt may know the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: God ordains both the means (Moses and Aaron) and the end (Egypt's knowledge of the LORD). His hardening of Pharaoh serves the revelation of his glory.
verseByVerse.examples: God's purpose in judgment is always self-revelation. Even his enemies will be made to know that he is the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The refrain "that they may know that I am the LORD" recurs throughout the plagues. Sproul stressed that the supreme purpose of the exodus is the glory of God — the vindication of his name before the watching nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses becomes God's representative, Aaron his prophet. God works through ordered means and appointed spokesmen. The pattern anticipates the prophetic office that culminates in Christ, the Prophet greater than Moses (Deut. 18:15; Acts 3:22).

verseByVerse.quote: But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,
verseByVerse.commentary: God declares his sovereign hardening in advance. Romans 9 takes up this very theme. The hardening is just judgment upon a willing rebel, not the corruption of an innocent — and it serves the multiplication of God's wonders and the display of his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — Aaron's Staff Swallows the Magicians'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent; Pharaoh's magicians replicate the sign, but Aaron's serpent swallows theirs. Pharaoh's heart is hardened.
verseByVerse.theology: The powers of darkness can imitate but never overcome the power of God. The swallowing serpent shows God's supremacy over all counterfeit spiritual power.
verseByVerse.examples: The enemy mimics God's works to deceive, but his power is always derivative and doomed. God's truth swallows up every counterfeit.

verseByVerse.quote: For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.
verseByVerse.commentary: A telling detail. The occult arts of Egypt can produce a counterfeit, but God's power devours it whole. Carson notes that Satan's imitations always serve only to harden, never to save. God's truth consumes every rival.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go."
verseByVerse.commentary: Here Pharaoh's hardness is described as his own refusal. Scripture holds together God's sovereign hardening and Pharaoh's culpable obstinacy without apology. Both are fully true: God ordains, and Pharaoh chooses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-25 — The Nile Turned to Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first plague: Moses strikes the Nile and it becomes blood; fish die, the river stinks, Egypt cannot drink. The magicians imitate it, and Pharaoh's heart remains hard.
verseByVerse.theology: The plague strikes at the heart of Egyptian religion and economy — the Nile was worshiped as a god and was the source of all life. God shows his lordship over what Egypt idolized.
verseByVerse.examples: The river of Hebrew infants' blood now runs with judgment-blood. God repays oppression in measure, yet his ultimate aim is that all should know he is the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood.
verseByVerse.commentary: The lifeblood of Egypt becomes literal blood. The god-river is shown to be no god at all. As Kidner observes, every plague unmasks an Egyptian deity as helpless before the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The magicians can mimic the plague but not reverse it; their counterfeit only deepens Pharaoh's hardness. As Carson notes, the devil's imitations of God's works serve always to harden, never to heal.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile.
verseByVerse.commentary: The worshiped river becomes undrinkable; Egypt scrambles for water on every side. The idol that promised life now yields only death — a parable of every false god that cannot finally satisfy or save.

verseByVerse.quote: Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The hardening refrain. Scripture says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it — a profound mystery of divine sovereignty and human responsibility that Romans 9 takes up directly. Pharaoh is never a victim; he is a willing rebel whom God justly gives over.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron shall tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land. But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, Pharaoh will not listen to you.
verseByVerse.commentary: God states at the outset what the outcome will be: Pharaoh will not listen. The ten plagues are not a graduated attempt to persuade a reasonable ruler; they are the systematic demonstration that the God of Israel is Lord over every domain Pharaoh and his gods claim to control. Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs — a first victory, easily overlooked. Pharaoh's heart is hardened and the pattern is established: sign, hardening, escalation. The hardening of Pharaoh's heart is both his own choice and God's judicial confirmation of it. He has set himself against God; God seals that choice. No one is hardened who has not first chosen to harden himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Go to Pharaoh in the morning, as he is going out to the water. Stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him, and take in your hand the staff that turned into a serpent. And you shall say to him, The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Nile was Egypt's god — Hapi, giver of life, source of fertility. The first plague turns it to blood. Every fish dies; the water stinks; there is nothing to drink. Egypt's source of life becomes death. The magicians duplicate the sign with their secret arts, which gives Pharaoh his excuse to harden his heart further. But note: the magicians can turn water to blood; they cannot turn it back. They can multiply the plague; they cannot remove it. Throughout the plagues, the magicians' power is only a power to worsen the crisis, not to resolve it. Only the God of Moses can do that.

7.theology:
The LORD over all gods. The plagues are judgments on the gods of Egypt (12:12). YHWH alone is God; every idol is exposed as powerless.

The hardening of the heart. Pharaoh hardens himself, and God hardens Pharaoh — a mystery Scripture holds together (Rom. 9). Human rebellion and divine sovereignty are both fully true.

Judgment as revelation. "That they may know that I am the LORD." Even God's acts of judgment serve to make his glory known.
7.examples:
Then: God began systematically to dismantle the gods of the world's greatest empire, turning its worshiped river to blood and swallowing the magicians' counterfeits, while Pharaoh hardened his heart.

Now: Our culture's idols — wealth, power, self — are no more able to save than Egypt's Nile. God still exposes every counterfeit and calls every heart to know that he alone is the LORD. The question is whether we will be softened or, like Pharaoh, hardened.

8.title: Escalating Judgment and a Line Drawn
8.text: <sup>10</sup>...Moses said, "...so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God." <sup>19</sup>Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said. <sup>22</sup>But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
8.overview:
The plagues escalate — frogs, gnats, flies — and two great themes come into focus. First, the incomparability of God: "that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God." Pharaoh's magicians can produce frogs but cannot remove them; soon they cannot even reproduce the plague of gnats and are forced to confess, "This is the finger of God." The counterfeit power of darkness reaches its limit and collapses before the living God.

Second, the distinction God makes between his people and the world. With the plague of flies, God sets apart Goshen, where Israel dwells, so that no swarms come there. This "making a difference" between Israel and Egypt is one of the great themes of the exodus: God knows his own and protects them in the day of judgment. As Ferguson observes, the God who pours out wrath also shelters his people from it — a foreshadowing of the Passover and, beyond it, of the cross where Christ bore the judgment so that none should fall on us.

Pharaoh begins to bargain — "sacrifice within the land," "do not go very far" — the classic half-repentance of a hard heart that wants relief without surrender.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-15 — Frogs and a Hollow Repentance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Frogs swarm the land and even Pharaoh's bedchamber. He begs Moses to remove them and promises to let Israel go, but when relief comes he hardens his heart again.
verseByVerse.theology: Pharaoh's repentance is mere remorse over consequences, not sorrow over sin. Relief from trouble does not change a hard heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Many cry out to God in crisis and forget him in calm. True repentance turns from sin itself, not merely from its painful effects.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Tomorrow." Moses said, "Be it as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God."
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the timing is granted by Pharaoh, so that the deliverance from frogs will plainly be God's act, not nature's. Begg notes the recurring purpose: every plague aims at knowledge of God — "there is no one like the LORD."

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, Let my people go, that they may serve me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The refrain sounds again: "Let my people go, that they may serve me." The purpose of every plague, every confrontation, is the worship of God by a freed people. Redemption's end is service to the Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh bargains under pressure, promising what he will not keep. The hard heart will say anything to escape pain yet repent of nothing. Crisis-prayers without conversion are the counterfeit of true repentance.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gnats cover the land. This time the magicians cannot reproduce the sign and confess to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." Still Pharaoh's heart is hardened.
verseByVerse.theology: The powers of darkness have a limit; they reach the end of their imitation and are forced to acknowledge God's hand. Yet acknowledgment is not submission.
verseByVerse.examples: Even God's enemies may recognize his power without bowing to him. Demons believe and tremble (James 2:19), but trembling is not faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The counterfeiters confess their defeat. Jesus would later cast out demons "by the finger of God" (Luke 11:20), claiming this very power. The hardened heart, though, can see the finger of God and still refuse to bend.

verseByVerse.quote: The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. So there were gnats on man and beast.
verseByVerse.commentary: The counterfeiters reach their limit and fail. There is a boundary beyond which the powers of darkness cannot go. God's power is original and infinite; every imitation is derivative and doomed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-32 — Flies and the Setting Apart of Goshen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Swarms of flies fill Egypt, but God sets apart Goshen so no flies come there. Pharaoh tries to negotiate a compromised worship; Moses refuses, Pharaoh relents under pressure, then hardens again.
verseByVerse.theology: God makes a distinction between his people and the world, sheltering his own in the day of judgment. He also refuses every half-obedience that Pharaoh proposes.
verseByVerse.examples: The separation of Goshen anticipates the Passover and the gospel: God shields his people from the wrath that falls on the world, for Christ has borne it in their place.

verseByVerse.quote: But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: God draws a line. The same providence that judges Egypt protects Israel. Calvin marveled that God can rain wrath on one place and peace on another at the same hour. This distinguishing mercy points to the cross, where the judgment passed over those covered by the Lamb's blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign shall happen."
verseByVerse.commentary: God Himself draws the dividing line — "my people" and "your people." The distinction is His doing, not Israel's merit. So in the gospel, what separates the saved from the lost is not their goodness but the redeeming grace of God.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you must not go very far away. Plead for me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh's compromises are instructive. "Don't go far." The world is willing to let us serve God a little, partially, on its terms. But God demands whole-hearted, unencumbered worship. Half-surrender is no surrender at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, Thus says the LORD, Let my people go, that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your country with frogs.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second and third plagues — frogs and gnats — attack the land itself. Frogs emerge from the Nile and cover everything: the beds, the ovens, the kneading bowls. Pharaoh asks Moses to pray for their removal and promises to let Israel go. Moses prays; the frogs die; the land stinks with rotting frogs. And Pharaoh's heart is hardened again. The pattern is painful to watch: relief brings hardening; the crisis is needed to sustain his momentary willingness. Sproul observes that Pharaoh is a portrait of the human heart under conviction: genuine discomfort in the crisis, genuine indifference once the discomfort passes.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, Say to Aaron, Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it may become gnats in all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third plague — gnats from the dust — is the first plague the magicians cannot duplicate. They tell Pharaoh: This is the finger of God. The magicians, Egypt's best practitioners of power, acknowledge what Pharaoh will not. There is a God whose power is beyond their skill. But Pharaoh does not listen even to his own experts. This is what hardness of heart looks like at its most advanced: the evidence is clear, the witnesses are his own advisors, and he refuses to draw the obvious conclusion.

verseByVerse.quote: But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: Beginning with the fourth plague — flies — God makes a distinction between Egypt and Goshen. The plagues no longer fall on Israel. This is a theological statement embedded in the geography of affliction: the God of Israel protects his people. Pharaoh bargains: go sacrifice to your God here, in Egypt. Moses refuses: our sacrifices are an abomination to the Egyptians. They must go into the wilderness. Pharaoh concedes, then retracts. The flies are removed; the hardening returns. Each cycle of negotiate-concede-retract is driving toward the one concession Pharaoh will never voluntarily make.

8.theology:
The incomparability of God. "There is no one like the LORD our God." The plagues expose every rival as powerless; even the magicians confess "the finger of God."

Distinguishing grace. God sets apart Goshen, sheltering his people in the day of judgment — a foreshadowing of Passover and the cross.

The hardened heart and false repentance. Pharaoh repents only of consequences, bargains for partial obedience, and hardens again when relief comes.
8.examples:
Then: As plagues escalated, Egypt's magicians confessed defeat, God shielded his people in Goshen, and Pharaoh offered the half-repentance and compromised obedience typical of a hardened heart.

Now: The world still offers God a partial obedience — "don't go too far." But God draws a line between his people and the world, and in Christ he shelters us wholly from the judgment to come. He calls not for bargaining but for surrender.

9.title: That My Name May Be Proclaimed in All the Earth
9.text: <sup>14</sup>"...so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth. <sup>16</sup>But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth." <sup>27</sup>Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong."
9.overview:
The plagues intensify toward life and death: livestock die, boils break out on man and beast, and then comes the devastating hail, the worst storm Egypt has ever seen. Again God distinguishes — no plague touches Goshen, and those Egyptians who fear the word of the LORD are spared by bringing their cattle indoors. Even among the Egyptians, the fear of God begins to bear fruit.

At the center of the chapter stands one of the most theologically weighty verses in all Scripture, quoted by Paul in Romans 9:17: "For this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth." Here is the ultimate purpose of Pharaoh's existence and the plagues' fury — the worldwide proclamation of God's name and power. Pharaoh is a vessel through whom God displays his glory. Sproul taught that this verse forces us to reckon with the absolute sovereignty of God over even the most hardened rebel.

Pharaoh utters his fullest confession yet — "I have sinned; the LORD is in the right" — but it dissolves the moment the hail stops. Words of repentance without a changed heart are worthless.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — Livestock, Boils, and a Deeper Distinction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Plagues on livestock and then boils strike Egypt, while Israel's animals are spared. The magicians cannot even stand before Moses because of the boils. The LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart.
verseByVerse.theology: The plagues now touch health and life itself, and the magicians are utterly defeated. Here Scripture first explicitly says the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart.
verseByVerse.examples: When men persistently resist God's revealed truth, he may judicially harden them, giving them over to the rebellion they have chosen (cf. Rom. 1:24-28).

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here the active divine hardening is stated plainly. After Pharaoh has repeatedly hardened himself (chs. 7-8), God now hardens him in judgment. Carson notes the pattern: God's hardening is never the corruption of an innocent but the judicial confirmation of a rebel in his chosen course.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, Let my people go, that they may serve me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Again the command, again the purpose: that they may serve me. God's patience in repeating the call exposes Pharaoh's guilt — he is warned again and again, and again and again refuses.

verseByVerse.quote: And the next day the LORD did this thing. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel died.
verseByVerse.commentary: The distinguishing mercy continues: Egypt's herds perish; Israel's are spared. God's judgments fall with surgical precision, sparing his own. The same providence that judges the world shelters the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13-21 — The Warning and the God-Fearers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the hail, God declares his purpose: to show his power that his name be proclaimed in all the earth. Some Egyptians fear the word of the LORD and shelter their servants and livestock.
verseByVerse.theology: Even in judgment, God gives warning and opportunity. And even among Egyptians, the fear of the LORD begins to take root — the first fruits of the nations.
verseByVerse.examples: God's wrath is never arbitrary; it comes with warning. And his mercy reaches beyond Israel, anticipating the day when his name is proclaimed among all nations.

verseByVerse.quote: But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes this in Romans 9:17 to teach God's sovereignty in salvation and judgment. The supreme end of all things — even of a tyrant's existence — is the proclamation of God's name. Sproul: the chief end of God is the glory of God, and even Pharaoh serves it.

verseByVerse.quote: For this time I will send all my plagues on you yourself, and on your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The plagues press toward a single goal: that Pharaoh and all the earth may know there is none like the LORD. Sproul stressed that God's incomparability is the great end of his mighty acts; he will be known as God alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-35 — Hail and a Confession That Melts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worst hailstorm in Egypt's history destroys crops and kills the unsheltered, but none falls on Goshen. Pharaoh confesses, "I have sinned; the LORD is in the right," yet when the storm stops, he hardens his heart again.
verseByVerse.theology: Pharaoh's confession is verbally orthodox but heart-empty. Conviction under pressure is not the same as repentance unto life.
verseByVerse.examples: Many make true confessions in the storm only to abandon them in the calm. Saving repentance endures; it is not merely a crisis reflex.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary: The words are flawless theology — God is righteous, I am wrong. Yet Begg warns that you can recite perfect doctrine and have an unchanged heart. The proof of repentance is not eloquence in the storm but obedience in the calm — which Pharaoh utterly lacks.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said to him, "As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease... so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's."
verseByVerse.commentary: "The earth is the LORD's" (cf. Ps. 24:1). Even the storms obey him. Moses' stretched-out hands toward heaven recall the posture of intercession and point to the One whose outstretched hands would still the storm of judgment for us.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart, he and his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary: The pattern is now sickeningly clear: relief comes, repentance evaporates, the heart hardens further. Begg warns that sin promised away in the storm is reclaimed in the calm. A heart unchanged by grace only grows harder with each reprieve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, Let my people go, that they may serve me... The livestock of Israel did not die.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fifth and sixth plagues — livestock disease and boils — escalate the economic and physical cost. The distinction between Israel and Egypt is now explicitly stated: not one of the livestock of Israel died (v.7). Pharaoh sends to check. It is confirmed. His heart is hardened. The boils afflict all of Egypt, including the magicians, who cannot even appear before Pharaoh because they are too sick. The medical establishment has been taken out of the contest. One by one, every human resource Egypt has is being neutralized.

verseByVerse.quote: For this time I will send all my plagues on you yourself, and on your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth. For by now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The hail plague is preceded by God's most explicit statement of purpose: I have raised you up for this very purpose, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth (v.16). Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9 to explain divine sovereignty. Pharaoh exists for a purpose beyond himself — to be the theater in which God's power is displayed to the nations. The hail is catastrophic: fire and hail together, the worst storm in Egypt's recorded history. Flax and barley are destroyed. Those who feared the word of the LORD among Pharaoh's servants sheltered their livestock — even in Egypt, there were those who responded to God's warning.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is Pharaoh's most explicit confession — and also his emptiest. The LORD is in the right; I have sinned. Moses prays; the thunder and hail stop. But verse 34 reports: when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart. The confession was real while the pain was real. The moment the pain stopped, so did the repentance. MacArthur notes that this is the portrait of worldly sorrow (2 Cor. 7:10) — grief about consequences rather than about the offense against God. It produces no change. True repentance changes the direction of the heart, not just the words of the mouth.

9.theology:
The sovereignty of God in hardening. The LORD himself now hardens Pharaoh (v. 12), and declares Pharaoh exists for the display of God's power (v. 16; Rom. 9:17).

The glory of God as the goal of all things. "That my name may be proclaimed in all the earth" is the supreme purpose behind the plagues and behind history itself.

The futility of false repentance. Pharaoh's perfect confession melts when the pressure lifts. Words without a changed heart save no one.
9.examples:
Then: God brought Egypt to its knees with disease and the worst hailstorm in its history, declaring that even Pharaoh existed to display God's power and proclaim his name in all the earth.

Now: God still governs even the hardest hearts toward the proclamation of his glory. And we are warned: it is possible to confess sin with flawless words in a crisis and remain unchanged. True repentance bears fruit when the storm has passed.

10.title: Darkness Over the Land
10.text: <sup>2</sup>"...that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians... that you may know that I am the LORD." <sup>21</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt." <sup>23</sup>...but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.
10.overview:
The eighth and ninth plagues — locusts and darkness — push Egypt toward the brink of un-creation. The locusts devour everything the hail left, stripping the land bare; then comes a darkness "to be felt," three days of thick blackness that strikes at Ra, the sun-god, the chief deity of Egypt. The God who said "Let there be light" now says, in effect, let there be darkness — and the cosmos of Egypt unravels.

This darkness is profoundly significant. As Keller notes, it anticipates the darkness that would cover the land at Calvary, when from the sixth hour to the ninth, darkness fell as the true Firstborn bore the judgment of God. At Calvary the darkness fell not on God's enemies but on God's own Son, in our place. The plague of darkness in Egypt is a shadow of the deeper darkness Christ entered for us, so that we might have light — for "all the people of Israel had light where they lived."

Pharaoh's bargaining grows more desperate: leave the children, leave the livestock. But God will accept no partial exodus. He claims his people whole.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends locusts that cover the land and eat every remaining plant. Pharaoh's own servants plead with him to relent. Pharaoh again offers a partial release — only the men — then hardens after the plague lifts.
verseByVerse.theology: God's purpose is generational: that fathers tell sons how the LORD dealt with Egypt, so that all may know he is the LORD. Pharaoh's servants crack before he does.
verseByVerse.examples: God means his mighty acts to be retold across generations. The exodus is to be catechized into children's hearts — a pattern for passing on faith.

verseByVerse.quote: and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: God designs the exodus to be retold — the seed of the Passover catechism (12:26-27). Faith is handed down by remembering and recounting God's deeds. As Begg often urges, we must tell the next generation what God has done.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?"
