verseByVerse.commentary: Even Pharaoh's court can see what he refuses to admit — Egypt is ruined. The hardened heart is the last to perceive its own destruction. Pride blinds the proud while everyone around them sees the catastrophe.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, that I may show these signs of mine among them,"
verseByVerse.commentary: God states plainly that he hardened Pharaoh's heart for the purpose of displaying his signs. The hardening serves revelation. Even the obstinacy of the rebel is overruled to magnify the glory of God.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: "How long will you refuse to humble yourself?" The root of Pharaoh's sin, and of all sin, is pride that will not bow. Humility before God is the beginning of deliverance; refusal to bow is the essence of ruin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21-29 — A Darkness to Be Felt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends three days of darkness so thick it can be felt, while Israel has light. Pharaoh offers to let the people go but keep the livestock; Moses refuses, and Pharaoh threatens him with death.
verseByVerse.theology: The darkness undoes creation and dethrones the sun-god Ra, while God's people dwell in light. It foreshadows the darkness of Calvary and the light of those in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: At the cross, darkness fell as Christ bore judgment, so that all who are in him might walk in light. The plague is a shadow; the cross is the substance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt."
verseByVerse.commentary: A darkness so dense it has weight — the very antithesis of "Let there be light." Ra, the supreme god of Egypt, is blotted out. Carson sees here the unmaking of Egypt's world, a foretaste of final judgment when light is withdrawn from those who reject the Light of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was pitch darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three days of darkness — a number that will echo at the cross and the empty tomb. Here darkness falls in judgment on Egypt; at Calvary it falls on the Son in our place, that the light of life might dawn for us at his rising.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.
verseByVerse.commentary: The decisive contrast: darkness for Egypt, light for Israel. So Paul writes, "you are all children of light" (1 Thess. 5:5). The darkness Christ endured at Calvary purchased the light in which his people now dwell.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sovereign hardening is restated as the contest nears its climax. God's purposes march forward through Pharaoh's resistance toward the great deliverance of the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said, "As you say! I will not see your face again."
verseByVerse.commentary: The final breach. Pharaoh's hardened heart has exhausted God's patience; the next word will be the death of the firstborn. There comes a point when the door of opportunity closes — a solemn warning to all who presume upon grace.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country, and they shall cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. And they shall eat what is left to you after the hail, and they shall eat every tree of yours that grows in the field.
verseByVerse.commentary: The eighth plague — locusts — strips the land of everything the hail left standing. Pharaoh's own servants beg him: Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined? He summons Moses and Aaron and makes another partial concession: the men may go, but not the women and children. Moses refuses. The locusts come and there was not a single green thing left. Pharaoh confesses again: I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you. The east wind brings the locusts; a west wind drives them into the sea. The precision of the wind is a signature of divine control over creation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt.
verseByVerse.commentary: The ninth plague — thick darkness for three days — is a direct assault on Ra, the sun god, Egypt's highest deity. The darkness is tactile: a darkness to be felt. For three days the Egyptians cannot see one another and cannot move. But all the people of Israel had light where they lived. The contrast between Israel in light and Egypt in darkness is the visible form of the entire narrative: God distinguishes his people. Pharaoh offers another partial concession: go, but leave your livestock. Moses refuses. Pharaoh's rage breaks through: get away from me; never see my face again, or you shall die. Moses responds: as you say; I will not see your face again. The tenth plague is already announced in the darkness.

10.theology:
The undoing of creation. Locusts and a tangible darkness reverse the order God established, dethroning Egypt's sun-god and showing the LORD's mastery over creation itself.

The darkness that prefigures Calvary. The three days of darkness anticipate the darkness over Golgotha, where the true Firstborn bore judgment so his people might have light.

Generational testimony. God designs the exodus to be retold to children and grandchildren, that every generation may know he is the LORD.
10.examples:
Then: God stripped Egypt bare with locusts and plunged it into a darkness that could be felt, dethroning the sun-god, while his people dwelt in light — yet Pharaoh still bargained and hardened.

Now: The darkness over Egypt points to the darkness over the cross, where Christ entered judgment for us. Those in him are children of light. And we, like Israel, are called to tell our children how the LORD has saved — that they too may know him.

11.title: The Announcement of the Last Plague
11.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here." <sup>4</sup>So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, <sup>5</sup>and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die...' <sup>7</sup>...that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel."
11.overview:
This brief chapter is the hush before the storm — the solemn announcement of the tenth and final plague: the death of every firstborn in Egypt, from Pharaoh's throne to the slave at the mill. It is the climactic judgment, the one that will finally break Pharaoh's grip. "Israel is my firstborn son," God had said (4:22); Pharaoh refused to release God's firstborn, and now the firstborn of Egypt will fall.

This is the most sobering plague because it confronts us with the wages of sin: death. The judgment that falls on Egypt is the judgment that justice requires of all. And the only thing that will make a difference between Israel and Egypt on that terrible night is not Israel's merit — for Israel deserves death as much as Egypt — but the blood of a lamb. The next chapter will reveal the means of escape. Here we are simply told that the LORD "makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel."

As Ferguson reflects, this distinction is the heart of grace: not that some are better, but that some are covered. The firstborn of Egypt die; the firstborn of Israel live — because a substitute will die in their place. The shadow of the cross falls across this whole chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-3 — Favor in the Eyes of the Egyptians
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God announces one final plague after which Pharaoh will drive Israel out. He gives Israel favor with the Egyptians, who give them silver and gold — the plundering of Egypt promised long before.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides for his redeemed people even from the wealth of their oppressors, fulfilling his word to Abraham (Gen. 15:14) that they would come out with great possessions.
verseByVerse.examples: God is able to turn the resources of the world toward the good of his people and the building of his worship (cf. the tabernacle materials).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary: God turns the hearts of the Egyptians toward his people. The God who hardens Pharaoh also softens the populace. The plundering of Egypt fulfills Genesis 15:14 — God keeps every word across centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely."
verseByVerse.commentary: God announces the end: one final plague, and then complete release. The deliverance long promised is now at the threshold. God's timing, though it tarries, never fails; the appointed hour has come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4-8 — The Death of the Firstborn Announced
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At midnight the LORD will go through Egypt, and every firstborn will die, from Pharaoh's son to the lowliest slave's. There will be a great cry, but not a dog will growl against Israel, that all may know God distinguishes between Egypt and Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: Sin's wages is death, and the firstborn — the pride and hope of every household — represents the whole. The distinction God makes is one of grace, not merit.
verseByVerse.examples: The death of the firstborn anticipates the death of God's own Firstborn, who would die so that the children of God might be spared.

verseByVerse.quote: and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle.
verseByVerse.commentary: Judgment is no respecter of persons — from palace to mill, all are exposed. Sproul stressed that the universality of judgment reveals the universality of sin. None can stand on social standing before the holy God; all need a substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt,'"
verseByVerse.commentary: "I will go out" — God himself comes in judgment at midnight. This is no impersonal disaster but the very presence of the holy God passing through the land. Only the blood of the lamb will turn that presence from wrath to mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever will be again.
verseByVerse.commentary: A cry like no other will rise from Egypt — the wail of a thousand deaths. Sin's wages, long deferred, fall in a single night. The horror of that cry measures the horror of judgment from which only the Lamb's blood can save.

verseByVerse.quote: But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The distinction is so complete that not even a dog will bark at Israel. Yet the next chapter makes clear the distinction is not Israel's worthiness but the blood of the lamb. Grace, not merit, draws the line between life and death.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.
verseByVerse.commentary: The proud who would not bow to God will yet bow, begging Israel to leave. God humbles the proud in his own time. And Moses departs in righteous anger — the holy indignation of a servant whose Master has been defied to the last.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by noting that Pharaoh would not listen, that God's wonders might be multiplied, and that the LORD had hardened his heart.
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereign hardening of Pharaoh serves the multiplication of his wonders and the display of his glory. Human rebellion is overruled for divine purposes.
verseByVerse.examples: What men intend for evil and obstinacy, God weaves into the tapestry of his redemptive glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
verseByVerse.commentary: The summary of the contest: many wonders, a hardened heart, a sovereign God. As Romans 9 teaches, God's purpose in election and judgment stands. The stage is now set for the Passover and the great deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry... For the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary: The plundering of Egypt before the Exodus is the fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 15:14: they will come out with great possessions. God gives Israel favor in Egyptian eyes — a miraculous reversal in the middle of a plague sequence. The Egyptians, broken and terrified by nine plagues, give freely. God confirms to Moses: Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied. The hardening has a purpose: to run the full number of signs so that every generation will know that the God who brought Israel out of Egypt is Lord over all.

11.theology:
The wages of sin is death. The final plague confronts us with judgment in its starkest form. The death of the firstborn shows that sin's just penalty is death.

Distinguishing grace. God makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel — not by merit but, as ch. 12 reveals, by the blood of a substitute.

God's faithfulness to ancient promises. The plundering of Egypt fulfills the word given to Abraham four centuries earlier (Gen. 15:14).
11.examples:
Then: God announced the climactic judgment — the death of every firstborn — a judgment that exposed all Egypt, palace and hovel alike, and could be escaped only by the distinction God himself would make.

Now: The death of the firstborn confronts us with the truth that sin's wage is death and that none can escape on the basis of merit. The only distinction that saves is the blood of the Lamb — Christ, the true Firstborn, who died that we might live.

12.title: Christ Our Passover
12.text: <sup>5</sup>"Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. <sup>7</sup>Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses... <sup>13</sup>The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt." <sup>14</sup>"This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations."
12.overview:
We come now to the beating heart of the book — the Passover. Here the gospel is preached in shadow with such clarity that the apostle Paul can simply say, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor. 5:7). On this night God delivers his people not by their strength, their worthiness, or their works, but by the blood of a lamb.

Consider the lamb: it must be without blemish, a male in its prime, set apart, slain at twilight, its blood applied to the doorposts, not a bone broken. Every detail points to Christ. He is the Lamb of God without spot or blemish (1 Pet. 1:19); his blood, applied to us by faith, turns away the wrath of God; "not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:36). The destroyer passes over every house marked by the blood. The Israelites inside were not safer than the Egyptians because they were better; they were safe because they were covered. Salvation is by substitution — a life for a life, the lamb for the firstborn.

As Sproul preached with trembling, the most important question that night was not "Are you an Israelite?" but "Is there blood on your door?" And the most important question now is not "Are you religious?" but "Are you covered by the blood of Christ?" This is the chapter that explains the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Lamb and the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God institutes the Passover: a lamb without blemish, selected, slain at twilight, its blood applied to the doorposts, its flesh eaten in haste. When God sees the blood, he will pass over that house.
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation is by the blood of a spotless substitute. The lamb dies in the place of the firstborn; the blood, not the merit of those inside, turns away judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Cor. 5:7), without blemish (1 Pet. 1:19), whose blood, applied by faith, shields us from the wrath of God. This is the gospel in shadow.

verseByVerse.quote: Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats,
verseByVerse.commentary: The lamb must be flawless — the best of the flock, in its prime. Only a perfect substitute will do. Peter draws the line straight to Christ, "a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet. 1:19). No imperfect sacrifice can bear away sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell all the congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month every man shall take a lamb according to their fathers' houses, a lamb for a household.
verseByVerse.commentary: A lamb for a household — redemption is personal yet familial, gathering whole houses under the blood. So the gospel comes to households (Acts 16:31), the covenant promise extending to believers and their children.

verseByVerse.quote: and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at twilight.
verseByVerse.commentary: The lamb is set apart for four days, then slain — examined, found without blemish, then offered. So Christ entered Jerusalem and was scrutinized by his enemies, who could find no fault in him, before being slain as our Passover at the appointed hour.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.
verseByVerse.commentary: It is not enough for the lamb to be slain; the blood must be applied. Keller notes that a slain lamb in the yard saves no one — the blood must be on the door. So too the cross saves only those who, by faith, have its blood applied to them.

verseByVerse.quote: The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: "When I see the blood, I will pass over you." The basis of safety is the blood, not the worthiness of those inside. God does not look at their record but at the blood of the substitute. This is the doctrine of atonement in a single sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike all the firstborn... and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The plague is the climactic judgment on the gods of Egypt. The LORD alone is God, and every idol falls before him. The Passover is the final, decisive blow in the battle of the gods.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands that the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread be kept perpetually, with instructions for teaching the meaning to children. The people bow and worship, then obey.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is to be remembered, celebrated, and taught to every generation. The removal of leaven pictures the call to holiness flowing from deliverance.
verseByVerse.examples: The Passover becomes the Lord's Supper, the perpetual memorial of our redemption by Christ's body and blood, to be kept until he comes (1 Cor. 11:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?'
verseByVerse.commentary: The Passover is built for catechism. Worship raises questions in children's hearts, and parents answer with the story of redemption. Begg urges that every generation must hear afresh, "This is what the LORD did for us."

verseByVerse.quote: you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary: The right response to redemption explained is worship. Having heard what God did, the people bow and adore. So the gospel rightly understood always issues in worship — the bowed head of the redeemed before the saving God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At midnight the LORD strikes every firstborn in Egypt. Pharaoh finally drives Israel out. They leave in haste with the plunder of Egypt, and the Passover ordinances are completed, including that no bone of the lamb be broken.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment falls, and the redemption long promised is accomplished in a single night. The unbroken bone is one more arrow pointing to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: John 19:36 cites the unbroken-bone command as fulfilled in Jesus: "Not one of his bones will be broken." The Lamb of God fulfills the Passover to the letter.

verseByVerse.quote: It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of the flesh outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones.
verseByVerse.commentary: Not a bone broken — a detail John records was fulfilled at the cross when the soldiers, finding Jesus already dead, did not break his legs (John 19:33-36). Across fifteen centuries, the Lamb of God answers the pattern perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt; so this same night is a night of watching kept to the LORD by all the people of Israel throughout their generations.
verseByVerse.commentary: A night of watching by the LORD himself. God did not merely command the Passover; he kept vigil over his people that night. The Redeemer watches over his redeemed — the same vigilance that would one day keep watch in Gethsemane and on Golgotha for our sake.

verseByVerse.quote: This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you... The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Passover is the founding sacrament of Israel's life. God restructures Israel's calendar: this is now the first month, the beginning of months. Time itself is reset around the act of redemption. A lamb without blemish, killed at twilight, its blood applied to the doorposts and lintel — the mark that causes the destroyer to pass over. The household gathers to eat the lamb in haste, loins girded, sandals on, staff in hand: ready to depart. The meal is eaten on the edge of departure. Every Passover thereafter would be eaten in memory: this is what the LORD did for us when he brought us out of Egypt. The lamb, the blood, the protected household, the night of judgment passing over — the entire gospel is here in outline, waiting for the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses, for if anyone eats what is leavened, from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Feast of Unleavened Bread is bound inseparably to the Passover: the night of the blood is followed by seven days of the bread of haste. No leaven — leaven works slowly, invisibly, through the entire loaf. Israel is to eat the bread of affliction and urgency, remembering that there was no time to wait for bread to rise. Paul will use this imagery to teach the church: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed; therefore let us celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:7-8). The feast and its theology travel forward into the New Covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock.
verseByVerse.commentary: The tenth plague falls at midnight — the hour of deepest darkness. From Pharaoh's palace to the prison cell to the cattle stall, every firstborn dies. The cry in Egypt that night is unlike any before or after — an entire nation in grief. Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron at night: Go, serve the LORD as you have said. Take your flocks and your herds. Go, and bless me also. The blessing he asks for is a desperate plea from a broken man. Israel leaves in haste, 430 years to the day from when they entered. They borrow silver, gold, and clothing — the plundering of Egypt accomplished peacefully, by the gift of God's favor. The mixed multitude who leaves with them — Egyptians and others who have seen what God did and choose to leave with Israel — is the first hint that the redemption of God was never only for one nation.

12.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The lamb dies in the place of the firstborn. "When I see the blood, I will pass over you." Salvation is by a substitute's blood, not by merit.

Christ our Passover. The spotless lamb, the applied blood, the unbroken bones — all fulfilled in Jesus (1 Cor. 5:7; 1 Pet. 1:19; John 19:36).

Redemption remembered. The Passover becomes a perpetual memorial, fulfilled in the Lord's Supper, by which the church proclaims Christ's death until he comes.
12.examples:
Then: On the night of judgment, every household covered by the blood of a spotless lamb was passed over, while Egypt's firstborn died — and God's people went free, not by their worth but by the blood.

Now: Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. The decisive question is not how good we are but whether we are covered by his blood. By faith we apply his blood to our hearts, and the judgment passes over us forever. Every Lord's Supper recalls this redemption until he comes.

13.title: Consecration and the Guiding Presence
13.text: <sup>2</sup>"Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine." <sup>21</sup>And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night. <sup>22</sup>The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
13.overview:
Redeemed people belong wholly to God. So the first command after the exodus is the consecration of the firstborn: "Whatever is the first to open the womb... is mine." Because God spared Israel's firstborn on Passover night, every firstborn now belongs to him — either given to his service or redeemed by a substitute. The principle is profound: those whom God has redeemed, he claims as his own possession. We are not our own; we were bought with a price.

The chapter also institutes the Feast of Unleavened Bread and the practice of teaching children — again the rhythm of remembering and recounting. Then comes one of the most tender images in all of Scripture: the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. God does not redeem his people and then leave them to find their own way. He goes before them, leading every step, never departing. The God who came down to deliver now travels with his people.

This guiding presence is the great comfort of the redeemed life. As Ferguson observes, the same God who saves us also leads us, and his presence — fulfilled in Christ who promised "I am with you always" and in the Spirit who indwells us — never departs.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God claims every firstborn of Israel because he spared them at Passover. The firstborn are to be consecrated or redeemed, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread is to be kept, with the meaning taught to children as a sign on hand and forehead.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption establishes ownership: those God spared belong to him. The firstborn are redeemed by substitution, reinforcing the Passover principle.
verseByVerse.examples: Because Christ has redeemed us, we are not our own (1 Cor. 6:19-20). The whole of life is to be consecrated to the God who bought us.

verseByVerse.quote: Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine.
verseByVerse.commentary: God claims what he has redeemed. The firstborn spared at Passover now belong to him. Calvin notes this teaches Israel that their very lives were a gift of grace, owed back to God. Redemption always issues in consecration.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Remember." The redeemed are a remembering people. Forgetfulness is the soil of ingratitude and idolatry; remembrance keeps the heart tender and thankful. We remember our redemption supremely at the Lord's table.

verseByVerse.quote: And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary: Redemption is to mark hand, eyes, and mouth — the whole life shaped by what God has done. The deliverance is not a private memory but a public, total reorientation of life around the saving God.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'
verseByVerse.commentary: "What the LORD did for me" — personal, grateful testimony passed to the next generation. The faith is not abstract doctrine but recounted experience of grace. Each believer must be able to say, "This is what God did for me."

verseByVerse.quote: And when in time to come your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you shall say to him, 'By a strength of hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Again the catechism of redemption: children ask, parents recount the mighty acts of God. Faith is handed down by the faithful retelling of what God has done. Each generation must learn to say, "the LORD brought us out."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17-22 — The Pillar of Cloud and Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God leads Israel not by the direct route but through the wilderness, carrying Joseph's bones in fulfillment of his oath. He goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, which never departs.
verseByVerse.theology: God leads his redeemed people personally and continually, choosing even the longer, harder road for their good. His guiding presence never leaves them.
verseByVerse.examples: The pillar prefigures Christ, the light of the world, and the indwelling Spirit who guides God's people. "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Heb. 13:5).

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary: God leads by the harder, longer way — out of tender wisdom, knowing their frailty. Carson observes that God's detours are mercies; he leads us not by the shortest path but by the path that will make us his people. His guidance is always loving, even when puzzling.

verseByVerse.quote: But God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea.
verseByVerse.commentary: God leads by the wilderness way — the longer, harder road that will become the path of his greatest deliverance. His leading is never careless; even his detours are designed for our good and his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones with you from here."
verseByVerse.commentary: Joseph's bones travel with Israel — a centuries-old act of faith fulfilled (Heb. 11:22). Joseph believed the promise of exodus before it came; now his bones journey to the land. God keeps faith across generations; no believing word spoken to him falls to the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night.
verseByVerse.commentary: God himself goes before them — visible, constant, leading. Sproul called this the visible Shekinah, the manifest presence of God among his people. The Redeemer is also the Guide. Day and night, light and shade, he never leaves them to wander alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine.
verseByVerse.commentary: The consecration of the firstborn is the memorial law that grows directly from the Passover night. The firstborn of Israel survived because the angel of death passed over the blood-marked houses; therefore every firstborn belongs to God as a living reminder. The firstborn animal is sacrificed; the firstborn child is redeemed by a substitutionary offering. The principle is theological: all life belongs to God; survival is mercy; substitution is the mechanism of grace. Every firstborn redeemed in Israel is a small re-enactment of the Passover, and every re-enactment points forward to the one Firstborn who would not be redeemed by a substitute but would himself be the substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out. And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month.
verseByVerse.commentary: The feast laws are given while Israel is still in the wilderness, still short of the Promised Land. God tells them: when I bring you into the land — it is assumed, certain, not in doubt. The feast will be kept in the land that is not yet possessed, because the God who promises it will deliver it. This is the pedagogy of covenant: God gives the law of celebration before the celebration is possible, training his people to live by promise rather than by present experience.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's route for Israel is not the shortest route but the necessary one. The coastal road through Philistia is close — it would have taken weeks. The wilderness route will take forty years. But God knows his people: they are not ready for immediate warfare. He takes them the long way because the long way is the only way that will produce a people fit for what is ahead. The pillar of cloud by day and pillar of fire by night is God's visible presence leading them — not a GPS but a Person, going before them, making the way. He never leaves them to find their own path.

13.theology:
Redemption and consecration. Those whom God redeems, he claims. The firstborn are his; we who are redeemed by Christ are not our own.

The wisdom of God's leading. God chooses the longer road for his people's good, sparing them what they cannot yet bear. His detours are mercies.

The guiding presence of God. The pillar of cloud and fire reveals a God who never departs from his people — fulfilled in Christ and the indwelling Spirit.
13.examples:
Then: Having redeemed his people, God claimed their firstborn as his own and led them out by a visible pillar of cloud and fire that never departed, choosing even the harder road for their good.

Now: Redeemed by Christ, we belong wholly to God and consecrate our lives to him. And we are never left to find our own way: he leads us by his Word and Spirit, choosing wise paths, promising never to leave us nor forsake us.

14.title: The LORD Will Fight for You
14.text: <sup>13</sup>And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today... <sup>14</sup>The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent." <sup>21</sup>...and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. <sup>22</sup>And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.
14.overview:
Trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea, Israel panics. There is no way forward, no way back, no human possibility of escape. And precisely there, in the place of utter helplessness, God works his greatest salvation. "Stand firm," Moses says, "and see the salvation of the LORD... The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent." This is the gospel posture: salvation is something we receive, not achieve. We do not contribute to it; we behold it.

God divides the sea, and Israel passes through on dry ground from death to life, while the same waters that saved them destroy their enemies. Paul tells us this crossing was a baptism: "all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Cor. 10:2). The Red Sea is the pattern of every believer's salvation — passing through the waters of judgment safely because we are united to our deliverer, our old enemies drowned behind us, emerging into new life on the other shore.

As Keller preached, the Red Sea teaches us that God's deliverance often comes only when we have run out of options — when we finally stop striving and stand still to see the salvation of the LORD. The enemy that terrified us at dawn lies dead on the shore by morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-14 — Trapped, Terrified, and Told to Stand Still
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God leads Israel into a trap to draw Pharaoh after them and gain glory. Pharaoh pursues; Israel panics and accuses Moses. Moses answers: stand firm, see the LORD's salvation, the LORD will fight for you.
verseByVerse.theology: God sometimes leads his people into seeming dead ends to display his glory and teach them to trust. Salvation is the LORD's work, received in faith, not achieved by striving.
verseByVerse.examples: When trapped with no human way out, the believer's call is to stand firm and behold God's salvation. "Be still, and know that I am God" (Ps. 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall never see again."
verseByVerse.commentary: "See the salvation of the LORD" — salvation is something to be beheld, not produced. Ferguson notes that here Israel does nothing but watch God save. So in the gospel, we contribute nothing to our redemption; we receive the finished work of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: Caught between the army and the sea, the people are terrified — and they cry out to the LORD. Even panic that turns Godward is the seed of faith. The cornered believer's best refuge is the cry to heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.
verseByVerse.commentary: One of the most freeing sentences in Scripture. The battle belongs to the LORD. Our striving adds nothing; our silence honors his sufficiency. As Sproul said, the Christian life begins by ceasing to trust ourselves and trusting wholly in the God who fights for us.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward."
verseByVerse.commentary: There is a time to pray and a time to march. Faith both cries out and steps forward at God's word. God commands them to advance toward the impossible sea, for he is about to make a way where there is no way.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved... and stood behind them,
verseByVerse.commentary: The presence of God moves between his people and the enemy — protection and shield. The same God who leads from the front also guards the rear. No foe can reach his people except through him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Moses to lift his staff; the pillar moves behind Israel to shield them; a strong east wind divides the sea, and Israel crosses on dry ground while the Egyptians follow into the seabed, where God throws them into confusion.
verseByVerse.theology: God's power over creation makes a path through the impossible. The same presence that lights Israel's way darkens the enemy's; God's salvation and judgment proceed from the same hand.
verseByVerse.examples: The crossing is our baptism (1 Cor. 10:2): passing through judgment-waters safely because united to our deliverer, into new life on the far shore.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
verseByVerse.commentary: God uses means — a strong east wind — yet the act is wholly his. Creation itself bends to make a way of salvation. The God who divided the waters at creation (Gen. 1) now divides them for redemption. The Redeemer is the Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.
verseByVerse.commentary: They walk through death and come out alive. Paul calls this a baptism (1 Cor. 10:1-2) — the great picture of dying and rising with our deliverer. The waters that would have drowned them become walls of safety because they go through with God.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its normal course when the morning appeared... and the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary: The waters that walled the path now become a flood of judgment. The same sea saves and destroys. At the cross, the same event — Christ's death — is salvation to those who believe and judgment to those who reject him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses stretches out his hand again; the waters return and drown Pharaoh's army. Israel sees the Egyptians dead on the shore, fears the LORD, and believes in him and in Moses his servant.
verseByVerse.theology: The same waters that save God's people destroy their enemies. The decisive defeat of the foe produces faith and the fear of the LORD in the redeemed.
verseByVerse.examples: Christ's death and resurrection is the true Red Sea: there our great enemy — sin, death, the devil — was drowned forever, and we emerge on the shore of new life.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians, so the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in Moses his servant.
verseByVerse.commentary: Salvation produces worship. Having seen God's power, they fear and believe. Begg observes that genuine deliverance always issues in faith and reverence — the redeemed cannot help but trust and tremble before such a God.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary: "The LORD saved Israel that day." The verb belongs to God alone. The enemy that terrified them at dawn lies dead by morning. So our great enemies — sin, death, and the devil — lie defeated on the shore of Christ's empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The crisis at the Red Sea is engineered by God: he tells Moses to camp in a position that will look like confusion to Pharaoh, drawing the Egyptian army after them. The plan is designed to bring Pharaoh to his final destruction and to be glorified over Pharaoh and all his host. Israel, trapped between the sea and the army, cries out to God — which is exactly what they should do. Then, understandably, they turn on Moses: Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? The fear is real; the complaint is understandable. God is not offended by their terror. He is about to answer it in a way they will never forget.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.
verseByVerse.commentary: The parting of the Red Sea is the defining miracle of the Old Testament — the act to which Israel will refer for all of subsequent history when speaking of God's power. A strong east wind all night: the mechanism is natural, the timing and precision are supernatural. Israel walks on dry ground between walls of water. The Egyptians pursue into the sea; the LORD looks down through the pillar of fire and panic-jams their chariot wheels. They say: Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians. They try to flee — and the waters return. The army that enslaved Israel for 400 years is swallowed by the sea that Israel crossed on dry ground. Not one remains.

14.theology:
Salvation belongs to the LORD. "The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent." Israel beholds; God acts. Redemption is received, not achieved.

The Red Sea as baptism. Passing through the waters from death to life, united to the deliverer, with the old enemy drowned behind — the pattern of Christian baptism (1 Cor. 10:1-2).

The same waters save and judge. God's deliverance of his people is simultaneously the destruction of his enemies. Salvation and judgment flow from one hand.
14.examples:
Then: Trapped between army and sea, Israel was told to stand still and see God save. He split the waters, brought them through from death to life, and drowned their enemies behind them.

Now: When we are cornered with no way out, the gospel call is the same: stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. At the cross our true enemies were drowned, and in Christ we have passed through the waters of judgment into new life. The battle belongs to the LORD.

15.title: The Song of the Redeemed
15.text: <sup>1</sup>"I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea. <sup>2</sup>The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him." <sup>11</sup>"Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?" <sup>18</sup>"The LORD will reign forever and ever."
15.overview:
Redeemed people sing. The first thing Israel does on the far shore of the sea is break into song — the Song of the Sea, the oldest hymn of salvation in Scripture. This is no dirge but an explosion of doxology: "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously!" Salvation accomplished leads inevitably to praise lifted up. As Sproul observed, theology that does not end in doxology is dead theology. Here the saved cannot keep silent.

The song celebrates the character of God: "The LORD is a man of war" — the warrior who fights for his people; "majestic in holiness" — incomparable in purity; "the LORD will reign forever and ever" — the everlasting King. It looks back at the sea and forward to the promised land, to the place God will plant his people, the sanctuary his hands will establish. The exodus is not an end but a beginning, leading to worship in God's dwelling place.

Revelation 15 tells us that the redeemed in glory sing "the song of Moses... and the song of the Lamb." The song begun on the shore of the Red Sea will be completed before the throne. And Miriam takes up her tambourine and leads the women in dancing — the joy of salvation overflowing into the whole community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — The LORD Is a Warrior
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses and Israel sing of the LORD's triumph over Pharaoh's army, exalting his strength, his right hand, his majesty in holiness, and his incomparability among the gods.
verseByVerse.theology: The redeemed respond to salvation with worship that magnifies God's character. He is the warrior who saves, majestic in holiness, beyond all comparison.
verseByVerse.examples: Salvation accomplished must lead to praise. The first instinct of the redeemed heart is to sing of the God who saved it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Personal and corporate worship fuse: "my God" and "my father's God." Salvation is intensely personal yet rooted in covenant history. Begg notes that to sing "he has become my salvation" is to make the redemption of the people one's own. The Redeemer is not merely Israel's but mine.

verseByVerse.quote: I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first word of the redeemed is song. Salvation accomplished cannot be met with silence. Sproul taught that theology must end in doxology — and here the saved break spontaneously into praise of the triumphant God.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary: The LORD is a warrior who fights for his people. This is no abstract deity but the God who bares his arm against his enemies. The same warrior-God conquers our foes at Calvary, leading captivity captive (Eph. 4:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?
verseByVerse.commentary: The great question of the song: who is like the LORD? None. He is incomparable, supremely in holiness. Sproul taught that holiness is the attribute Scripture emphasizes above all others — the very thing the seraphim cry day and night. The redeemed worship a holy God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song looks ahead: God will lead his redeemed people in steadfast love, plant them on his mountain, and bring them to his sanctuary, where he will reign forever.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption has a destination: the dwelling place of God, where his people worship him as everlasting King. Salvation is for the sake of communion with God.
verseByVerse.examples: The goal of redemption is always God's presence — fulfilled in Christ and consummated in the New Jerusalem where God dwells with his people forever (Rev. 21).

verseByVerse.quote: You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode.
verseByVerse.commentary: Redemption is the fruit of God's steadfast love (hesed), and its destination is his holy dwelling. Keller notes that God saves us not merely from something but to himself — to his presence, his abode, his everlasting joy.

verseByVerse.quote: You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O LORD, which your hands have established.
verseByVerse.commentary: The song already looks to the sanctuary — God's dwelling with his people, the goal of the whole book. Redemption leads to the place where God abides. We are saved to dwell with him forever (Rev. 21:3).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary: The climax of the song: an eternal kingdom. The exodus is a window onto the everlasting reign of God. Revelation echoes it: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord" (Rev. 11:15). The God who reigned over the sea reigns forever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Miriam, the prophetess, takes a tambourine and leads the women in song and dance, echoing the refrain of the LORD's glorious triumph.
verseByVerse.theology: The joy of salvation overflows into the whole community, women and men together. Worship is not the privilege of leaders alone but the response of all the redeemed.
verseByVerse.examples: Salvation produces communal, embodied joy — a foretaste of the worship of the great multitude before the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The joy cannot be contained; it spills into music and dancing. Miriam leads the women in answering song. Salvation is not a private sentiment but a shared celebration — the whole redeemed community caught up in praise.

verseByVerse.quote: And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary: Miriam answers the men's song with the women's refrain — antiphonal praise rising from the whole community. The joy of salvation is too great for one voice; it must be answered, echoed, multiplied among all the redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water.
verseByVerse.commentary: From the height of song to the test of thirst — the redeemed life moves quickly from triumph to trial. The wilderness will prove whether the praise of the shore endures in the parched places. Faith must learn to sing in the desert too.

verseByVerse.quote: Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea... Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?
verseByVerse.commentary: The Song of Moses is Israel's first great hymn. It is theology set to music: the acts of God celebrated, his character declared, his future purposes anticipated. Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? This is not a question; it is a declaration that the question has been answered by what just happened. The gods of Egypt — Hapi of the Nile, Ra of the sun, Pharaoh himself who claimed divinity — have all been exposed as nothing before the God who parts seas and swallows armies. The song reaches forward to the conquest: terror and dread fall on Canaan; the LORD will bring his people in and plant them on his holy mountain. They are singing the end before they have lived the middle.

verseByVerse.quote: They went three days in the wilderness and found no water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter... And the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three days after the greatest miracle in their history, Israel complains about water. The transition is jarring and human. The bitter waters of Marah are their first wilderness test. Moses cries to the LORD; God shows him a log; the log sweetens the bitter water. Then comes the first wilderness law: if you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God and do that which is right in his eyes... I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer. The physical healing of the water becomes the announcement of a healer-God. The early church saw the wood cast into Marah as a type of the cross — Christ the log that transforms bitter water into sweet, curse into blessing.

15.theology:
Doxology as the response to redemption. The redeemed sing. Salvation accomplished overflows into worship. Theology rightly ends in praise.

The incomparability and holiness of God. "Who is like you, majestic in holiness?" The song magnifies the unique, holy, warrior-King.

The everlasting reign of God. "The LORD will reign forever and ever." The exodus opens onto the eternal kingdom, fulfilled in Christ.
15.examples:
Then: Standing on the far shore with their enemies dead behind them, the redeemed people broke into the oldest song of salvation, exalting the warrior-God, majestic in holiness, who reigns forever.

Now: The proper response to redemption is song. We who have been brought through the waters in Christ join the song of Moses and the Lamb. Our worship now is the rehearsal of the eternal praise we will sing before the throne.

16.title: Bread from Heaven
16.text: <sup>4</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you..." <sup>15</sup>...It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. <sup>18</sup>...whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat. <sup>35</sup>The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land.
16.overview:
Barely a month out of Egypt, the redeemed people grumble — not against Pharaoh now, but against God, even wishing they had died in Egypt where at least there was bread. The human heart, even the redeemed heart, is prone to forget grace and crave the security of its old slavery. Yet God responds not with judgment but with mercy: he rains "bread from heaven."

The manna is a daily miracle of provision and a daily lesson in dependence. It must be gathered each morning; it cannot be hoarded; what is kept overnight breeds worms — except on the day before the Sabbath, when a double portion keeps. God teaches his people to trust him one day at a time, to rest on the Sabbath, and to learn that "man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD" (Deut. 8:3).

And then Jesus takes up this very manna in John 6: "I am the bread of life... your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died... I am the living bread that came down from heaven." The manna was a shadow; Christ is the substance. As Ferguson reflects, the daily bread of the wilderness points to the One who alone can satisfy the deepest hunger of the soul. We feed on him by faith, and we shall never hunger again.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the wilderness the people grumble against Moses and Aaron, longing for Egypt's food. God promises to rain bread from heaven and send quail, that they may know he is the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.theology: The redeemed are prone to forget grace and idealize their old bondage. Yet God meets even ungrateful grumbling with patient provision, to reveal himself as their God.
verseByVerse.examples: How quickly we forget past deliverances and crave the security of former sins. God's patience with murmuring people is itself a wonder of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."
verseByVerse.commentary: Astonishing ingratitude — they romanticize slavery for the sake of full stomachs. Calvin observed that unbelief always exaggerates past comforts and forgets present mercies. The flesh would rather have bread in bondage than freedom with faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Quail come in the evening and manna in the morning. The people gather it daily; each has enough, none has lack, and it cannot be stored overnight without spoiling.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides daily bread to teach daily dependence. The equalizing of much and little teaches contentment and trust in God's sufficiency rather than hoarding.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul applies the equity of the manna to Christian generosity (2 Cor. 8:15). God's people are to trust him for each day and share with one another.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Bread from heaven" — the very phrase Jesus claims in John 6. The daily gathering is a test of trust. Will they depend on God for each day's portion? So we pray, "Give us this day our daily bread," learning the same dependence.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread, then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the provision answers the great refrain: "that you may know that I am the LORD." God feeds his people not merely to fill their stomachs but to reveal himself. Every mercy is a means of knowing God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said, "...your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: To grumble against God's servants is to grumble against God. Murmuring is not a small sin; it is unbelief aimed at heaven. The redeemed are called to trust, not to complain against the God who saved them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Manna" means literally "What is it?" — a mystery bread from heaven. Jesus declares the answer: he himself is the true bread (John 6:32-35). The wilderness manna sustained the body for a day; Christ, the living bread, gives eternal life. He is the answer to "What is it?"

verseByVerse.quote: But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul cites this very verse on Christian generosity (2 Cor. 8:15): in God's economy, abundance and need are balanced by sharing. The manna teaches both daily trust and open-handed care for one another.

verseByVerse.quote: Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.
verseByVerse.commentary: The manna could not be hoarded; it had to be gathered fresh each day. So grace is received daily, not stockpiled. Yesterday's manna will not feed today's hunger; we must come to God anew each morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-36 — The Sabbath Provision and a Memorial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the sixth day a double portion comes and keeps over the Sabbath, when no manna falls. Some disobey and find none. A jar of manna is kept as a memorial of God's provision throughout the generations.
verseByVerse.theology: God builds Sabbath rest into the rhythm of provision, teaching trust and rest in him. The preserved manna memorializes his faithful care.
verseByVerse.examples: The Sabbath principle of rest and trust endures; we labor and rest in dependence on God, who provides all we need. The preserved manna anticipates Christ, our enduring bread.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary: Forty years of unfailing provision — a daily testimony to God's faithfulness through the whole wilderness journey. The God who began to feed them did not stop until they reached the land. He sustains his people the whole way home.

verseByVerse.quote: And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, and the people of Israel said to them, Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second great complaint: hunger. Six weeks into the wilderness, the people are ready to trade liberation for full stomachs. This is not ingratitude born of comfort; it is desperation born of real hunger. The extraordinary aspect is God's response: he does not rebuke them but rains bread from heaven. Quail in the evening, manna in the morning — daily provision, never too much, never too little. God tells Moses: I will test them, whether they will walk in my law or not. The manna is not merely food; it is a curriculum. Dependence on daily bread from heaven is the shape of the covenant life. Jesus will teach his disciples to pray: give us today our daily bread — and will declare: I am the bread of life.

verseByVerse.quote: When the layer of dew lifted, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground. When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, What is it? For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.
verseByVerse.commentary: Manna — the word itself means What is it? — is the mystery-provision of the wilderness years. It must be gathered fresh each morning, except on the sixth day when a double portion is collected for the Sabbath. Those who try to keep it overnight find it rotten and wormy. Those who try to gather on the Sabbath find nothing. The manna disciplines the people into the rhythm of creation: six days of labor, one day of rest, daily dependence on God for sustenance. Deuteronomy 8:3 will explain the lesson: he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. Jesus quotes this verse when Satan tempts him with bread in the wilderness.

16.theology:
The grumbling heart and patient grace. The redeemed forget grace and idealize bondage, yet God answers murmuring with merciful provision.

Daily dependence. The manna teaches trust for each day, contentment, Sabbath rest, and the truth that man lives by every word of God.

Christ the bread of life. The manna is fulfilled in Jesus (John 6), the living bread from heaven who alone satisfies the soul's hunger forever.
16.examples:
Then: When the redeemed grumbled and longed for Egypt's bread, God rained manna from heaven, feeding them daily for forty years and teaching them to depend on him one day at a time.

Now: We still crave the security of our old slaveries and forget past mercies. God still calls us to daily dependence — "give us this day our daily bread" — and offers us himself, the true bread from heaven. Feeding on Christ by faith, we shall never hunger.

17.title: The Rock and the Uplifted Hands
17.text: <sup>6</sup>"Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel. <sup>11</sup>Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed. <sup>15</sup>And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner.
17.overview:
Two scenes, both pointing to Christ. First, the people thirst and quarrel, testing God: "Is the LORD among us or not?" God commands Moses to strike a rock at Horeb, and water gushes out to give the people life. Paul interprets it unmistakably: "they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10:4). The Rock must be struck for the water of life to flow — and at Calvary, Christ our Rock was struck by the rod of God's judgment, that the living water of the Spirit might pour out to a thirsting people. Strikingly, God says, "I will stand before you there on the rock" — God himself takes the place of judgment as the rock is struck.

Second, Amalek attacks, and as long as Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails; when his hands grow weary, Israel falters — so Aaron and Hur hold up his hands until sunset. Here is a picture of intercession: the battle below is won by the uplifted hands above. Moses the mediator, with arms outstretched, prevails for his people — prefiguring the greater Mediator whose arms were outstretched on a cross and who "always lives to make intercession" for us (Heb. 7:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Water from the Struck Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Rephidim the people thirst and quarrel with Moses, testing whether the LORD is among them. God stands on the rock at Horeb; Moses strikes it, and water flows. The place is named Massah and Meribah.
verseByVerse.theology: The people's testing of God is unbelief; yet God graciously provides life-giving water from a struck rock. The striking of the rock is the means of the water.
verseByVerse.examples: The Rock is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4), struck by God's judgment that the living water of salvation might flow to a thirsting people. "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink" (John 7:37).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Astonishing: God says "I will stand before you... on the rock" as it is struck. The blow that brings water falls, as it were, where God himself stands. Sproul saw here a shadow of the cross, where the rod of divine justice fell upon God incarnate, that the water of life might flow to us.

verseByVerse.quote: All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary: They camp where God commanded — and find no water. Obedience does not guarantee ease. God sometimes leads his people into thirsty places to teach them that he, not the circumstances, is their supply.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Is the LORD among us or not?" — the question of unbelief in the face of mountains of evidence. Hebrews 3 warns us not to harden our hearts as at Meribah. The redeemed must beware the rebellion that doubts God's presence despite his proven faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go."
verseByVerse.commentary: The same staff that struck the Nile in judgment now brings water in mercy. The instrument of judgment becomes the means of grace — as the cross, an instrument of death, becomes the fountain of life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Uplifted Hands and the Battle with Amalek
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amalek attacks. Joshua fights below while Moses holds up the staff of God on the hill. When his hands are up, Israel prevails; Aaron and Hur hold up his weary hands until sunset, and Israel wins.
verseByVerse.theology: The victory is won not merely by the sword below but by the uplifted hands above — a picture of prevailing intercession and dependence on God's power.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses' outstretched arms prefigure Christ, our great Intercessor with arms stretched out on the cross, who ever lives to pray for us (Heb. 7:25). The church wins its battles on its knees.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The outcome of the battle hangs on the uplifted hands. Begg notes this is a vivid parable of intercession: the real battle is fought in prayer. The hands lifted to God determine the victory of the people below.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand."
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua fights below while Moses intercedes above — the work of the church in two hands: faithful labor and prevailing prayer. Neither alone wins the day; the battle is won where action and intercession meet.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the mediator grows weary and needs support — a beautiful picture of bearing one another's burdens. Yet it also points beyond Moses to the Mediator whose hands never grow weary, who ever lives to intercede. The church is called to hold up one another's arms in prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary: The victory below is real, won by Joshua's sword — yet it depended wholly on the uplifted hands above. So our efforts matter, but their fruit hangs on the intercession of our great Mediator, who ever lives to pray for us.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
verseByVerse.commentary: The enemy of God's people is the enemy of God himself, and the LORD pledges perpetual war against him. Our battles are his; the victory is sure, for the One on the throne fights for us until every foe is subdued.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-16 — The LORD Is My Banner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God declares perpetual war against Amalek and tells Moses to record it. Moses builds an altar named "The LORD Is My Banner."
verseByVerse.theology: God himself is the banner under which his people fight and the one who secures their victory. The war against his enemies is his own.
verseByVerse.examples: Our battles are the LORD's; we rally under his banner, and the victory is his. "In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us" (Rom. 8:37).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner,
verseByVerse.commentary: The victory is credited entirely to God; the altar bears his name as banner. We do not fight for victory but from victory — rallying under the standard of the LORD who fights for us. The triumph is his, and so is the glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, Give us water to drink. And Moses said to them, Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?
verseByVerse.commentary: The third great complaint: no water. The pattern is establishing itself — need, complaint, provision — but each iteration intensifies. At Marah the water was bitter; here there is no water. The people quarrel with Moses so fiercely that he cries to God: What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me. The escalation reveals the fragility of the people's faith but also the remarkable patience of God. He does not abandon them; he does not destroy them; he provides. Faithfulness meets faithlessness with grace, again and again, as it must — because the God who made the promise to Abraham cannot let the promise fail because of the people's weakness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim... Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The battle with Amalek introduces the theology of intercessory prayer as warfare. Moses stands on the hill with his hands raised; Israel prevails. When his hands drop, Amalek gains ground. Aaron and Hur hold up his arms until sunset; Israel wins. The interceding mediator, arms stretched wide, sustaining a people in battle through prayer alone — the image is impossible to read without thinking of the one who stretched out his arms on the cross. The victory over Amalek is to be remembered forever: write it in a book, recite it to Joshua. The memory of God's deliverance is itself a weapon against future enemies.

17.theology:
Christ the struck Rock. The rock struck for water (1 Cor. 10:4) is Christ, struck by God's judgment that living water might flow to thirsting sinners.

The ministry of intercession. Moses' uplifted hands win the battle below, prefiguring Christ's ever-living intercession and the church's call to prevailing prayer.

The LORD our Banner. The battle and the victory are God's. We fight under his standard and credit the triumph to him alone.
17.examples:
Then: God brought water from a struck rock to a thirsting, doubting people, and gave victory over Amalek through the uplifted hands of Moses, held steady by Aaron and Hur until sundown.

Now: Christ our Rock was struck that the living water of the Spirit might flow to us; he ever lives, with hands once outstretched on the cross, to intercede for us. And the church wins its battles under the LORD's banner, holding up one another in prayer.

18.title: Wise Counsel and Shared Burdens
18.text: <sup>11</sup>"Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people." <sup>18</sup>"You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone." <sup>21</sup>"Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people..."
18.overview:
After the great deliverance comes a quieter but vital chapter on leadership and community. Jethro, Moses' Midianite father-in-law, hears all that God has done, comes to Moses, and rejoices, confessing, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods." Here is an early fruit of the exodus among the nations — a Gentile priest worshiping the God of Israel. The mighty acts of God draw the watching world to praise.

Then Jethro observes Moses single-handedly judging the people from morning to evening and gives wise counsel: this will wear you out; the burden is too heavy to bear alone. Appoint capable, God-fearing, trustworthy men who hate a bribe, and share the load. The principle is profound for every leader and every church: ministry is not a solo performance but a shared calling. As MacArthur notes, the wise leader multiplies himself through others, raising up and entrusting godly people with real responsibility.
