God appeals to memory and empathy: you know how it feels to be the outsider, the powerless one at the mercy of others' fairness. Let that memory make you just. A society is weighed by how it treats those who cannot repay or retaliate — and God is watching the scales.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-13 — The Sabbath Year and the Sabbath Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rhythm of rest that governs Israel's week now governs its years. Every seventh year the land itself must lie fallow, and whatever grows wild is left for the poor and the wild animals. Every seventh day, rest — so that servant and sojourner and even the ox may be refreshed. Rest is woven into creation, and it overflows in mercy: God's Sabbath is not only for the strong but for the weak and the weary.
verseByVerse.theology: Sabbath is an act of faith: to stop working is to confess that the world is upheld by God, not by our striving (cf. Ps 127:2). The seventh-year rest for the land trusts God to provide, and turns the margins over to the poor. All of it points beyond itself to the deeper rest promised in Christ: "Come to me, all who labor... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28), and finally the sabbath rest that remains for the people of God (Heb 4:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the farmer who let his field lie fallow every seventh year staked his bread on the faithfulness of God, and the poor gleaned freely from the trust.

Now: a life that never rests is a life that quietly believes everything depends on us. Sabbath rest — and the deeper rest of the gospel — frees us to stop, because Another holds the world and has finished the work that saves.

verseByVerse.quote: For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield, but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat... that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sabbath principle stretches from the day to the year, and everywhere it lands, mercy grows. Rest the land every seventh year — and notice who benefits: "the poor of your people may eat," the wild beasts too, and the fields recover. Rest every seventh day — and notice who is named: the ox, the servant's son, the sojourner, the ones most likely to be worked to the bone. God builds rest into the world and aims it especially at the weak and the weary. Behind it lies a quiet trust: the God who fed Israel with manna can be trusted to provide through a fallow year. And behind that trust stands the true rest — Christ, in whom the striving soul finally lays its burden down.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three times a year every Israelite man is to appear before the LORD: at Unleavened Bread (tied to Passover and the exodus), at the Harvest (Weeks, later Pentecost), and at Ingathering (Booths, the final harvest). Israel's calendar is a gospel calendar, a yearly rehearsal of redemption — deliverance, firstfruits, and final in-gathering — all of it fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The feasts are prophecy in the form of a calendar. Unleavened Bread proclaims redemption from bondage by the Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7); the Feast of Harvest/Weeks becomes Pentecost, the firstfruits of the Spirit's harvest (Acts 2); Ingathering looks to the great final harvest when God gathers his people home (Matt 13:39). "None shall appear before me empty-handed" (v.15) — worship comes with a gift, because grace received longs to give back.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: three times a year the roads filled with pilgrims singing their way up to the LORD, hands full of firstfruits, hearts full of the story of their rescue.

Now: every Lord's Day is our pilgrim feast — we gather before God through the true Passover Lamb, in the power of the Pentecost Spirit, longing for the final Ingathering when the harvest is home.

verseByVerse.quote: Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me... the Feast of Unleavened Bread... the Feast of Harvest... the Feast of Ingathering. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary: God fixes three yearly appointments with his people, and together they tell the whole story of salvation. Unleavened Bread looks back to the night of the exodus, redemption by the blood of the lamb. The Feast of Harvest (Weeks, which the Greeks would call Pentecost) celebrates the firstfruits of the wheat — and would one day mark the outpouring of the Spirit and the firstfruits of the church (Acts 2). Ingathering, at year's end, gathers in the full harvest, a picture of the last day when God brings all his people home. Israel's calendar was never merely agricultural; it was a rehearsal, three times a year, of what God had done, was doing, and would do. To keep the feasts was to keep telling the gospel until the Gospel himself should come.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened... The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three closing rules guard the purity of worship. Keep leaven — a picture of corruption — away from the blood of sacrifice. Bring "the best of the firstfruits," not the leftovers, for God is worthy of the first and finest. And the curious command not to "boil a young goat in its mother's milk" — likely a Canaanite fertility rite, and in any case a grotesque mingling of life (the mother's milk) with death (her kid) — a cruelty God's people must not imitate. Worship is not casual; God cares how he is approached, what we bring, and whether our devotion is tangled up with the practices of the world around us. Give him the best, and keep it clean.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-33 — The Angel and the Promise of Conquest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant book ends with a promise that thrills and warns. God will send his Angel before Israel — "my name is in him" — to guard them on the way and bring them to the land. If they obey his voice, God will be an enemy to their enemies and drive out the nations, "little by little," before them. But they must make no covenant with those nations or their gods, lest idolatry become a snare. Grace goes before them; holiness must follow.
verseByVerse.theology: The Angel in whom God's own name dwells (v.21), who must be obeyed and can pardon or refuse to pardon transgression, is no ordinary messenger — many see here a preincarnate appearing of the Son, God himself going before his people (cf. 1 Cor 10:4). The conquest "little by little" (v.30) teaches the pattern of sanctification: God gives the victory, but progressively, so that his people grow into it rather than being overwhelmed. And the ban on covenant with the nations guards the first commandment — compromise with idols is always a snare (v.33).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel marched not alone but behind the Angel of the LORD, promised victory if they would trust and obey, warned that the land's idols would trap them if they made peace with them.

Now: Christ goes before us, and our conquest of sin comes "little by little" — real, God-given, but gradual (Phil 1:6). And still the warning stands: make no peace treaty with the idols you were sent to drive out.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice... for my name is in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's parting promise is a Person. He sends his Angel ahead — but this is no ordinary messenger. "My name is in him"; he must be obeyed; he can refuse to pardon transgression. The Name of God dwells in him, the authority of God belongs to him. Many across the church have heard in these words the voice of the preincarnate Son, God himself going before his people to guard and guide them (cf. 1 Cor 10:4, "the Rock was Christ"). What comfort for pilgrims: we do not find our own way to the place God has prepared; he goes before us, bearing his own name, to bring us safely home. "I go to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2) is the same promise, from the same Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do... You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise comes with a hard line: no bowing to Canaan's gods, no imitating Canaan's ways. God will not share his people's worship, and idolatry is not a private preference but a fatal betrayal. To the obedient, rich promises follow — bread and water blessed, sickness removed, no miscarriage or barrenness, full lifespans. These are not a prosperity formula but the shape of covenant life under God's care in the land. The deep principle endures: wholehearted worship of the true God is the fountain of every real blessing, and the idols that promise life can only deliver a snare.

verseByVerse.quote: I will send my terror before you... little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land... You shall make no covenant with them and their gods... lest they make you sin against me.
verseByVerse.commentary: God promises the victory — but "little by little." He could have swept Canaan clean in a day; instead he gives the land gradually, so the wilderness will not overrun the fields and so Israel will grow into their inheritance rather than be swamped by it. Here is the pattern of the Christian life: God gives real, certain victory over sin, but progressively, teaching us to trust and to grow (Phil 1:6). And here is the perennial warning: "make no covenant with them and their gods," for tolerated sin becomes a snare (v.33). The nations you make peace with, you will one day bow to. The covenant book ends where the Christian fight always stands — sure of God's promise, sober about compromise, marching behind the Angel who bears God's name.

24.title: The Blood of the Covenant
24.text: <sup>8</sup>And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words." <sup>10</sup>and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone... <sup>11</sup>...they beheld God, and ate and drank.
24.overview:
The covenant is solemnly ratified, and the means is blood. Moses builds an altar, sacrifices are offered, and the blood is divided: half thrown against the altar (representing God), half thrown on the people, with the words "Behold the blood of the covenant." A covenant relationship between a holy God and a sinful people can be sealed only in blood. As Hebrews says, "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Heb. 9:22).

Jesus deliberately echoes this very moment at the Last Supper: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt. 26:28). The blood of bulls at Sinai could only point forward; the blood of Christ actually cleanses. Sinai's covenant is sealed in animal blood; the new covenant is sealed in the blood of the Lamb of God. Every drop at the altar of Sinai was a signpost to Calvary.

Then comes one of the most astonishing scenes in all Scripture: the elders go up the mountain and "they saw the God of Israel," and they "ate and drank" in his presence. A covenant meal in the presence of God — fellowship restored, sinners feasting before the holy One and not consumed. This covenant meal anticipates the Lord's Supper and ultimately the marriage supper of the Lamb, when the redeemed will see God face to face and eat and drink in his everlasting presence.

sections.title: The Covenant Confirmed
sections.commentary:
Moses relays all the LORD's words and rules, and the people respond with one voice: "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do." Moses writes down the words of the LORD, building an altar and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes. The covenant is not a vague spiritual sentiment but a concrete, recorded, binding agreement between God and his people, with clear terms and a wholehearted response. The written word grounds the covenant in objective, enduring revelation.

The people's confident pledge — "all that the LORD has spoken we will do" — is sincere, yet the rest of Exodus (the golden calf!) will show how quickly human resolve fails. This is precisely why the covenant must be sealed in blood: forgiveness and atonement, not human performance, will be its foundation.

sections.title: The Blood of the Covenant
sections.commentary:
Burnt offerings and peace offerings are sacrificed, and Moses takes the blood, throwing half against the altar and reading the Book of the Covenant. When the people again pledge obedience, Moses throws the other half of the blood on them: "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you." The covenant binds God and people together in blood. Sin has made a barrier that only sacrificial blood can bridge; the relationship is sealed by death.

Jesus' words at the Last Supper deliberately echo this scene: "This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt. 26:28). Hebrews makes the connection explicit (Heb. 9:18-22): the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sin, but pointed forward to the blood of Christ. Sinai's altar is a signpost to Calvary. Every covenant with God is sealed in blood — and the only blood that finally cleanses is the blood of the Lamb.

sections.title: The Covenant Meal
sections.commentary:
Then the astonishing happens: Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up the mountain and "they saw the God of Israel," with what looked like a pavement of sapphire under his feet, clear as the sky. And the text marvels: "he did not lay his hand on the chief men... they beheld God, and ate and drank." Sinners feast in the presence of the holy God and are not consumed. The covenant sealed in blood opens the way to fellowship and communion.

This covenant meal in God's presence anticipates the Lord's Supper, where we commune with the risen Christ, and ultimately the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9), when the redeemed will see God face to face and eat and drink in his everlasting joy. Ferguson notes that the goal of redemption is always communion — to see God and live, to feast in his presence forever. What was glimpsed on Sinai is our eternal destiny in Christ.

sections.title: Moses Enters the Glory
sections.commentary:
God calls Moses up to receive the tablets of stone, and the glory of the LORD settles on Sinai like a devouring fire. Moses enters the cloud and remains forty days and forty nights. The mediator goes up into the very presence of God on behalf of the people, who wait below. This pattern — a mediator ascending into God's glory for the people — points forward to Christ, who has gone up into the true sanctuary, into the presence of God, on our behalf (Heb. 9:24).

The glory like a devouring fire reminds us that this is the same holy God of the burning bush and the trembling mountain. Yet now, through covenant blood, a mediator may dwell forty days in that fire and live. The barrier of sin is being addressed; the way into God's presence is opening — a way fully opened only when Christ entered heaven itself for us.

24.theology:
The covenant sealed in blood. "Behold the blood of the covenant." A holy God and sinful people can be bound only through sacrificial blood — fulfilled in Christ's blood of the new covenant (Matt. 26:28).

Communion with God as the goal. The elders see God and eat and drink in his presence — a covenant meal anticipating the Lord's Supper and the marriage supper of the Lamb.

The mediator who ascends. Moses enters God's glory for the people, prefiguring Christ who entered heaven itself on our behalf (Heb. 9:24).
24.examples:
Then: The covenant was ratified in blood thrown on altar and people, and the elders ascended to see God and eat and drink in his presence — sinners feasting before the holy One and not consumed.

Now: The blood of bulls pointed to the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins. By that blood we are brought into communion with God, feasting at the Lord's table now and at the marriage supper of the Lamb forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-8 — The Blood of the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The laws have been given; now the covenant is sealed. The people hear all God's words and answer with one voice, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars, offers sacrifices, and does something startling: he takes the blood, throws half against the altar, reads the Book of the Covenant aloud, and throws the other half over the people, declaring, "Behold the blood of the covenant." A covenant is cut in blood — and the words Moses speaks here will fall from the lips of Jesus on the night he is betrayed.
verseByVerse.theology: Covenants in Scripture are sealed with blood, because fellowship between a holy God and sinful people can only be founded on atonement. Moses' words, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you" (v.8), are deliberately echoed by Christ: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many" (Matt 26:28; Heb 9:19-20). The blood on the people binds them to God and God to them. The old covenant's blood pointed forward; the new covenant's blood, the blood of Jesus, actually cleanses the conscience and secures the promise forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel stood sprinkled with the blood of oxen, pledged to a covenant they would soon break.

Now: we come to "the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24). At the Lord's Table we hear Moses' very words on the lips of Christ, and know that this covenant, sealed in better blood, can never be broken.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Moses, 'Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship from afar. Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but the others shall not come near.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Even in the moment of covenant, the distance is preserved. The elders may come up the mountain, but they must "worship from afar"; only Moses, the mediator, may come near. This is the great problem the whole book is circling: a holy God has drawn near to save, yet sinners cannot simply stroll into his presence. There must be a mediator, and even he approaches with trembling. All of it aches for the day when the true Mediator would come near for us and bring us near with him — "through him we... have access in one Spirit to the Father" (Eph 2:18). What the elders could only glimpse from a distance, we are invited to enter, because One went near in our place.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, 'Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Watch the covenant being sealed. The people pledge, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do and we will be obedient." Moses writes the words down, builds an altar with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, and sacrifices are offered. Then the blood: half thrown against the altar (God's side), half thrown over the people (their side) — one blood binding the two together. And Moses lifts his voice: "Behold the blood of the covenant." Hold those words, and then hear them again on a darker night, from the true Mediator: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt 26:28). Israel's vow to obey would shatter within weeks at the golden calf. But the new covenant does not rest on our fragile "we will do"; it rests on his blood, and his finished obedience in our place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-11 — They Beheld God and Ate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then something almost too wonderful to write. Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders go up, and "they saw the God of Israel." Under his feet, a pavement like sapphire, clear as the sky itself. And God "did not lay his hand" on them — sinners saw God and did not die. Instead, "they beheld God, and ate and drank." A meal, in the presence of God, sealing the covenant. This is fellowship restored, if only for an hour — a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb.
verseByVerse.theology: "No one has ever seen God" in his unveiled essence (John 1:18); what the elders saw was a gracious, veiled manifestation of his glory. The wonder is not the seeing but the surviving — "he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people." And they ate and drank: covenant fellowship is table fellowship. This meal on the mountain looks forward to the Lord's Supper and beyond it to the wedding feast of the Lamb (Rev 19:9), when the redeemed will see his face (Rev 22:4) and live.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: seventy elders sat down to eat in the presence of the God whose glory blazed above them, and lived to tell of it — covenant sealed with a shared meal.

Now: every time we come to the Table we sit and eat in the presence of God, unharmed, welcomed, at peace — because the hand that should have fallen on us fell on Christ instead.

verseByVerse.quote: and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness. And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.
verseByVerse.commentary: Pause here in wonder. Sinful men "saw the God of Israel" — not his unveiled essence, which no one can see and live (John 1:18), but a real and gracious manifestation of his glory, a pavement beneath his feet like sapphire, clear as heaven itself. And the miracle is stated almost quietly: "he did not lay his hand" on them. They should have died; they did not. Instead, "they beheld God, and ate and drank." Think of it: a meal in the presence of the Holy One, the covenant sealed not only in blood but around a table. This is what God has wanted all along — to dwell with his people and eat with them in peace. It points straight to the upper room, to the Table where we still eat in his presence, and on to the day when "they will see his face" (Rev 22:4) and sit down at the marriage supper of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 — Into the Cloud of Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls Moses higher still, to receive the stone tablets written by God's own hand. Leaving the elders and taking Joshua partway, Moses climbs into the cloud that covers the mountain. To Israel below, the glory of the LORD looked "like a devouring fire" on the summit. Moses enters the cloud and remains there forty days and forty nights, alone with God — and Israel waits at the foot of the mountain, where trouble is already brewing.
verseByVerse.theology: The tablets "written with the finger of God" (v.12; 31:18) ground the law in God's own authorship, not human invention. The glory like "a devouring fire" warns that our God "is a consuming fire" (Heb 12:29) — to draw near unatoned is to be consumed. Forty days and nights (a span echoed in Israel's wandering, Elijah, and our Lord's fast) mark a time of testing and preparation. Moses enters the fire and lives, because he goes as mediator — a shadow of the greater Mediator who entered the fire of judgment for us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses vanished into the cloud of fire for forty days, mediating between God and a people who could not bear to come near.

Now: we "have not come to a mountain that... is burning with fire" to be kept at a distance, but "to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant" (Heb 12:18, 24). The fire that would consume us fell on him; the way up the mountain is open.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, 'Come up to me on the mountain and wait there, that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction.' ... The glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai... Now the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain... Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
verseByVerse.commentary: Higher and higher God draws his servant. Moses is to receive the tablets "which I have written" — the law is not Moses' invention but God's own hand. Leaving the elders, taking Joshua partway, Moses climbs alone into the cloud, while below, Israel watches the summit blaze "like a devouring fire." Our God is glorious and holy; "our God is a consuming fire" (Heb 12:29), and no unclean thing can stand before him unconsumed. Yet Moses enters the fire and lives — because he goes as mediator, at God's own call. For forty days and nights he is hidden in the glory. It is a mountaintop of unspeakable privilege — and at its very foot, out of patience and out of sight, the people are about to melt their gold into a calf. The higher the glory on the mountain, the darker the sin in the camp. Grace and rebellion, side by side — and only a Mediator standing between.

25.title: That I May Dwell in Their Midst
25.text: <sup>8</sup>"And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst. <sup>9</sup>Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle, and of all its furniture, so you shall make it." <sup>22</sup>"There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat... I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel."
25.overview:
We arrive at the great theme that crowns the book of Exodus: God's desire to dwell with his people. "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst." The God who came down to deliver now wants to come down to stay. The whole apparatus of the tabernacle exists for one stunning purpose — that the infinite, holy God might dwell among his redeemed people. This is the heartbeat of the gospel: God with us.

The instructions begin with a freewill offering — God's house is built by willing hearts — and then with the most sacred objects. First the Ark of the Covenant, overlaid with gold, with the mercy seat above it and two cherubim, where God promises, "There I will meet with you." The mercy seat (the kapporet) is where the blood of atonement is sprinkled — and Paul says Christ is our "mercy seat" (Rom. 3:25, hilasterion), the place where God's justice and mercy meet. Then the table of the bread of the Presence and the golden lampstand, each rich with meaning.

Crucially, everything must be made "exactly as I show you concerning the pattern." The tabernacle is a copy of a heavenly reality (Heb. 8:5). It points beyond itself — first to the incarnation, where the Word "tabernacled among us" (John 1:14), and finally to the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man" (Rev. 21:3). All of it whispers: God wants to be with you.

sections.title: The Freewill Offering
sections.commentary:
God begins not by conscripting materials but by inviting them: "from every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution." God's dwelling is built by willing, generous hearts — a principle Paul takes up in 2 Corinthians 9:7, "God loves a cheerful giver." The materials are listed in lavish detail: gold, silver, bronze, fine linen, precious stones. The redeemed give back to God from the very wealth he provided when they plundered Egypt. Grace received overflows in generous giving.

The purpose is breathtaking: "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst." Here is the goal of the whole exodus. God did not redeem his people merely to free them from Egypt but to dwell among them forever. And it must be built "exactly as I show you concerning the pattern" — the earthly tabernacle is a copy of a heavenly reality (Heb. 8:5), pointing beyond itself to greater things.

sections.title: The Ark of the Covenant
sections.commentary:
The most sacred object comes first: the Ark, an acacia chest overlaid inside and out with pure gold, containing the testimony (the tablets of the law). Upon it rests the mercy seat (kapporet), with two cherubim of gold facing one another, their wings overshadowing it. Here, above the mercy seat, between the cherubim, God promises to meet with his people: "There I will meet with you... I will speak with you." The throne of God on earth is a throne of mercy resting upon the law.

The mercy seat is where, on the Day of Atonement, the blood of sacrifice was sprinkled, covering the broken law beneath. Paul declares that Christ is our hilasterion — our mercy seat (Rom. 3:25) — the place where the blood is applied and God's wrath is propitiated. Sproul taught that here, supremely, the justice of God (the law) and the mercy of God (the blood-covered seat) meet. The Ark is a gospel sermon in gold and acacia: God meets sinners only at the place of atonement, fulfilled in Christ.

sections.title: The Table of the Bread of the Presence
sections.commentary:
The golden table holds the bread of the Presence — twelve loaves representing the twelve tribes, continually before the LORD. It signifies that God's people live always in his presence and that he provides for them, feeding them and welcoming them to his table. The bread set before God's face speaks of fellowship and communion: a perpetual meal in the presence of God.

The bread points forward to Christ, the bread of the Presence and the bread of life (John 6:35), and to the table of the Lord where we commune with him. God's people are always before his face, always provided for, always invited to feast in his presence. The table foreshadows the eternal communion of the redeemed.

sections.title: The Golden Lampstand
sections.commentary:
The lampstand (menorah) of pure hammered gold, with its branches like an almond tree in bloom, gives light continually in the holy place. It signifies God as the light of his people and the light of his presence that never goes out. The intricate beauty — buds, blossoms, almond flowers — reflects the glory and life of God's presence. Light in the sanctuary means life, guidance, and the radiance of God himself.

The lampstand anticipates Christ, the light of the world (John 8:12), and the church, called to be lampstands bearing his light (Rev. 1:20). In the New Jerusalem there will be no need of sun or lamp, "for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb" (Rev. 21:23). The light that burned in the holy place will blaze forever in the presence of God. And again the refrain: make it "after the pattern" shown on the mountain — earthly worship copying heavenly reality.

25.theology:
God's desire to dwell with his people. "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst." The goal of redemption is God's presence — fulfilled in the incarnation and the New Jerusalem.

The mercy seat and atonement. God meets sinners only at the blood-covered mercy seat, where justice and mercy meet — fulfilled in Christ our hilasterion (Rom. 3:25).

Worship after the heavenly pattern. The tabernacle is a copy of a heavenly reality (Heb. 8:5), pointing beyond itself to Christ and to the eternal dwelling of God with man.
25.examples:
Then: God commanded a sanctuary, built by willing hearts after a heavenly pattern, so that he might dwell among his redeemed people — with the Ark and its blood-covered mercy seat as the throne where he would meet them.

Now: God's great desire is still to dwell with his people. The tabernacle pointed to Christ, in whom the fullness of God tabernacled among us, and to the day when the dwelling of God will be with man forever. We meet God only at the mercy seat — at the cross of Christ, where mercy and justice embrace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The Freewill Offering and the Pattern
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new movement begins that will fill most of the rest of Exodus: the building of the tabernacle, God's tent among his people. It opens not with a tax but with an invitation — an offering from "every man whose heart moves him." God funds his dwelling with willing gifts. And the reason is breathtaking: "let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst" (v.8). The whole exodus has been driving toward this — not merely to get Israel out of Egypt, but to get God into their midst.
verseByVerse.theology: The purpose of redemption is the presence of God: "that I may dwell in their midst." The tabernacle is built "after the pattern" shown to Moses (v.9), the earthly copy of a heavenly reality (Heb 8:5) — which means every detail is prophecy, pointing to Christ, in whom "the Word became flesh and dwelt [tabernacled] among us" (John 1:14). God delights in freewill giving, not grudging duty (2 Cor 9:7): grace in the heart overflows as gladness in the hand.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the people brought gold, blue and purple yarn, ram skins and acacia wood — Egypt's plunder now poured out for God's house, each gift moved by a willing heart.

Now: God still builds his dwelling — now a temple of living stones (1 Pet 2:5) — from willing gifts. And the goal is unchanged: God with us, God in us, God forever in our midst.

verseByVerse.quote: Speak to the people of Israel, that they take for me a contribution. From every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution for me... And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst. Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle... so you shall make it.
verseByVerse.commentary: Everything the book has been building toward is spoken in one line: "let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst." God did not rescue Israel from Egypt merely to be free; he rescued them to live among them. The whole point of the exodus is a Presence. And how is his house funded? Not by compulsion but by generosity — "from every man whose heart moves him." God loves a willing gift (2 Cor 9:7). The materials are Egypt's plunder (12:36), the wealth of their captivity now consecrated to their Deliverer. Above all, it must be built "according to the pattern" God shows Moses on the mountain — for this tent is a copy of a heavenly original (Heb 8:5). That means every board and basin is a sermon, and the whole structure whispers one Name. When John writes that the Word "dwelt among us" (literally, "tabernacled," John 1:14), he is telling us who the tabernacle was always about.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-22 — The Ark and the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the very center, in the Most Holy Place, stands the ark: a gold-covered chest holding the testimony (the tablets of the law), crowned by the mercy seat and two cherubim of hammered gold. Here God makes his promise: "There I will meet with you... from between the two cherubim" (v.22). The mercy seat — the atonement cover — is the throne of God on earth, where blood would cover the broken law beneath, and where holiness and mercy meet.
verseByVerse.theology: The mercy seat (Hebrew kapporet, "place of atonement") is where God meets sinners — over the broken law, but under the sprinkled blood (Lev 16:14-15). Paul takes its Greek name, hilasterion, and gives it to Christ: God "put [him] forward as a propitiation [the mercy seat] by his blood" (Rom 3:25). The law inside accuses; the blood on top atones; the God enthroned above meets his people in mercy. Christ is all three at once — the law kept, the blood shed, the meeting place opened. This little golden box is the gospel in gold.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: once a year the high priest sprinkled blood on the mercy seat, and God met Israel there and did not consume them.

Now: "we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus" (Heb 10:19). The true mercy seat is a Person; the meeting place is thrown open, and we come not once a year but every hour.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold... And you shall put the mercy seat on the top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the testimony that I shall give you. There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here, at the heart of the tent, is the throne of God on earth. The ark is a chest of acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, holding "the testimony" — the tablets of the law. On top sits the mercy seat, the atonement cover, with two cherubim of hammered gold bowed over it, their wings touching, their faces down. And God speaks the great promise: "There I will meet with you." Consider what this means. Inside the box is the law we have broken, our accusation in stone. But God does not meet us at the law; he meets us at the mercy seat above it — and on the Day of Atonement that cover would be drenched in blood (Lev 16). Between the broken law below and the holy God above, blood and mercy. This is the exact shape of the gospel. Paul reaches for the Greek name of this very object, hilasterion, when he writes that God set forth Christ "as a propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25). Jesus is the true mercy seat, where the law we shattered is covered by the blood he shed, and where God meets us and does not condemn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-30 — The Table of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the Holy Place stands a golden table bearing twelve loaves, the "bread of the Presence," set out before the LORD continually. Twelve loaves for twelve tribes, always on the table, always before God's face. It is a picture of covenant fellowship — God's people kept perpetually in his presence, and God spreading a table before them.
verseByVerse.theology: The bread of the Presence (literally "bread of the face") keeps all Israel — twelve tribes, twelve loaves — continually before God, a standing sign of covenant communion. It anticipates the One who is "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and the table he spreads for his people. Where God dwells, there is a table; fellowship with God is feast, not famine (Ps 23:5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: fresh loaves lay before God's face week by week, the twelve tribes represented, fed, remembered, never out of his sight.

Now: Christ is our bread, and he sets a table before us. To be his is to be kept perpetually in the presence of God and fed from his own hand.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall make a table of acacia wood... and overlay it with pure gold... And you shall set the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly.
verseByVerse.commentary: Across from the lampstand stands a golden table, and on it, always, the "bread of the Presence" — literally the "bread of the face," bread set before the very face of God. There were twelve loaves (Lev 24:5-6), one for each tribe, laid out fresh each Sabbath and never absent. Think of what it pictures: all Israel, all the time, kept before God's face — remembered, represented, welcomed to his table. Where the LORD dwells, he does not merely tolerate his people; he feeds them and keeps them in his presence. The table is a standing promise of communion. And it points forward to the One who said, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger" (John 6:35), and who still spreads a table before us in the presence of our God (Ps 23:5). Fellowship with God is not a bare audience; it is a feast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Opposite the table stands the lampstand (the menorah), a single piece of hammered pure gold, its central shaft branching into six arms, each cup shaped like an almond blossom, its seven lamps giving light in the Holy Place. There is no window here; the only light is this golden tree of flame. It speaks of God as the light of his sanctuary, and points to Christ the true light and to his people who shine with his.
verseByVerse.theology: The lampstand is the sanctuary's only light — a golden, living tree of fire, hammered from one piece, blossoming like almond (the first tree to wake in spring, Jer 1:11-12). It images God as the light in whom his people see (Ps 36:9), fulfilled in Christ, "the light of the world" (John 8:12). In Revelation the lampstands become the churches (Rev 1:20) — called not to make their own light but to bear his, burning with oil the Spirit supplies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: in a room with no window, the golden lampstand burned continually, the only light by which the priests could serve.

Now: Christ is our light, and we are his lampstands (Rev 1:20; Matt 5:14) — not the source, but the vessel, shining in a dark place with a borrowed, Spirit-fed flame.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand shall be made of hammered work: its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers shall be of one piece with it... You shall make seven lamps for it... And see that you make them after the pattern... which is being shown you on the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Holy Place has no window; its only light is this — a lampstand of pure gold, hammered from a single piece, its central stem branching into six arms, every cup shaped like an almond blossom, seven lamps burning at the top. It is a golden tree of fire. The almond is striking: it is the first tree to flower in spring, the "watching" tree (Jer 1:11-12), so the lampstand blossoms like life waking from winter. In a windowless room, God provides the light by which his servants may see and serve — a picture of the God "in [whose] light do we see light" (Ps 36:9). It points to Jesus, "the light of the world" (John 8:12), and to his people: in Revelation these lampstands become the churches (Rev 1:20), called to shine — not with light of our own, but bearing his, kept burning by the oil of his Spirit. Once more comes the refrain: make it "after the pattern" shown on the mountain. Nothing here is human invention; it is all heaven's design, and it all leads to Christ.

26.title: The Way into the Presence
26.text: <sup>1</sup>"Moreover, you shall make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns; you shall make them with cherubim skillfully worked into them." <sup>33</sup>"And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy."
26.overview:
The instructions turn to the structure of the tabernacle itself — its curtains, frames, and coverings, and above all its veil. To modern readers the architectural detail can seem tedious, but every measurement and material preaches a sermon about how a holy God may be approached by sinful people. The tabernacle is a graded structure of increasing holiness: the outer court, the Holy Place, and the Most Holy Place where God's presence dwells above the Ark.

The most theologically charged feature is the veil — "the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy." This thick curtain, embroidered with cherubim, barred the way into God's immediate presence. Only the high priest could pass through it, and only once a year, and only with blood. The veil declared, in fabric, the great problem of the universe: sinners cannot come to a holy God. There is a barrier, guarded by cherubim, just as cherubim guarded the way back to Eden (Gen. 3:24).

And here the gospel breaks in with glory. When Christ died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt. 27:51). The veil that barred the way was rent — by God, from the top — when Christ's flesh was torn. Hebrews says we now enter the Most Holy Place "by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh" (Heb. 10:20). The whole structure of the tabernacle cries out: there is a way into the presence of God, and it is Christ.

sections.title: The Inner Curtains
sections.commentary:
The tabernacle's beauty is hidden, seen only from within. The innermost curtains are of fine twined linen in blue, purple, and scarlet, with cherubim skillfully woven in — a glimpse of heavenly glory for those who draw near. Over these are layers of goats' hair, ram skins dyed red, and durable leather, protecting the glory within from the harsh wilderness. The most glorious things are reserved for those who enter; the outside is plain and weather-worn.

So it is with the things of God: the world sees a humble exterior, but those who draw near behold glory. The cherubim woven into the curtains remind the worshiper that he is entering the realm of heaven, the dwelling of the God whom angels serve. Every fiber of the tabernacle is saturated with meaning, declaring that this is holy space, set apart for the presence of God.

sections.title: The Framework
sections.commentary:
The frames of acacia wood overlaid with gold, set in silver bases, give the structure its standing strength. Each board fits precisely into its neighbor, bound together with bars, forming one stable dwelling. The careful joinery preaches the unity and order of God's house — many parts fitted into one structure to house the divine presence. Paul will later describe the church as a building "joined together" and "growing into a holy temple in the Lord" (Eph. 2:21).

And again the standard is exactness: "set up the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain." Nothing is left to human invention. Worship is to be ordered by God's revelation, not human imagination — a principle that runs through all of Scripture. God determines how he is to be approached.

sections.title: The Veil and the Most Holy Place
sections.commentary:
The climax of the chapter is the veil: "the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy." This thick curtain, embroidered with cherubim, hung between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place where the Ark and the presence of God dwelt. Only the high priest could pass through it, only once a year, only with blood. The cherubim woven into it recall the cherubim guarding Eden (Gen. 3:24): the way back to God's immediate presence is barred to sinners.

The veil proclaimed the great problem of the cosmos in cloth: sinful humanity cannot come to the holy God. But when Christ died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt. 27:51) — torn by God himself, from heaven down, as the flesh of Christ was torn. Hebrews 10:19-20 declares that we now have confidence to enter the holy places "by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh." The barrier is gone. In Christ, the way into the presence of God is open forever.

sections.title: One House, One People, One Way
sections.commentary:
The tabernacle's many parts — curtains, frames, bars, veil — are fitted into a single dwelling for the one God, foreshadowing the church, "joined together" and "growing into a holy temple in the Lord" (Eph. 2:21). The hidden glory within, seen only by those who enter, pictures the truth that the world sees a humble exterior while those who draw near behold the glory of God.

Above all, the veil declares both the barrier of sin and, in light of the cross, the open way. What Sinai's fire and the tabernacle's veil kept closed, the torn flesh of Christ has opened forever (Heb. 10:19-20). The whole structure preaches the gospel: there is one God, one people, and one way into his presence — and that way is Christ.

26.theology:
The holiness of God and the barrier of sin. The graded structure and the veil declare that sinners cannot casually approach the holy God; there is a barrier, guarded by cherubim as at Eden.

Christ the torn veil. At the cross the veil was torn from top to bottom (Matt. 27:51). We enter God's presence through the new and living way of Christ's flesh (Heb. 10:20).

Worship after the pattern. The tabernacle is built exactly as God commanded — worship is governed by God's revelation, not human invention.
26.examples:
Then: God commanded a tabernacle of hidden glory, ordered exactly to his pattern, whose veil — embroidered with cherubim like those guarding Eden — barred the way into his immediate presence.

Now: The veil declared that sinners cannot approach a holy God. But at the cross that veil was torn from top to bottom. Through the torn flesh of Christ, the way into God's presence is open forever. We who once stood outside now draw near with confidence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tent itself takes shape. Ten inner curtains of fine linen, embroidered blue and purple and scarlet with cherubim, form the beautiful ceiling seen from within. Over them, curtains of goats' hair; over those, a covering of ram skins dyed red; and over all, an outer layer of tough weatherproof hide. Glory within, plainness without — the humble outside gives no hint of the shimmering beauty inside, where God dwells.
verseByVerse.theology: The layered tent preaches a pattern that runs to the incarnation: outside, nothing to attract the eye; inside, the beauty of God. So it was with Christ, who had "no form or majesty that we should look at him" (Isa 53:2), yet was full of glory (John 1:14). The cherubim woven into the ceiling remind the worshiper that heaven itself overshadows this place. Beauty and holiness belong together in God's house, but the glory is within, seen only by those who enter.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a traveler passing by saw only a plain tent of dark hides; the priest who entered stood beneath a canopy of angels and glory.

Now: the world sees little to admire in Christ or his church from the outside; but those brought within discover "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (Eph 3:8) — a glory hidden to the casual eye, unveiled to the one who enters.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, you shall make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns; you shall make them with cherubim skillfully worked... You shall also make curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle... a covering of tanned rams' skins and a covering of goatskins on top.
verseByVerse.commentary: God cares about the details of his dwelling, down to the loops and clasps. The innermost layer, the ceiling the priests would look up into, is a masterpiece: fine linen shot through with blue, purple, and scarlet, and worked all over with cherubim — so that inside, the worshiper stands beneath a woven heaven of angels. But over that beauty lie three plainer coverings: goats' hair, red ram skins, and a tough outer hide against the weather. From outside, the tabernacle looked like nothing — a dark, unimpressive tent. All its glory was inside, hidden, for those who entered. Here is a pattern God loves. His Son would come with "no form or majesty that we should look at him" (Isa 53:2), his glory veiled in ordinary flesh — and only those who came near beheld "glory as of the only Son from the Father" (John 1:14). God's richest beauty is often wrapped in the plainest exterior, and is found by those who go in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tent needs a skeleton. Upright frames of acacia wood, overlaid with gold, stand in sockets of silver, joined by golden bars running through golden rings. Each board rests on two bases of silver — and that silver came from the atonement money of the people (30:11-16). The whole structure literally stands on redemption. Beauty needs a frame; glory needs a foundation, and the foundation is silver bought with the price of ransomed lives.
verseByVerse.theology: Every gold-covered frame rests on silver bases drawn from the census "ransom" money (30:11-16, 38:25-28) — so the dwelling of God stands, quite literally, upon the price of atonement. The many separate boards, joined by bars into one structure, picture the many members made one house (Eph 2:21-22). Individually they would fall; bound together and grounded on redemption, they stand as the dwelling place of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: not one gold frame touched the desert sand; each stood on silver bought with ransom money — the whole house upheld by the price of redeemed souls.

Now: the church is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Eph 2:20). We stand only on redemption, joined to one another, or we do not stand at all.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall make upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood... And you shall make bars of acacia wood... you shall overlay the frames with gold... their bases of silver... Then you shall erect the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary: The shimmering curtains need a frame to hold them up, and here it is: tall boards of acacia wood, each overlaid with gold, standing upright and joined by gilded bars threaded through golden rings into one rigid, gleaming wall. But look down at what every board stands on — bases of solid silver. That silver is not random: it came from the atonement money, the half-shekel "ransom for his life" each Israelite paid (30:11-16; 38:25-28). So the entire house of God rests, board by board, on the price of redemption. Not one frame touches the bare ground; all of it is upheld by the silver of ransomed lives. And notice the boards are many but bound into one. Alone, a single frame would topple; joined together and grounded on atonement, they become the dwelling of God. It is the very picture Paul draws of the church, "joined together... into a holy temple in the Lord... a dwelling place for God by the Spirit" (Eph 2:21-22). And once more: "according to the plan... shown on the mountain."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-37 — The Veil and the Screen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two hangings divide the tent. The veil — blue, purple, scarlet, worked with cherubim — separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, barring the way to the ark and the presence of God. A second screen hangs at the entrance. The message of the veil is solemn: the way into God's presence is not yet open. But the day would come when that veil, in the true temple, would be torn from top to bottom.
verseByVerse.theology: The veil, embroidered with cherubim like the angel who guarded Eden (Gen 3:24), says plainly: sinners may not simply enter God's presence — "the way into the holy places" was "not yet opened" (Heb 9:8). But when Jesus died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt 27:51) — torn by God, from heaven down, His own hand opening the way. "By the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh" (Heb 10:20), we now enter with boldness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the veil hung like a closed door, cherubim woven across it, warning every worshiper that the presence beyond was barred.

Now: the veil is torn. The barred road into the Holiest is a highway. "Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace" (Heb 4:16) — a boldness bought with the tearing of Christ's flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall make a veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It shall be made with cherubim skillfully worked into it... And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy... And you shall make a screen for the entrance of the tent.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two hangings guard the way inward. At the tent's entrance, a screen; and deeper in, the veil — a thick, beautiful curtain of blue, purple, and scarlet, worked all over with cherubim, dividing the Holy Place from the Most Holy, where the ark and the mercy seat stand. Do not miss the cherubim woven into it. Ever since Eden, cherubim have stood guard over the way to God, sword in hand at the gate of the garden (Gen 3:24). The veil says the same thing they said: you cannot come in. The way to the presence of God is barred to sinners — "the way into the holy places is not yet opened" (Heb 9:8). For centuries that curtain hung like a closed door. Then, on the day the true sacrifice died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt 27:51) — not ripped by human hands from below, but by God's hand from above, the whole barrier undone in an instant. Christ's flesh, torn on the cross, is the new and living way through the veil (Heb 10:19-20). The cherubim have stepped aside. The road home is open.

27.title: The Altar Where Blood Is Shed
27.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square... <sup>2</sup>and you shall overlay it with bronze." <sup>20</sup>"...that they may bring to you pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn."
27.overview:
The first thing a worshiper encountered upon entering the courtyard of the tabernacle was the great bronze altar — and this placement is no accident. Before anyone could draw near to God, before any approach to the Holy Place, there had to be sacrifice. The altar of burnt offering stood at the entrance, declaring that the way to God begins at the place where blood is shed. There is no fellowship with the holy God except through atonement.

The altar was made of acacia wood overlaid with bronze — bronze, the metal that can endure fire, for here the fire of God's judgment fell upon the substitute. Day after day, sacrifice after sacrifice, the blood flowed. Hebrews reminds us that these endless sacrifices could never finally take away sin (Heb. 10:11); they pointed forward to the one sacrifice that would. The bronze altar at the gate is a signpost to the cross at the entrance of our salvation.

The chapter also describes the courtyard with its linen hangings and the oil for the lamp that must burn continually. The court sets apart sacred space; the perpetual light signifies God's unceasing presence and the worship that never stops. As MacArthur observes, every detail of the tabernacle preaches the same gospel: a holy God, sinful people, and the blood that opens the way between them — all fulfilled in Christ, who is at once the altar, the sacrifice, and the light.

sections.title: The Bronze Altar
sections.commentary:
The altar of burnt offering, five cubits square and overlaid with bronze, stood at the very entrance of the tabernacle court. Its placement preaches a sermon: before anyone could approach the presence of God, they had to pass the altar of sacrifice. The way to God begins at the place where blood is shed. There is no entry into fellowship with the holy God except through atonement — a truth woven into the very geography of worship.

Bronze is the metal that endures fire, and here the fire of divine judgment fell — not on the worshiper, but on the substitute laid upon the altar. The horns of the altar, the basins for blood, the grate for the fire: every feature served the shedding and offering of blood. Hebrews teaches that these endless sacrifices could never finally take away sin (Heb. 10:11), but pointed to the one sacrifice of Christ, who bore the fire of judgment in our place. The bronze altar is the cross in shadow.

sections.title: The Court of the Tabernacle
sections.commentary:
The courtyard, enclosed with fine linen hangings on bronze-based posts, sets apart sacred space from the common world. Within this enclosure stood the altar and the laver, and beyond, the tent of meeting. The single gate on the east side — one way in — reminds us that there is one appointed way to approach God, not many. Jesus declares, "I am the door" (John 10:9) and "I am the way" (John 14:6). There is one entrance to the presence of God.

The white linen surrounding the court speaks of the purity required to approach God, a purity no sinner possesses in himself but which is provided through the sacrifice within. The boundary declares that God's presence is holy ground; one cannot wander in carelessly. Access is real, but it is on God's terms — through the one gate, past the one altar.

sections.title: The Oil for the Lamp
sections.commentary:
The people are to bring pure beaten olive oil so that the lamp may burn continually, from evening to morning, before the LORD. The perpetual light signifies the unceasing presence of God among his people and the worship that never ceases. Even in the darkness of night, the light burns in the holy place — God's presence does not sleep, and the worship of his people is to be constant.

The continual light anticipates Christ, the light that shines in the darkness and is never overcome (John 1:5), and the church, called to keep the lamp of witness burning. It points to the eternal day of the New Jerusalem, where the Lamb is the lamp and there is no night at all (Rev. 21:23-25). The light that burned in the tent foreshadows the unending light of God's presence among his redeemed.

sections.title: From Altar to Presence: The Gospel Geography of Worship
sections.commentary:
The court of the tabernacle lays out the gospel in space. One enters through a single gate, comes first to the bronze altar of sacrifice, then to the laver of cleansing, and only then approaches the holy place lit by the continual lamp. Sacrifice, cleansing, and light — the order is the order of salvation: atonement, purification, and the illumination of God's presence.

Every step points to Christ, who is the one door (John 10:9), the sacrifice on the altar, the cleansing water, and the light of the world (John 8:12). MacArthur notes that nothing in the tabernacle is arbitrary; the very layout preaches that the way to God runs through the blood, leads through cleansing, and ends in the light of his presence — fulfilled wholly in Christ.

27.theology:
No approach to God without sacrifice. The bronze altar at the gate declares that the way to God begins at the place of shed blood — fulfilled in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.

One appointed way. The single gate and altar prefigure Christ, the one door and the one way to the Father (John 10:9; 14:6).

The unceasing presence and light of God. The continual lamp signifies God's constant presence and unending worship, fulfilled in Christ the light and the eternal day of the New Jerusalem.
27.examples:
Then: At the entrance to God's dwelling stood the bronze altar, where the fire of judgment fell on the substitute — declaring that no one approaches the holy God except through shed blood, past the one appointed gate.

Now: The cross stands at the entrance of our salvation: there is no fellowship with God except through the sacrifice of Christ, the true altar and Lamb. He is the one door, the one way, and the light that burns forever. We approach God only through him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before anyone reaches the beauty within, they meet the altar. Standing in the courtyard, the great bronze altar of burnt offering is the first thing encountered on the way to God — and it is a place of blood and fire. There is no approach to the holy God except by sacrifice. The road to the mercy seat begins at the altar.
verseByVerse.theology: The altar's position teaches the order of the gospel: the way to God begins with atoning sacrifice. Bronze, which endures fire, speaks of judgment borne. No one enters the courtyard, let alone the Holy Place, without first passing the place where a substitute dies. It all points to the cross, the true altar, where "Christ... gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2). We come to God only over the ashes of a sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the worshiper's first step toward God was a slain animal on a bronze altar, smoke rising, blood poured out.

Now: we come to God by one sacrifice, once for all (Heb 10:12). The altar still stands at the entrance — but the offering has been made, and we come through the blood already shed.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square... and you shall overlay it with bronze... You shall make it hollow, with boards.
verseByVerse.commentary: Step through the gate into the courtyard, and the very first thing you meet is not beauty but an altar — a large square structure of acacia wood sheathed in bronze, with horns at its corners and a grate for the fire. This is the altar of burnt offering, and its position preaches. Before a worshiper can reach the golden furniture, before he can approach the veil, he must pass this place of blood and fire. There is no way to the holy God except over a sacrifice. Bronze is the metal that stands up to fire; it speaks of judgment endured. Here the substitute died and burned in the sinner's place, its smoke rising as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD." Every approach to God began here, at the cost of a life. And it all points to the cross, the true altar, where "Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2). We still come to God only one way: past the altar, through the blood of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-19 — The Court of the Tabernacle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Around the tent stretches a courtyard, enclosed by hangings of fine linen on bronze posts, with a single gate on the east side. The white linen wall marks off holy space from common ground; the one gate says there is a way in — but only one. God is separate, yet God has opened an entrance.
verseByVerse.theology: The white linen wall (righteousness, cf. Rev 19:8) marks the boundary between the holy and the common; the single gate declares that access is real but exclusive — "I am the door" (John 10:9), "no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). The courtyard holds together two truths the world tries to divide: God is holy and set apart, and God has opened a way in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: an Israelite could not scale the linen wall wherever he pleased; he came through the one appointed gate, or not at all.

Now: there is one way to God, and he stands open like a door: "whoever enters by me will be saved" (John 10:9). The exclusivity is not cruelty; it is a gate flung wide.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall make the court of the tabernacle... the hangings for the court shall be of fine twined linen... And for the gate of the court a screen of twenty cubits, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns... All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use... shall be of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary: A wall of brilliant white linen, hung on bronze posts, encloses the sacred space — a clean boundary between the holy and the common, the courtyard of God marked off from the dust of the ordinary world. That white linen speaks of purity and righteousness (cf. Rev 19:8): to come near, one must cross into cleanness. But the wall is not unbroken. On the east side is a gate, a colorful screen of blue and purple and scarlet, and it is the only way in. Not many gates — one. You could not slip in at any point you chose; you came through the appointed entrance or you did not enter at all. This is not narrowness for its own sake; it is grace with an address. Jesus takes the image and makes it personal: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved" (John 10:9); "no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). One gate — but it stands wide open to all who will come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with a small, tender command: the people are to bring pure beaten olive oil so that the lamp may burn continually, tended by Aaron and his sons "from evening to morning before the LORD." In the darkness, the light must never go out — a perpetual flame kept burning through every night.
verseByVerse.theology: The continual lamp, fed by pure oil and tended by the priests, pictures worship and witness that must never be allowed to die — kept burning through the dark hours. Oil throughout Scripture is a sign of the Holy Spirit (cf. Zech 4:2-6); the light shines only as the oil is supplied. So the church's light endures not by its own resources but by the Spirit's continual provision, and by the faithful, nightly tending of those who serve.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: every evening the priests trimmed and fueled the lamp so that a flame burned before God all night long, never extinguished.

Now: the light of witness is kept alive by the oil of the Spirit and the faithfulness of God's servants through the long night of this age — "let your light shine" (Matt 5:16), and keep it fed.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall command the people of Israel that they bring to you pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn. In the tent of meeting... Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening to morning before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: After the grand structures, a small and beautiful instruction: bring pure, beaten olive oil so the lamp will never go dark. The oil must be the best — "pure beaten" — and the priests must tend the flame "from evening to morning," all through the night, so that a light always burns before God. In the windowless Holy Place, and through the dark hours, the flame is never allowed to die. There is gospel comfort in this perpetual light: God is never in the dark, and his testimony never goes out. Oil, all through Scripture, is a picture of the Holy Spirit (Zech 4:2-6), and the lamp shines only as long as the oil is supplied. So the light of God's people burns not by our own strength but by the Spirit's constant provision, tended by faithful hands through the night of this world — until the morning breaks and we need the lamp no more, "for the Lord God will be their light" (Rev 22:5).

28.title: Israel on the High Priest's Heart
28.text: <sup>12</sup>"And you shall set the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. And Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance." <sup>29</sup>"So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD."
28.overview:
God now turns to the priesthood, designing garments for Aaron the high priest "for glory and for beauty." Every thread is rich with meaning, but the most moving detail is this: the names of the twelve tribes of Israel are engraved on precious stones and worn by the high priest — on his shoulders and over his heart — whenever he enters the presence of God. The high priest carries the people into God's presence, bearing them on the place of strength (the shoulders) and the place of love (the heart).

What a tender picture of mediation. Aaron does not enter for himself alone; he enters representing the people, bearing their names before the LORD "for remembrance." When God looks upon the high priest, he sees his people named and carried into his presence. This is the very essence of the gospel: we come to God not on our own standing but borne upon the heart of our Great High Priest.

For Jesus is the fulfillment. He is the High Priest who has "passed through the heavens" (Heb. 4:14), bearing our names — bearing us — into the very presence of God. He carries his people on his shoulders like the shepherd seeking the lost sheep, and on his heart like the bridegroom cherishing his bride. As Ferguson says, the believer's deepest comfort is that Christ ever lives, with our names engraved on his heart, to appear in the presence of God for us (Heb. 9:24). The breastpiece also bore the Urim and Thummim for discerning God's will, and a gold plate on the turban read "Holy to the LORD" — for the priest must represent a holy people to a holy God.

sections.title: Garments for Glory and Beauty
sections.commentary:
God sets apart Aaron and his sons to serve as priests and commands holy garments "for glory and for beauty," made by craftsmen filled with the Spirit of skill. The priesthood is God's gracious provision: sinful people cannot approach him directly, so he appoints mediators to stand between. The beauty and glory of the garments reflect the dignity of the office and the holiness of the God they serve. Nothing shabby or careless will do in the presence of the Holy One.

The very existence of the priesthood declares a profound truth: we need a mediator. Left to ourselves, we cannot come to God. The whole institution points forward to the one who would be both priest and sacrifice — Christ, our Great High Priest, who needs no successor because he lives forever (Heb. 7:24-25).

sections.title: The Ephod and the Breastpiece
sections.commentary:
The most moving feature of the priestly garments is the bearing of Israel's names. Two onyx stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod are engraved with the names of the twelve tribes, "stones of remembrance," so that "Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance." And the breastpiece of judgment, set with twelve precious stones, also bears the tribal names, so that "Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart" whenever he enters the Holy Place.

Here is mediation at its most tender. The high priest carries the people into God's presence — on his shoulders, the place of strength, and on his heart, the place of love. When God looks upon the priest, he sees his people named, carried, remembered. Jesus fulfills this perfectly: our Great High Priest bears us on his shoulders like the shepherd who finds his lost sheep, and on his heart like the bridegroom who cherishes his bride. Our names are engraved on his heart as he appears in the presence of God for us (Heb. 9:24). The breastpiece also held the Urim and Thummim, by which God's will was discerned — the priest mediated not only the people to God but God's guidance to the people.

sections.title: The Robe, the Turban, and the Holy Crown
sections.commentary:
The robe is fringed with golden bells and pomegranates, so that the sound is heard when the priest enters and leaves the Holy Place — a sign that he goes in and comes out alive, accepted on behalf of the people. Most striking is the gold plate on the turban, engraved "Holy to the LORD," worn on Aaron's forehead so that he may "bear any guilt" connected with the holy things and the people be accepted before the LORD.

The plate declares the necessity of holiness in approaching God, and the priest's role in bearing the guilt of the people so they may be accepted. This points unmistakably to Christ, who bore our guilt (Isa. 53:6) and is himself "Holy to the LORD," the spotless High Priest who makes us acceptable to God. Every garment, from the engraved stones to the holy crown, declares that we are brought to God only through a mediator who bears us, bears our guilt, and is himself holy. That mediator is Christ.

sections.title: The High Priest as a Portrait of Christ
sections.commentary:
Taken together, the priestly garments form a complete portrait of mediation fulfilled in Christ. The names borne on shoulder and heart show the priest carrying his people into God's presence by strength and love; the Urim and Thummim show him mediating God's guidance to the people; the plate "Holy to the LORD" shows him bearing their guilt that they might be accepted. Every element points beyond Aaron to a greater High Priest.

Hebrews gathers it all into Christ, who has passed through the heavens (4:14), bears us into the presence of God (9:24), is himself holy and undefiled (7:26), and ever lives to intercede for us (7:25). The believer's deepest comfort, as Ferguson says, is that our names are engraved on the heart of our great High Priest, who appears in the presence of God on our behalf — and is himself "Holy to the LORD."

28.theology:
The necessity of a mediator. The priesthood exists because sinners cannot approach God directly. We need one to stand between — fulfilled in Christ, our Great High Priest.

Borne on the heart of the priest. The high priest carries Israel's names on his shoulders and heart into God's presence — a picture of Christ who bears us, by strength and love, before the Father (Heb. 9:24).

Holiness and the bearing of guilt. "Holy to the LORD" and the bearing of the people's guilt point to Christ, who is holy and who bore our guilt that we might be accepted.
28.examples:
Then: God clothed the high priest in garments of glory, engraving Israel's names on stones worn over his shoulders and heart, so that he carried the people into God's presence and bore their guilt that they might be accepted.

Now: Jesus is our Great High Priest, who bears us into the very presence of God — on his shoulders like the shepherd, on his heart like the bridegroom. Our names are engraved on his heart. He bore our guilt and is himself "Holy to the LORD," so that we are accepted in him forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-5 — Garments for Glory and for Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God now clothes the men who will serve him. Aaron and his sons are set apart as priests, and God commands holy garments "for glory and for beauty" — woven of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet by skilled hands he himself has gifted. The priest cannot come as he is; he must be clothed. And every thread of that clothing points beyond Aaron to a greater High Priest, and to the righteousness in which he clothes his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest must be clothed "for glory and for beauty" — no one approaches God in his own ordinary state; he must be robed by God's design. This anticipates our great High Priest, Jesus, and the "garments of salvation... the robe of righteousness" in which he clothes us (Isa 61:10). We do not manufacture our fitness to draw near; we receive it, put on like a robe (Zech 3:3-5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Aaron could not serve in his own clothes; he was dressed head to toe in garments God designed, that he might stand before the Holy One.

Now: we come to God "found in him, not having a righteousness of [our] own" (Phil 3:9) but clothed in Christ (Gal 3:27) — glorious and beautiful in the eyes of God, not by our merit but by his gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Then bring near to you Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the people of Israel, to serve me as priests... And you shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty... that he may serve me as priest.
verseByVerse.commentary: God chooses the men and God designs their clothes. Aaron and his sons are drawn out from among the people to serve as priests — a calling they did not seize but received. And they may not serve in their everyday clothes; God commands "holy garments... for glory and for beauty," to be made by craftsmen he has filled "with a spirit of skill" (v.3). Even the ability to weave the priest's robes is God's gift. The lesson runs deep: no one comes to serve or to worship God dressed in himself. The priest must be clothed by God, for God's glory and in God's beauty. It is a picture of the gospel, where the sinner is stripped of filthy garments and dressed in "the robe of righteousness" (Isa 61:10; Zech 3:3-5). And it points to the true High Priest, Jesus, glorious and beautiful, who clothes his people in himself so that they may draw near.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6-14 — The Ephod: Israel on the Shoulders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ephod is the priest's central garment, a richly woven apron of gold and colored yarn. On its two shoulder pieces are set two onyx stones, and engraved on them are the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, six on each. So when the high priest goes in before the LORD, he carries the whole people on his shoulders — "as a memorial before the LORD." Israel is borne into God's presence on the strength of their priest.
