Then: Moses offered his own soul for his people — but a sinner cannot ransom sinners, and God did not accept the trade.

Now: what Moses could only offer, Christ accomplished. He was "blotted out" — cut off from the land of the living (Isa 53:8) — that our names might never be. "Rejoice that your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:20).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses returned to the LORD and said, 'Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. They have made for themselves gods of gold. But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written.' But the LORD said to Moses, 'Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is one of the most breathtaking prayers in the Bible. Moses climbs back up to God, names the sin plainly — "a great sin" — and then makes an offer that stops the heart. He cannot even finish the sentence: "if you will forgive their sin —." The thought is too large; he breaks off. And then: "but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written." Moses offers to be damned in their place. Take my name out of your book, he says, but spare them. It is the love of a true shepherd, willing to perish for his sheep — and Paul would one day echo it, wishing himself accursed for his kinsmen (Rom 9:3). But God will not take the trade: "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book." Moses is himself a sinner; he cannot ransom sinners. No mere man can bear another's guilt. And so the offer hangs in the air, aching, unfulfilled — until One comes who is sinless, and who can. Jesus was truly "cut off out of the land of the living" (Isa 53:8), blotted out under the wrath we deserved, so that our names might stand forever in the Lamb's book of life (Rev 21:27). Moses could only offer it. Christ did it.

33.title: If Your Presence Will Not Go
33.text: <sup>14</sup>And he said, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." <sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." <sup>18</sup>Moses said, "Please show me your glory." <sup>20</sup>..."you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live."
33.overview:
After the golden calf, the deepest question is no longer survival but presence. God offers to send Israel to the promised land with an angel — but to withdraw his own presence, lest his holiness consume this stiff-necked people on the way. And here Moses utters one of the most magnificent prayers in all of Scripture: "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than the promised land without him. He understands that the land without God's presence is no blessing at all.

This is the very heart of true religion. As Keller has said, the difference between a believer and a moralist is this: the believer wants God himself, not merely God's gifts. Moses does not want the milk and honey; he wants the God who gives it. "Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people?" The presence of God is what sets his people apart — it is everything.

Then Moses dares to ask the unaskable: "Please show me your glory." And God answers with infinite grace and infinite reserve: he will cause all his goodness to pass before Moses and proclaim his name, but Moses cannot see his face and live. So God hides him in the cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand, and lets him see only his back. Sproul saw here both the unapproachable holiness of God and his astonishing condescension. We could never bear the full glory — but in Christ, "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6), we behold what Moses longed to see.

sections.title: The Threat of God's Absence
sections.commentary:
God commands Israel to depart for the promised land, flowing with milk and honey, and promises to send an angel before them. But there is a terrible catch: "I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people." The very holiness that makes God's presence the greatest blessing also makes it dangerous to a sinful people. When the people hear this disastrous word, they mourn and strip off their ornaments. The prospect of the land without God's presence is felt as catastrophe.

This is the crisis the golden calf created: the holy God cannot simply dwell among an unholy people without consuming them. The problem demands a solution that chapter 33 cannot yet fully provide — a way for a holy God to dwell with sinful people without destroying them. That way is found only in Christ, in whom God dwells among us in grace, having dealt with our sin at the cross.

sections.title: Moses' Prayer for the Presence
sections.commentary:
Moses pitches the tent of meeting outside the camp, and the LORD speaks with him "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." Then Moses prays the great prayer: pleading for God's presence, he says, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people?" And God grants it: "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest."

Here is the heart of true faith. Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than Canaan without him. As Keller observed, the difference between a true believer and a mere moralist is that the believer wants God himself, not merely God's gifts. Moses does not crave the milk and honey; he craves the God who gives them. The presence of God is what makes his people distinct — it is everything. To have God's gifts without God himself would be the deepest poverty; to have God's presence in a desert is the greatest wealth.

sections.title: Show Me Your Glory
sections.commentary:
Emboldened, Moses asks the unaskable: "Please show me your glory." God answers with both grace and holy reserve. He will make all his goodness pass before Moses and proclaim his name, the LORD, declaring his sovereign grace and mercy. But "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." So God hides Moses in the cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand as his glory passes by, and lets him see only his back.

Here is the unapproachable holiness of God and his astonishing condescension held together. No sinner can behold the unveiled glory of God and survive; yet God graciously grants Moses a glimpse, sheltering him in the rock. Many have seen the rock that shelters Moses as a picture of Christ, our refuge from the consuming glory. And what Moses could not see — the face of God — is now beheld in Christ: "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). In the incarnate Son, the glory Moses longed for has drawn near, veiled in flesh, so that we may behold it and live.

sections.title: The Crisis and the Cry: A Holy God and a Sinful People
sections.commentary:
The whole chapter turns on a single, unbearable tension: how can a holy God dwell among a sinful people without consuming them? The golden calf created the crisis; Moses' prayer presses it; God's reserve in revealing his glory deepens it. The land without God's presence is no blessing, yet God's presence among the unholy is mortal danger.

This crisis is resolved only in Christ. In him the holy God dwells among sinners in grace, because at the cross our sin was borne and atoned. The glory Moses could not see in full is beheld in "the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). And the deepest cry of faith — "if your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up" — is answered forever in Immanuel, God with us, whose presence will never depart from his people.

33.theology:
The supreme value of God's presence. Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than the promised land without him. True faith wants God himself, not merely his gifts (Keller).

The problem of a holy God dwelling with sinners. God's presence among an unholy people would consume them — a crisis resolved only in Christ, who deals with our sin so God can dwell with us.

The unseeable glory revealed in Christ. No one can see God's face and live, yet in Christ we behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6).
33.examples:
Then: After the calf, God threatened to send Israel onward without his presence, but Moses pleaded, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here," and dared to ask, "Show me your glory."

Now: The mark of true faith is that we want God himself, not merely his blessings. "If your presence will not go, do not send me." And the glory Moses could not fully see has drawn near in Christ, the face of God among us. To have God's presence is everything; in Christ, that presence is ours forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-6 — 'I Will Not Go Up Among You'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Israel to leave Sinai for the promised land — flowing with milk and honey — but adds a devastating word: "I will not go up among you, lest I consume you." He will give them the land but withhold himself. And that, to a people who have tasted his presence, is unbearable news. They mourn, and strip off their ornaments. A land without God is no gift at all.
verseByVerse.theology: God's threat to send Israel on "with an angel" but without his own presence (v.3) exposes the heart of true religion: the gift is nothing without the Giver. A promised land without God would be a golden cage. The people "mourned" (v.4) — a sign of real repentance, for they now grieve God's absence more than any hardship. Moses will refuse to move an inch without the Presence (v.15). The deepest blessing is never God's gifts but God himself (Ps 73:25).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the promise of milk and honey turned to ashes at the words "I will not go up among you." Israel mourned, for they had learned that the land was worthless without its God.

Now: we can want heaven's blessings while forgetting heaven's God. But "whom have I in heaven but you?" (Ps 73:25). Better a wilderness with God than a paradise without him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey; but I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people.' When the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned, and no one put on his ornaments.
verseByVerse.commentary: God keeps his promise of the land — milk and honey, everything they were journeying toward — and then speaks the most terrible sentence they could hear: "I will not go up among you." He will send an angel, he will give the land, but he will withhold himself, "lest I consume you," for they are a stiff-necked people and his holy presence among sinners is deadly. Here is the crisis the golden calf created: how can a holy God dwell in the midst of an unholy people without destroying them? And notice Israel's response — "when the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned." This is the turning point, the mark of real repentance. They do not grieve over a hard road or a lost comfort; they grieve over the loss of God. The land itself has become worthless to them if he will not be in it. They strip off their ornaments in mourning. A soul that has tasted the presence of God can never again be content with his gifts alone. "Whom have I in heaven but you?" (Ps 73:25). Better the desert with God than Canaan without him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-11 — The Tent of Meeting, and a Friend of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses pitches a tent outside the camp, and there the LORD meets with him. When Moses enters, the pillar of cloud descends to the door, and the people rise and worship. And the wonder is stated simply: "the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." In the aftermath of the calf, God still speaks with his mediator — a friendship that keeps hope alive for the whole nation.
verseByVerse.theology: "Face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (v.11) describes an intimacy of communion unmatched under the old covenant (Num 12:8; Deut 34:10) — though even Moses could not see God's face unveiled (v.20). It anticipates the friendship Christ extends: "No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends" (John 15:15), and the day when "we shall see face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). The young Joshua lingering in the tent (v.11) is a quiet picture of the next generation learning to seek God's presence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the people watched the cloud come down to the tent door and worshiped from their own doorways, longing for the intimacy their mediator enjoyed.

Now: through Christ that intimacy is opened to us; he calls us friends (John 15:15), and by the Spirit we "behold the glory of the Lord" and are transformed (2 Cor 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting... When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance... Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even after the calf, God does not go silent. Moses pitches a tent outside the camp, and there the LORD comes down to meet him. When Moses enters, the pillar of cloud descends to the doorway, and all the people rise and worship from their own tent doors — watching, longing, worshiping at a distance. And then the line that takes your breath away: "the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." Not thunder from a mountaintop now, but conversation — the intimacy of friendship. In a chapter about God threatening to withdraw his presence, here is proof that the door is not shut: God still speaks, still befriends his mediator, and through that friendship keeps hope alive for the whole guilty nation. Yet even this is not the fullness; Moses could not see God's unveiled face and live (v.20). It all leans forward to the One who says, "No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends" (John 15:15), and to the day when "we shall see face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). Note too the young Joshua, who "would not depart from the tent" — a new generation already learning to linger in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — 'If Your Presence Will Not Go'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Emboldened by friendship, Moses presses God with holy boldness. He will not settle for an angel; he wants God himself. "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." The very thing that marks Israel out from every other people on earth is not the land, not the law, but this: "Is it not in your going with us?" And God yields: "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest."
verseByVerse.theology: Moses' argument is the essence of prayer: he holds God to his own words and his own grace, and asks for God himself as the one indispensable gift (vv.13-16). What distinguishes God's people from all others is the presence of God among them (v.16) — not superior virtue, but a Presence given by grace. God's answer, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest" (v.14), is the gospel promise that runs to Christ, "Immanuel" (Matt 1:23), and his word, "I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses staked everything on one request — God's own presence — and would rather stay in the desert with God than march to Canaan without him.

Now: the one thing that makes the church the church is Christ with us: "I am with you always" (Matt 28:20). Seek his presence above every other blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people on the face of the earth?' And the LORD said to Moses, 'This very thing that you have spoken I will do.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Friendship makes Moses bold, and he presses in with the holiest kind of daring. He will not be content with an angel escort; he wants God himself, and he says so plainly: "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." Then he lays bare the deepest truth about God's people: what makes Israel different from every nation on earth is not their land, their law, or their goodness — it is the presence of God in their midst. "Is it not in your going with us?" Strip that away and they are just another tribe wandering the desert. This is the one thing worth asking for, the one gift that contains every other. And God, moved by his servant's plea and his own grace, gives the tender promise: "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." Hold those words, for they are the heartbeat of the whole Bible. They run straight to Bethlehem, to "Immanuel, God with us" (Matt 1:23), and to the Savior's invitation, "Come to me... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28). The presence that Moses begged for is the presence we are freely given in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having secured God's presence, Moses asks for more still: "Please show me your glory." It is the boldest request in Scripture. God answers by promising to make "all my goodness" pass before him and to proclaim his name — but "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." So God will hide Moses in a cleft of the rock, cover him with his hand, and let him see only his back as his glory passes by. Grace lets a sinner glimpse God and live — sheltered in the rock.
verseByVerse.theology: God's glory, when unveiled, is unbearable to sinners: "man shall not see me and live" (v.20). Yet grace makes a way — Moses is hidden "in a cleft of the rock" and covered by God's hand while the glory passes (vv.22-23). The rock that shelters from the glory is a picture of Christ, the Rock (1 Cor 10:4), in whom alone we are safe before the holiness of God. And what God shows is chiefly moral glory — "all my goodness," his name and character (v.19) — fully unveiled at last in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6; John 1:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses, hidden in the rock and shielded by God's own hand, saw the afterglow of the glory and lived — a sinner sheltered to behold his God.

Now: we behold the glory of God safely, "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6), hidden in the true Rock. What Moses glimpsed from behind, we see full-face in the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said, 'Please show me your glory.' And he said, 'I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name, The LORD... But,' he said, 'you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live.'... 'Behold, there is a place by me where you shall stand on the rock... I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I have passed by.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses has secured God's presence; now, greatly daring, he asks for the summit of all desire: "Please show me your glory." Who would dare pray such a prayer? And how does God answer? He promises to make "all my goodness" pass by and to proclaim his own name — for the truest glory of God is not raw blazing power but his moral splendor, his goodness and grace and character. But there is a limit even grace cannot cross for now: "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." Unveiled deity would incinerate a sinner. So God devises a way for Moses to see and yet survive: he will hide him "in a cleft of the rock," cover him with his own hand while the glory passes, and let him see only the afterglow, his back. Do not miss the tenderness — God's own hand shielding his servant so that he can bear the unbearable. And do not miss the rock. To behold the glory of God and live, a sinner must be hidden in a rock, sheltered by God himself. That Rock is Christ (1 Cor 10:4). Hidden in him, we are safe before the holiness that would otherwise consume us — and what Moses saw only from behind, we now behold full-face, "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6).

34.title: The LORD, the LORD, a God Merciful and Gracious
34.text: <sup>6</sup>The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, <sup>7</sup>keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty..."
34.overview:
This is the high point of divine self-revelation in the Old Testament. Having asked to see God's glory, Moses is given new tablets and meets God on the mountain again. And God reveals his glory not first by sight but by proclamation — by declaring his name, his character: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness." This is who God is at the deepest level, the answer to Moses' prayer. The glory of God is supremely the glory of his grace.

This proclamation becomes the most-quoted text in the rest of the Old Testament, echoed again and again (Num. 14, Neh. 9, Pss. 86, 103, 145, Joel 2, Jonah 4, Nah. 1). It is Israel's creed about the heart of God. And notice the perfect balance: God is overflowing with steadfast love and forgiveness, yet "will by no means clear the guilty." His mercy does not cancel his justice; his justice does not quench his mercy. How can both be fully true? The answer comes at the cross, where, as Sproul never tired of saying, God is shown to be "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26) — where guilt is not cleared by being ignored but by being borne.

The covenant is renewed; God's grace triumphs over Israel's sin. And Moses comes down from the mountain with his face shining, radiant from being in God's presence — a glory Paul says is surpassed by the greater glory now shining in the gospel of Christ (2 Cor. 3). The God who is merciful and gracious has, in Christ, drawn infinitely near.

sections.title: The New Tablets
sections.commentary:
God commands Moses to cut two new tablets like the first, which he shattered, and to ascend the mountain again. As God's glory passes by, he proclaims his name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty." Moses bows and worships, pleading for God to pardon and to go with his stiff-necked people.

This is the climax of divine self-revelation in the Old Testament. God answers Moses' request to see his glory not chiefly by sight but by the proclamation of his character — and the heart of that character is grace, mercy, steadfast love (hesed), and faithfulness. Yet held together with mercy is justice: he "will by no means clear the guilty." Here is the great tension of the gospel: how can God be both abundantly forgiving and perfectly just? Sproul taught that this tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is shown to be "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom. 3:26). Guilt is not cleared by being overlooked but by being borne by a substitute.

sections.title: The Covenant Renewed
sections.commentary:
God graciously renews the covenant, promising to do marvels and to drive out the nations before Israel. He warns sternly against idolatry and intermarriage with the surrounding peoples, against making covenants with them or worshiping their gods, for "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." He reaffirms the feasts, the firstborn, the Sabbath, and the firstfruits. The covenant broken by the golden calf is restored — entirely by God's grace, not Israel's merit.

The renewal of the covenant after such a grievous breach is a stunning display of mercy. Israel had forfeited everything; God restores everything. This is the pattern of grace throughout Scripture: not that we keep covenant with God, but that God keeps covenant with us despite our unfaithfulness. The warnings against idolatry remind us that grace is never a license to return to the idols from which we were rescued; the God who forgives is also the God who is jealous for the undivided love of his people.

sections.title: The Shining Face of Moses
sections.commentary:
When Moses comes down from the mountain, his face shines because he has been talking with God — so brightly that the people are afraid to come near, and Moses must veil his face. The radiance is the reflected glory of having been in God's presence. Even a glimpse of God's glory transforms and radiates from the one who beholds it.

Paul takes up this scene in 2 Corinthians 3, showing that the glory on Moses' face — though real — was fading, and was surpassed by the far greater and permanent glory of the new covenant. Under the gospel, "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Cor. 3:18). The fading glory of Moses gives way to the surpassing, transforming glory of Christ. To behold him is to be changed into his likeness — the radiance Moses reflected is now, by the Spirit, being worked into all who behold the glory of God in the face of Christ.

sections.title: The Name Above All Names: Grace and Justice Meet
sections.commentary:
At the center of the chapter, and of the whole Old Testament's self-revelation of God, stands the proclamation of the divine name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness... forgiving iniquity... but who will by no means clear the guilty." Here grace and justice stand side by side, both absolute, both true.

How can God be both abundantly forgiving and perfectly just? The chapter cannot yet say; the cross alone resolves it, where God is shown "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom. 3:26). Guilt is not cleared by being ignored but by being borne. And the glory of this name, reflected fadingly on Moses' face, now shines unfading in Christ, transforming all who behold him from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18).

34.theology:
The glory of God is the glory of his grace. God reveals his glory by proclaiming his name: "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love." This is the most-quoted text in the rest of the OT.

Mercy and justice held together. God forgives yet "will by no means clear the guilty." The tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26).

Transforming glory. Moses' shining face is surpassed by the greater glory of the gospel; beholding Christ, we are transformed from glory to glory (2 Cor. 3:18).
34.examples:
Then: God answered Moses' plea to see his glory by proclaiming his name — "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious" — renewing the covenant after the calf and sending Moses down with a face shining from God's presence.

Now: This is the God we worship: merciful and gracious, yet perfectly just. At the cross his mercy and justice meet, for there our guilt was borne, not ignored. And beholding the glory of God in the face of Christ, we are being transformed from one degree of glory to another by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The LORD Proclaims His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls Moses back up with two new stone tablets to replace the ones he shattered. And there, as his goodness passes by, God does the very thing he promised — he proclaims his own name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness... forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty." This is God's self-revelation, the most quoted description of God's character in the whole Bible. Moses bows and worships.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the fullest self-portrait God gives in the Old Testament (vv.6-7), echoed again and again across Scripture (Num 14:18; Ps 86:15; 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). Its center is hesed — "steadfast love," God's loyal, covenant-keeping mercy — held together with justice: he forgives iniquity, yet "will by no means clear the guilty." How can both be true at once? The tension is only resolved at the cross, where God is "just and the justifier" (Rom 3:26) — guilt not cleared but borne, love and justice meeting in the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: at Israel's lowest moment, just after the calf, God reveals himself not chiefly as wrath but as "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love."

Now: this is still who God is toward all who come to him in Christ. His mercy is not reluctant; it is his glory. Yet he does not wink at sin — he laid it on his Son, that mercy and justice might kiss.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, 'The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty...' And Moses quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary: God cuts two new tablets of stone — grace rewriting the law Israel had broken — and then keeps the promise he made in the cleft of the rock. As his goodness passes by, God proclaims his own name, and it is the most treasured description of God's character in all of Scripture: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness." Feel the timing. This comes not at Israel's best moment but at their worst, days after the golden calf. And God reveals himself first and foremost not as fury but as mercy — patient, gracious, overflowing with hesed, his loyal covenant love. This one verse becomes the church's confession of God, quoted again and again down the Old Testament (Ps 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). Yet the same breath adds, he "will by no means clear the guilty." God is merciful, and God is just, and he will not pretend sin does not matter. How can both stand together? Not here — only at Calvary, where God proves himself "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom 3:26). The guilt was not waved away; it was carried by the Son, so that mercy and justice could embrace. No wonder Moses "quickly bowed his head... and worshiped."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the ground of his mercy, God renews the covenant, promising to do "marvels" never before seen and to drive out the nations of Canaan. But the warning is urgent: make no covenant with the peoples of the land, tear down their altars, for their idolatry will become a snare. And God tells them his name: "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." The God who forgives is also the God who will not share his people's hearts.
verseByVerse.theology: God's "jealousy" (v.14) is not petty envy but the fierce, protective love of a husband for his bride — he will not tolerate rivals for a heart that belongs to him (cf. Deut 4:24; 2 Cor 11:2). The ban on covenants and mixed worship guards against the snare of syncretism, blending the worship of the LORD with idols (as the calf tried to do). The molten gods forbidden in v.17 name the very sin just committed. Grace renews the covenant, but grace also demands undivided loyalty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: forgiven and restored, Israel was warned that peace-treaties with Canaan's idolatry would become a trap — tolerated idols always are.

Now: the God who saved us is jealous for us, in the best sense — he wants all our heart, not a share of it. "You cannot serve God and money" (Matt 6:24). His jealousy is the measure of his love.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth... Take care, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest it become a snare in your midst... for you shall worship no other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: On the sheer ground of his mercy, God renews the broken covenant — undeserved, astonishing grace — and promises to do "marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth." But renewal comes with a solemn charge. When they enter Canaan, they must make no covenant with its peoples and must tear down their altars, "lest it become a snare." Why so severe? Because tolerated idolatry never stays contained; make peace with it and you will end up bowing to it. Then God tells them one of his names: "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." We must hear that rightly. This is not the mean jealousy of a small heart, but the burning, protective love of a husband who will not share his bride with another (2 Cor 11:2). God's jealousy is the fire of his love. He forbids the molten gods (v.17) — naming the exact sin they had just committed — because a heart that belongs to him cannot be split. The God who abounds in steadfast love is the same God who says: all of you, not part. And that total claim is not a burden but the truest freedom, for we were made to be wholly his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The renewed covenant restates the rhythms of a life lived before God: keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, redeem every firstborn, rest on the Sabbath even in plowing time and harvest, keep the feasts of Weeks and Ingathering, and bring the best firstfruits. Israel's calendar is re-consecrated. A people brought back from ruin are re-taught how to walk with God through the year.
verseByVerse.theology: These repeated laws (cf. ch. 23) re-establish covenant life after the rupture of the calf: redemption of the firstborn (v.20) confesses that all life is forfeit and must be bought back; the Sabbath even in "plowing time and in harvest" (v.21) tests trust at the busiest, most tempting seasons; the feasts keep the story of grace before the people year by year. Restored people need re-formed rhythms — grace rebuilds a life of ordered worship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even in plowing and harvest — when every hour counted — Israel must rest, trusting God to provide what their labor could not.

Now: the busiest, most pressured seasons are exactly where our trust is tested. Sabbath rest still preaches that our provision comes from God, not from the hours we refuse to stop working (Ps 127:2).

verseByVerse.quote: 'You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread... All that open the womb are mine... Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest. In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest... The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: A restored people must relearn how to live, and so God re-establishes the rhythms of covenant life — the same feasts and firstfruits given before (ch. 23), now spoken again after the fall and the forgiveness. Keep Unleavened Bread, remembering the exodus. Redeem every firstborn, for "all that open the womb are mine" — a confession that every life is forfeit to God and must be bought back. Keep the feasts of Weeks and Ingathering. And rest on the Sabbath — with a pointed addition: "in plowing time and in harvest you shall rest." Those are precisely the seasons when a farmer can least afford to stop, when the weather is right and every hour is money. That is the test. Will you trust God enough to lay down your tools when the work screams to be done? The busiest, most pressured moments are where faith is proved. God re-forms his people's calendar because restored hearts need re-ordered lives — a whole year structured to keep the story of grace, and the trust it demands, always before them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27-28 — Forty Days, the Ten Words
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses is with the LORD forty days and forty nights, neither eating bread nor drinking water, and God writes on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments. The law broken at the foot of the mountain is graciously given again. Grace does not lower the standard; it restores the covenant and writes the words afresh.
verseByVerse.theology: The forty-day fast (v.28), echoed by Elijah and supremely by Christ (1 Kgs 19:8; Matt 4:2), marks a season of unique communion and mediation. That God writes the Ten Words again after they were shattered shows grace restoring what sin destroyed — the same holy law, re-given. Ultimately the law would be written not on stone but on hearts, in the new covenant Christ secures (Jer 31:33; 2 Cor 3:3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the broken tablets were replaced, the law re-written by God's own word — grace giving again what rebellion had smashed.

Now: the law we could never keep on stone is written by the Spirit on the hearts of God's people (2 Cor 3:3), and kept for us by the One who fulfilled it perfectly (Matt 5:17).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, 'Write these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.' So he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary: For forty days and forty nights Moses is alone with God, sustained without food or water — a span of unique, undistracted communion, later echoed by Elijah on the same mountain and by Christ in the wilderness (1 Kgs 19:8; Matt 4:2). And God writes again the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, on the fresh tablets. Do not rush past the wonder of this. Israel had taken God's law and shattered it, both in the calf and in the broken stones. And God simply gives it again. Grace does not water down the commandments — they are the same holy words — but grace re-gives what rebellion destroyed. This is the pattern of God's dealings with sinners: not lowering his righteousness, but restoring the covenant by his mercy. And it reaches its goal only when the law is written no longer on cold stone but on living hearts, in the new covenant sealed by Christ: "I will write it on their hearts" (Jer 31:33; 2 Cor 3:3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-35 — The Shining Face of Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses comes down not knowing that his face shines from being with God. The people are afraid to come near, so he veils his face — unveiling it only when he goes in to speak with the LORD. The glory was real but fading, borrowed, and veiled. Paul will take up this scene to show the surpassing glory of the new covenant, where we behold the Lord with unveiled faces and are changed.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul interprets this scene at length (2 Cor 3:7-18): Moses' shining but fading glory is the glory of the old covenant, veiled and passing; the new covenant's glory is greater and permanent. And its wonder is this: "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Cor 3:18). What was Moses' alone is now every believer's — and it does not fade.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the afterglow of God's presence shone on Moses' face, so bright the people shrank back, and he veiled it — a glory real but fading.

Now: to gaze on Christ is to be changed into his likeness, brightness that grows rather than fades, "from one degree of glory to another" (2 Cor 3:18). Time with God still leaves its shine.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai... Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God. Aaron and all the people of Israel saw Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him... And Moses would put the veil over his face.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses comes down the mountain glowing — and, beautifully, "Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone." Real time in the presence of God leaves a mark the person himself may not even notice; others see it before he does. The shine is the afterglow of glory, so bright that the people are afraid to come near, and Moses veils his face, uncovering it only when he goes back in to speak with the LORD. Centuries later Paul lifts this very scene to explain the gospel (2 Cor 3:7-18). That shining glory, he says, was real — but it was fading, and veiled, the glory of a covenant that would pass. The new covenant is greater. And here is its marvel: the shining is no longer for one mediator alone. "We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Cor 3:18). What Moses had for a moment, and had to hide, every believer now has in Christ — a glory that does not fade but grows, as we behold him. The face that beholds God is changed by what it sees.

35.title: The Willing Heart
35.text: <sup>5</sup>"Take from among you a contribution to the LORD. Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution..." <sup>21</sup>And they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, and brought the LORD's contribution... <sup>29</sup>All the men and women, the people of Israel, whose heart moved them to bring anything... brought it as a freewill offering to the LORD.
35.overview:
After the dark chapters of the golden calf and the renewal of the covenant, the building of the tabernacle finally begins — and it begins with the willing heart. Moses gathers the people and calls for contributions, but not by compulsion: "Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution." And the response is a flood of generosity. Men and women alike, "everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him," bring gold, silver, fine cloth, precious stones, and skilled labor — so much that Moses will soon have to tell them to stop (ch. 36).

What a contrast to the golden calf! There, they tore off their gold to make an idol; here, they freely give their gold to build God's dwelling. The same wealth that fueled idolatry now fuels worship — when the heart is right. As MacArthur observes, true worship flows from a willing, stirred, moved heart, not from coercion or duty alone. God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7), and the building of his house is a community project of joyful, Spirit-stirred generosity.

Notice too the breadth of involvement: men and women, skilled craftsmen and weavers, leaders and common people — the whole community is caught up in the work. Bezalel and Oholiab are again named as Spirit-filled craftsmen who will also teach others. The tabernacle is not built by a few professionals but by the whole Spirit-led community, each contributing as their hearts move them and their gifts allow. This is the church at its best: a willing-hearted people, gifted by the Spirit, building together for the glory and dwelling of God.

sections.title: The Sabbath and the Call for Offerings
sections.commentary:
Moses first reminds the people of the Sabbath — even the great work of building God's dwelling must honor the rhythm of rest — and then issues the call for contributions: "Take from among you a contribution to the LORD. Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution." He lists all that is needed: gold, silver, bronze, fine yarns, skins, oil, spices, and precious stones, along with skilled work for every part of the tabernacle. The work is comprehensive, and the call is to willing hearts.

That the Sabbath is mentioned first, even before the building begins, underscores that our work for God must never crowd out our rest in God. We do not earn his favor by ceaseless labor; we serve from rest, not for rest. The call for offerings is rooted in grace: God invites his redeemed people to give back from what he has provided, and only the generous, willing heart is sought.

sections.title: The Flood of Generosity
sections.commentary:
The response is overwhelming. "Everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him" brings contributions — men and women alike, bringing brooches, earrings, rings, gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, fine linen, goats' hair, skins, silver, bronze, and precious stones. The women spin the yarn with their hands; the leaders bring the precious stones. "All the men and women, the people of Israel, whose heart moved them... brought it as a freewill offering to the LORD."

The contrast with the golden calf is stunning. There, they tore off their gold to make an idol; here, they freely give their gold to build God's dwelling. The same wealth that fueled idolatry now fuels worship — for the heart has been turned back to God. True worship flows from a willing, stirred, Spirit-moved heart, not from compulsion. "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor. 9:7). And the breadth is beautiful: men and women, leaders and common folk, the whole community caught up in joyful generosity for the house of God.

sections.title: The Spirit-Gifted Craftsmen
sections.commentary:
Moses announces that the LORD has called Bezalel by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill and intelligence and knowledge in every craft, and has appointed Oholiab with him. Crucially, God has also "inspired him to teach" — the gifted are to equip others. The Spirit gives not only ability but the capacity to multiply ability in others, so that the whole community of craftsmen can share in the work.

Here is a beautiful picture of the church: a Spirit-gifted people, with leaders who not only exercise their gifts but teach and equip others to exercise theirs (cf. Eph. 4:11-12). The tabernacle is built not by a few professionals but by the whole Spirit-led community, each contributing willingly according to their gifts. This is the body of Christ at work — every member supplied by the Spirit, building together for the glory and dwelling of God.

sections.title: The Redeemed Community at Worship
sections.commentary:
The chapter paints a picture of the redeemed community at its best: a people resting in God (the Sabbath), giving from willing hearts (the freewill offering), and serving with Spirit-given gifts (the craftsmen). Men and women, leaders and common folk, the skilled and the generous — all are caught up together in building the dwelling of God.

This is the church as God designed it (Eph. 4:11-16): a body in which every member, gifted by the Spirit, contributes willingly to the common work, while the gifted equip others. What sin corrupted in the golden calf — gold torn off for an idol — grace now redirects to worship. The redeemed community gives, serves, and builds together for the glory and dwelling of God.

35.theology:
Worship from a willing heart. The tabernacle is built by freewill offerings from hearts stirred and moved by the Spirit, not by compulsion. "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor. 9:7).

Redemption redirects what idolatry corrupted. The same gold that made the calf now builds God's dwelling. A heart turned back to God turns its resources to worship.

The Spirit-gifted community. Men and women, leaders and craftsmen, all contribute their gifts; the Spirit equips and the gifted teach others — a picture of the church building together (Eph. 4:11-12).
35.examples:
Then: After the golden calf, the building of God's dwelling began with willing hearts — men and women freely bringing gold, cloth, and skilled labor, so generously that the same wealth once given to an idol now built the house of God.

Now: True worship and generosity flow from a willing, Spirit-stirred heart, not from compulsion. The church is built when the whole community, gifted by the Spirit, gives joyfully and serves together. What sin once corrupted, grace redirects to the glory of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the great work of building begins — and God opens it, as he opened the instructions (31:12-17), with the Sabbath. Six days for labor, but the seventh a holy rest; not even a fire is to be kindled for work. However urgent and sacred the project, it must never swallow the day God has hallowed. Worshipful rest guards worshipful work.
verseByVerse.theology: Bracketing the tabernacle's construction with the Sabbath (31:12-17; 35:1-3) makes an enduring point: zeal for God's work must never trample God's rest. Rest is not laziness but a weekly confession that God, not our striving, sustains us and sanctifies us — a shadow of the gospel rest in Christ (Heb 4:9-10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even builders eager to raise God's house had to lay down their tools each seventh day.

Now: good work, even ministry, can become an idol that crowds out rest in God. The Sabbath principle still says: stop, and trust the God who works while you rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days work shall be done, but on the seventh day you shall have a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD... You shall kindle no fire in all your dwelling places on the Sabbath day.
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel is finally ready to build the tabernacle, and God's very first word is not about gold or cloth but about rest. As he framed the instructions with the Sabbath, so he frames the construction. However holy the task, it must not override the holy day. The point is deliberate and searching: the work of God must never crowd out rest in God. It is possible to be so busy serving the Lord that we stop trusting him — to let even good work become a quiet idol. The Sabbath breaks that spell every seventh day, preaching that our holiness and our provision come from God's hand, not from our unbroken labor. It points on to the deeper rest of the gospel, where we cease from our works and rest in Christ's finished work (Heb 4:9-10). First rest, then build.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4-19 — The Call for Freewill Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls for the materials, and the key phrase is "whoever is of a generous heart." The tabernacle is to be funded not by taxation but by willing gifts — gold and silver, yarn and skins and wood and oil and precious stones. God, who owns everything, invites his people into the joy of giving to his house.
verseByVerse.theology: "Whoever is of a generous heart" (v.5) sets the tone: God loves willing gifts, not extracted ones (2 Cor 9:7). The offering flows from the heart before it flows from the hand. God did not need Israel's gold; he invited it, that they might have the joy of giving to the One who gave them everything (1 Chr 29:14). Grace received longs to give back.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the materials for God's dwelling came from open hearts and open hands, each one bringing as he was moved.

Now: God still funds his work through cheerful, willing givers — "each one must give as he has decided in his heart... for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor 9:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Take from among you a contribution to the LORD. Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution: gold, silver, and bronze... And let every skillful craftsman among you come and make all that the LORD has commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses lists all that will be needed to build the tabernacle — metals, dyed yarns, skins, wood, oil, spices, gems — but the heartbeat of the appeal is one phrase: "whoever is of a generous heart." God funds his dwelling not by compulsion but by willingness. He owns the gold already; he owns the cattle on a thousand hills. He does not need Israel's contributions — he invites them, so that his people might taste the joy of giving to the God who gave them everything. As David would later pray, "all things come from you, and of your own have we given you" (1 Chr 29:14). The gift that pleases God begins in the heart before it ever reaches the hand. This is the pattern of all true giving to God's work: not grudging, not pressured, but the glad overflow of a heart that has received grace and cannot help but give back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The response is overwhelming. Men and women, "all whose heart moved them," come streaming in with gold jewelry, fine yarn, skins, silver, bronze, and precious stones. The women spin with their own hands; the leaders bring the onyx and the gems. Again and again the text repeats: they brought "a freewill offering to the LORD." A people so recently guilty of the golden calf now pour out their treasure for God's house — grace turning greed into generosity.
verseByVerse.theology: The lavish, joyful giving (vv.21-22, 29) is the fruit of grace and forgiveness: the same gold that made a calf now builds a sanctuary. Redeemed hearts give freely (2 Cor 8:2-5). Note the dignity given to the women's skilled labor (vv.25-26) and to every willing contributor — God receives the gift of the humble spinner as gladly as the leader's gemstones. The measure is the heart, not the amount (Mark 12:43-44).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: hearts once bent toward an idol now overflowed toward God, and the gifts poured in faster than they could be used.

Now: when grace grips a heart, generosity follows — "in a severe test of affliction... their abundance of joy... overflowed in a wealth of generosity" (2 Cor 8:2). Forgiven people are open-handed people.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, and brought the LORD's contribution... So they came, both men and women. All who were of a willing heart... All the men and women, the people of Israel, whose heart moved them to bring anything for the work... brought it as a freewill offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The response is a flood. The text can hardly stop repeating it: everyone "whose heart stirred him," everyone "whose spirit moved him," "all who were of a willing heart," men and women alike, came streaming in with gold and yarn and skins and silver and gems. The women spun the goats' hair with their own skilled hands; the leaders brought the precious stones. Over and over the words ring out: "a freewill offering to the LORD." Now feel the wonder of it. This is the same nation that, only chapters ago, tore off its gold to make a calf. The very impulse that ran toward an idol now runs toward the living God. That is what grace and forgiveness do to a heart — they turn hoarding into giving, greed into generosity. And notice how God dignifies every gift: the humble spinner and the wealthy chief bring together, and both are received. God weighs the heart, not the amount (Mark 12:43-44). Redeemed people become generous people, for "their abundance of joy... overflowed in a wealth of generosity" (2 Cor 8:2).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses names Bezalel and Oholiab again, filled by God "with skill to do every sort of work" — engraving, weaving, designing — and gifted, too, "to teach." God supplies not only willing hearts and abundant materials but the very skill to shape them, and the ability to pass that skill on. The whole project, from gift to gold to craft, is the work of God through willing people.
verseByVerse.theology: God fills the craftsmen "with skill... and with the ability to teach" (vv.34-35) — gifting not only for the work but for equipping others, a pattern the New Testament carries into the church (Eph 4:11-12). Every ability to make, design, and instruct is a Spirit-given stewardship (1 Cor 12:4-7). The beauty of God's house is the fruit of God's own gifts, returned to him in service.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the skill in the artisans' hands and the ability to train others were themselves gifts of God, poured back into building his house.

Now: your abilities — and your capacity to teach and equip others — are God's gifts for building his people (Eph 4:12). Use them for him, and hand them on.

verseByVerse.quote: See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel... and he has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, with intelligence, with knowledge, and with all craftsmanship... And he has inspired him to teach, both him and Oholiab... He has filled them with skill to do every sort of work.
verseByVerse.commentary: God has stirred willing hearts and gathered abundant materials; now he supplies the skill to shape them. Bezalel and Oholiab are named again, filled with the Spirit of God for "every sort of work" — engraving, weaving, designing, working gold and stone and cloth. And God adds one more gift: he has "inspired him to teach." The Spirit gives not only the ability to do the work but the ability to train others to do it too. Nothing in the whole enterprise is self-generated. The willingness is from God, the wealth is from God, the skill is from God, even the gift of passing on the skill is from God. The people simply return to him what he first supplied. It is a beautiful picture of how God builds anything worth building — gifting his people, then equipping them to equip others, so that the body grows by every member's God-given gift (Eph 4:11-12; 1 Cor 12:4-7). The beauty of God's house is, from first to last, the work of God's own generosity.

36.title: More Than Enough
36.text: <sup>5</sup>..."The people bring much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD has commanded us to do." <sup>6</sup>So Moses gave command... "Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution for the sanctuary." So the people were restrained from bringing, <sup>7</sup>for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more.
36.overview:
Here is one of the most delightful problems in all of Scripture: the people give so generously that Moses has to command them to stop. "The people bring much more than enough," the craftsmen report, and so "the people were restrained from bringing." When was the last time a congregation had to be told to stop giving? This is what happens when redeemed hearts overflow with gratitude — generosity becomes a flood that must be restrained, not coaxed.

The chapter then describes the skilled craftsmen, led by Bezalel and Oholiab, beginning the actual construction — the curtains, the frames, the veil, all made exactly according to the pattern God had shown. The work proceeds with painstaking obedience and exquisite skill, every detail conforming to God's command. The Spirit-gifted workers translate God's design into reality with reverent care.

As Ferguson reflects, generosity that must be restrained is the fruit of hearts captivated by grace. The Israelites had been slaves with nothing; now, having been redeemed and provided for, they pour out their wealth with joy. This is the gospel pattern: "You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor. 8:9). When we grasp how much we have received in Christ, our giving overflows. The building of God's dwelling is funded not by reluctant duty but by grateful, abundant, joyful love.

sections.title: Bezalel and the Willing Workers
sections.commentary:
Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person "in whom the LORD has put skill and intelligence" set to work on the sanctuary. They come from their various tasks to do the work, and Moses gives them all the freewill offerings the people have brought. The work is a partnership: God supplies the skill, the people supply the materials, and the craftsmen supply the labor — all under God's command and design. Every part of the community has a role in building the dwelling of God.

The emphasis that God "put skill" in the workers reminds us that even our abilities are gifts of grace. There is no room for pride in service to God; the craftsman's skill, like the giver's generosity, comes from God himself. All the glory returns to the One who equips and provides. The workers are stewards of God-given gifts, deployed for God-given purposes.

sections.title: Restrained from Giving
sections.commentary:
Then comes the delightful problem: the craftsmen report to Moses, "The people bring much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD has commanded us to do." So Moses commands throughout the camp, "Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution for the sanctuary," and "the people were restrained from bringing, for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more." When has a congregation ever had to be told to stop giving?

This is the overflow of redeemed hearts. The Israelites, once slaves with nothing, now pour out their wealth with such joy that the giving must be restrained. As Ferguson notes, generosity that must be checked is the fruit of hearts captivated by grace. This is the gospel pattern: when we grasp the immeasurable riches we have received in Christ — who became poor that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9) — our giving overflows. The building of God's house is funded not by reluctant duty but by grateful, abundant love.

sections.title: The Curtains, Frames, and Veil
sections.commentary:
The construction begins in earnest. The skilled workers make the ten curtains of fine twined linen with cherubim, the coverings of goats' hair and skins, the acacia frames overlaid with gold set in silver bases, the bars, the veil of blue and purple and scarlet with cherubim, and the screen for the entrance. Every element is made precisely according to the pattern God had revealed on the mountain. The detailed repetition of the instructions, now in the form of execution, underscores the painstaking obedience of the workers.

The careful conformity to God's design teaches that worship is to be ordered by God's revelation, not human preference. Nothing is left to improvisation; everything is done "as the LORD had commanded." The beauty and precision of the work reflect the glory of the God it is built to house. And the cherubim woven throughout remind the worshiper that this is the threshold of heaven, the dwelling place of the God whom angels serve — all of it pointing forward to the greater dwelling of God with man in Christ and in the New Jerusalem.

sections.title: The Overflow of Grace
sections.commentary:
The defining image of the chapter is generosity that must be restrained. When have God's people ever had to be told to stop giving? This is the overflow of hearts captivated by grace — the gospel pattern of those who, having received much, cannot help but give much. The same hands that once tore off gold for a calf now give it freely for God's house.

Paul names the principle: "You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor. 8:9). When we grasp the immeasurable riches we have in Christ, our giving overflows. Generosity that must be restrained is the natural fruit of a heart that has truly tasted grace.

36.theology:
Generosity that must be restrained. The people give more than enough, until Moses commands them to stop — the fruit of hearts captivated by grace and the gospel pattern of overflow (2 Cor. 8:9).

Skill as a gift of grace. God "put skill" in the workers; even our abilities are graces, leaving no room for pride in service.

Worship ordered by God's pattern. Every element is made exactly as God commanded — worship is governed by his revelation, not human improvisation.
36.examples:
Then: The people gave so generously to build God's dwelling that Moses had to command them to stop, while Spirit-gifted craftsmen built every curtain, frame, and veil precisely according to God's pattern.

Now: When hearts grasp the riches we have in Christ — who became poor to make us rich — generosity overflows and must be restrained, not coaxed. Our gifts and skills are graces from God, deployed for his glory, and our worship is to be shaped by his revelation, offered with reverent, joyful care.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The work begins, and something wonderful happens: the people bring so much that the craftsmen have to stop them. Every morning the freewill gifts keep coming, until Bezalel and the workers tell Moses, "The people bring much more than enough." So a proclamation goes out through the camp: stop giving. It may be the only place in Scripture where God's people had to be restrained from generosity.
verseByVerse.theology: "The people bring much more than enough" (v.5) is a rare and lovely problem. When hearts are gripped by grace, generosity overflows past all requirement. It is the exact opposite of the grudging, calculating heart. Here is a foretaste of the church at its best, where giving springs from joy, not pressure (2 Cor 8:2-3), and God's work never lacks because his people's hearts are full.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the offering had to be halted — the people's generosity outran the need.

Now: imagine a church that had to be told to stop giving. That is what grace does to open hearts. "Each one must give as he has decided... for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor 9:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And they received from Moses all the contribution that the people of Israel had brought for doing the work... They still kept bringing him freewill offerings every morning... 'The people bring much more than enough for doing the work.' So Moses gave command... 'Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution.' So the people were restrained from bringing, for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more.
verseByVerse.commentary: The building begins, and we meet one of the happiest problems in all of Scripture. The people keep bringing their freewill offerings "every morning," gift after gift, until the craftsmen themselves come to Moses and say, in effect, "Please make them stop — the people bring much more than enough." And a proclamation actually goes out through the camp: no more giving. Stop. Where else in the Bible do we find God's people having to be restrained from generosity? This is what grace looks like when it floods a heart. The same people who grumbled in the wilderness and melted their gold into a calf now give so freely that the offering has to be halted. Generosity is the fingerprint of a forgiven heart. It runs past duty, past the minimum, past what is strictly needed, because it is not really about the tabernacle at all — it is about love for the God who gave first. Would that every church had this problem: hearts so full that the giving had to be capped.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the skilled workers make exactly what God commanded in chapter 26: the ten linen curtains embroidered with cherubim, the goats'-hair curtains, and the coverings of ram skins and hide. What God spoke on the mountain now takes shape in cloth and thread. Instruction becomes obedience; the pattern becomes the tabernacle.
verseByVerse.theology: The construction chapters echo the instruction chapters almost word for word, and the repetition is the point: Israel does exactly "as the LORD had commanded Moses." Obedience is not creativity; it is faithful reproduction of God's revealed pattern. The beauty of the tent — glory within, cherubim overhead — is built precisely to God's design (cf. Heb 8:5), not human preference.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the workers did not improvise; they made the curtains exactly as God had said, and the woven heaven of cherubim took shape as commanded.

Now: we serve God best not by reinventing worship to our taste but by faithfully following what he has revealed. Obedience honors the Designer.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the craftsmen among the workmen made the tabernacle with ten curtains. They were made of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns, with cherubim skillfully worked... He also made curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle... a covering of tanned rams' skins and a covering of goatskins.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the words spoken on the mountain become thread and cloth. The craftsmen make the ten beautiful linen curtains, embroidered all over with cherubim, to form the glory-ceiling of the tent; then the goats' hair curtains, and the outer coverings of ram skins and hide — precisely as God commanded in chapter 26. If you read the instruction and the construction side by side, they match almost word for word, and that echo is the whole point. Faithful service is not improvisation; it is the careful, joyful reproduction of what God has revealed. The workers add nothing of their own design and subtract nothing; they build exactly to the heavenly pattern (Heb 8:5). There is deep wisdom here for the church. We honor God not by remaking his worship to suit our tastes, but by doing faithfully what he has shown us. The beauty of God's house — its hidden glory, its canopy of angels — came from following the Designer to the letter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-38 — The Frames, the Veil, the Screen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The workers make the upright acacia frames overlaid with gold, standing on their silver bases, joined by golden bars; then the veil of blue and purple and scarlet, worked with cherubim, to divide the Holy Place from the Most Holy; and the screen for the entrance. The skeleton and the dividing curtains of God's dwelling are complete, each exactly as commanded.
verseByVerse.theology: Every gold-covered frame stands on silver bases from the atonement money (38:25-28): God's dwelling rests on the price of redemption. The veil, woven with guardian cherubim, again marks that the way into God's presence is "not yet opened" (Heb 9:8) — a barrier that Christ's torn flesh would one day remove (Matt 27:51; Heb 10:19-20). The obedient building of it all testifies that access to God comes only on God's terms.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the golden frames rose on their silver bases and the guarded veil hung exactly as commanded — God's house built on redemption, its inmost room still curtained off.

Now: the veil that Israel could not pass has been torn in Christ. We enter the Holiest "by the blood of Jesus... through the curtain, that is, through his flesh" (Heb 10:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he made the upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood... and their forty bases of silver... And he made the veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen; with cherubim skillfully worked into it he made it... He also made a screen for the entrance of the tent.
verseByVerse.commentary: The tent takes its shape. The workers raise the tall acacia frames, overlaid with gold, each one standing on bases of silver — and that silver came from the atonement money every Israelite paid (38:25-28), so that the whole house of God literally rests on the price of redemption. They join the frames with gilded bars into one gleaming structure. Then they weave the veil — blue, purple, scarlet, worked with cherubim — to hang between the Holy Place and the Most Holy, and a screen for the entrance. The cherubim on the veil are the old guardians of Eden's gate (Gen 3:24), and they say what they have always said: the way into the presence of God is barred to sinners, "not yet opened" (Heb 9:8). All of it is built exactly as God commanded — access to God strictly on God's terms. And all of it waits for the day when the true veil, the flesh of Christ, is torn on the cross (Matt 27:51), and the road into the Holiest is flung wide at last (Heb 10:19-20).

37.title: Obedience in Every Detail
37.text: <sup>1</sup>Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood... <sup>6</sup>And he made a mercy seat of pure gold... <sup>7</sup>And he made two cherubim of gold... <sup>9</sup>The cherubim spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, with their faces one to another...
37.overview:
This chapter recounts the actual making of the most sacred furnishings — the Ark and its mercy seat, the table of the bread of the Presence, the golden lampstand, and the altar of incense. What is striking is the repetition: nearly everything described in the commands of chapters 25 and 30 is now repeated in the language of fulfillment — "he made." God commanded; Bezalel made. The pattern shown on the mountain becomes reality in gold and acacia, exactly as God ordained.

This careful repetition is not tedious; it is theological. It declares that obedience matters in every detail. Bezalel did not improve upon God's design or add his own creative flourishes where God had spoken; he made it exactly as commanded. As Sproul taught, true worship is regulated by God's word, not by human invention. The Spirit-filled craftsman submits his considerable skill to the revealed will of God. Excellence and obedience go together.

And every object preaches Christ. The mercy seat, where God meets his people and the blood is sprinkled, is fulfilled in Christ our propitiation (Rom. 3:25). The bread of the Presence points to Christ the bread of life. The lampstand points to Christ the light of the world. The altar of incense points to the prayers of the saints rising through Christ our Intercessor. The whole sanctuary, built with obedient care, is a gallery of gospel portraits — every detail a finger pointing to the One in whom God dwells with us. Bezalel's faithful obedience in the small things is itself a form of worship.

sections.title: The Ark and the Mercy Seat
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the Ark of acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, with its rings and poles, and the mercy seat of pure gold with two cherubim of hammered gold at its ends, their wings overshadowing it and their faces toward one another, gazing down upon the mercy seat. The most sacred object is made first and with the greatest care — the throne of God on earth, the place where he meets his people above the blood-sprinkled mercy seat.

Every detail conforms exactly to God's command in chapter 25. The cherubim gaze down upon the mercy seat as if contemplating the mystery of atonement — "things into which angels long to look" (1 Pet. 1:12). The mercy seat, where the blood of atonement covers the broken law beneath, is fulfilled in Christ our propitiation (Rom. 3:25), the place where God's justice and mercy meet. Bezalel's faithful making of this object is the crafting of a gospel sermon in gold.

sections.title: The Table and the Lampstand
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the table of the bread of the Presence, overlaid with gold, with its dishes and vessels, and the lampstand of pure hammered gold with its branches, cups shaped like almond blossoms, buds, and flowers, and its seven lamps — all of a talent of pure gold. The exquisite craftsmanship reflects the glory of the God whose house this is. Beauty and excellence are offered to God, not as ends in themselves but as fitting expressions of his worth.

The table points to Christ, the bread of the Presence and the bread of life (John 6), and to the communion we have at his table. The lampstand points to Christ, the light of the world (John 8:12), and to the church called to bear his light. Made exactly as commanded, these furnishings declare that God's people live always in his presence, fed and enlightened by him. The almond-blossom design, recalling Aaron's budding staff, speaks of life and resurrection — the living light of God's presence among his people.

sections.title: The Altar of Incense and the Holy Oils
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the golden altar of incense with its horns, rings, and poles, and the holy anointing oil and the fragrant incense, blended as by a perfumer. The altar of incense, standing before the veil, is where the prayers of God's people rise as a sweet aroma before him. Everything is made according to God's precise specification, with reverent skill.

The altar of incense fulfilled in the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8; Ps. 141:2) reminds us that our prayers ascend acceptably to God only through the mediation of Christ, our great High Priest. The holy oil, used to consecrate the priests and furnishings, points to the anointing of the Spirit. Every object in this chapter, made in careful obedience, is a portrait of Christ and the worship he secures. Bezalel's obedience in every detail is itself an act of worship — a reminder that faithfulness in small things glorifies God.

sections.title: A Gallery of Gospel Portraits
sections.commentary:
The sacred furnishings of this chapter together form a gallery of gospel portraits, each one a finger pointing to Christ. The mercy seat is Christ our propitiation (Rom. 3:25); the bread of the Presence is Christ the bread of life (John 6:35); the lampstand is Christ the light of the world (John 8:12); the altar of incense is the place where our prayers rise through Christ our Intercessor (Rev. 5:8).

And every object is made in exact obedience — "he made it as the LORD commanded." Faithfulness in the smallest detail is itself worship. Bezalel's reverent craftsmanship teaches that we serve God on his terms, with our best skill submitted to his revealed will. The whole sanctuary, built in obedient care, declares the glory of the God who dwells with his people through the Christ to whom every detail points.

37.theology:
Obedience in every detail. Bezalel makes each furnishing exactly as God commanded — true worship is regulated by God's word, not human invention. Faithfulness in small things is worship.

Every object points to Christ. The mercy seat (Rom. 3:25), the bread (John 6), the lampstand (John 8:12), the incense (Rev. 5:8) — the whole sanctuary is a gallery of gospel portraits.

Excellence offered to God. The exquisite craftsmanship reflects the worth of the God whose house this is; beauty and skill are offered in his service.
37.examples:
Then: Bezalel made the Ark, mercy seat, table, lampstand, and altar of incense exactly as God had commanded, his Spirit-given skill submitted entirely to God's revealed design — every object a portrait of Christ.

Now: Faithful obedience in every detail is itself worship; we serve God on his terms, not ours. And the sacred furnishings preach the gospel still: Christ our mercy seat, our bread, our light, and our Intercessor through whom our prayers rise as sweet incense before God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bezalel himself makes the ark — the acacia chest overlaid with pure gold, the mercy seat of solid gold, and the two cherubim of hammered gold overshadowing it with their wings, their faces turned toward the mercy seat. The throne of God on earth, the place of atonement, is fashioned exactly as commanded. What God designed in chapter 25 is now made real.
verseByVerse.theology: Bezalel makes the mercy seat (kapporet, place of atonement) and the cherubim exactly as God prescribed — the very object Paul names for Christ, our "propitiation" (Rom 3:25). The cherubim gaze down toward the blood-sprinkled cover, as if heaven itself leans in to look at the place where mercy meets the broken law (cf. 1 Pet 1:12). It is made, not invented; the way of atonement is God's design, not ours.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the golden mercy seat took shape under Bezalel's hands, the cherubim bowing over the place where God would meet his people in blood.

Now: the true mercy seat is Christ, and even the angels long to look into these things (1 Pet 1:12). At the cross, holiness and mercy meet.

verseByVerse.quote: Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood... And he overlaid it with pure gold... And he made a mercy seat of pure gold... He made two cherubim of hammered gold... The cherubim spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, with their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat were the faces of the cherubim.
