verseByVerse.commentary: Bezalel himself builds the holiest object of all: the ark, overlaid inside and out with pure gold, holding the tablets of the law; and above it the mercy seat of solid gold, with two cherubim of hammered gold spreading their wings over it. Notice the direction of their faces — turned inward and downward, gazing toward the mercy seat. It is as if heaven itself is leaning in to look at this one spot, the place where, on the Day of Atonement, blood would be sprinkled and a holy God would meet sinful people without destroying them. Peter says the angels "long to look" into the things of our salvation (1 Pet 1:12), and here they are, cast in gold, doing exactly that. The mercy seat — in Greek, the hilasterion — is the very word Paul gives to Christ, whom God set forth as "a propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25). And it is made, not invented. The way sinners come to God is designed by God himself, and it has always pointed to the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Next the golden table is made, with its rings and poles and its dishes for the bread of the Presence — the table on which twelve loaves would always sit before the face of God. Fellowship with God has a table, and it is built exactly as commanded.
verseByVerse.theology: The table of the Presence, made as God prescribed, keeps all twelve tribes continually "before the LORD" (25:30) — covenant communion pictured as a shared table. It anticipates the Bread of Life (John 6:35) and the table Christ spreads for his people (Ps 23:5; Luke 22:30).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the golden table was fashioned to hold the bread that kept Israel perpetually before God's face.

Now: in Christ we are kept perpetually in the presence of God and fed at his table — fellowship that is feast, not famine.

verseByVerse.quote: He also made the table of acacia wood... and overlaid it with pure gold... And he made the vessels of pure gold that were to be on the table, its plates and dishes for incense, and its bowls and flagons with which to pour drink offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary: The golden table is made, complete with its poles for carrying and its dishes for the bread of the Presence — the twelve loaves that would sit before God's face continually, one for each tribe (25:30). Built exactly to command, it quietly preaches a great truth: fellowship with God has a table. God does not merely tolerate his people in his presence; he sets bread before them, keeps them before his face, and welcomes them to eat. The table anticipates the One who would call himself "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and the table he still spreads for his people (Ps 23:5; Luke 22:30). To belong to God is to be fed by God, kept always in his presence — communion that is a feast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The golden lampstand is hammered from a single talent of pure gold — its base, stem, branches, cups, and almond-blossom calyxes all of one piece, with seven lamps to light the Holy Place. The living tree of gold and flame, the only light in that windowless room, is made exactly as God showed.
verseByVerse.theology: The lampstand, one piece of pure gold blossoming like almond, gives the sanctuary's only light — a picture of God as the light of his people (Ps 36:9), fulfilled in Christ, "the light of the world" (John 8:12), and reflected in the churches, the lampstands of Revelation (Rev 1:20), burning by the oil of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: in a room with no window, the golden lampstand was made to burn as the only light — God providing sight for those who serve him.

Now: Christ is our light, and we are his lampstands (Matt 5:14; Rev 1:20) — shining not our own light but his, kept burning by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: He also made the lampstand of pure gold. He made the lampstand of hammered work. Its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers were of one piece with it... and its seven lamps... He made it and all its utensils of a talent of pure gold.
verseByVerse.commentary: The lampstand is beaten from a single talent of pure gold — base, stem, six branches, cups shaped like almond blossoms, and seven lamps, all of one piece, no joints or welds. It is a golden tree of light, and in the windowless Holy Place it is the only light there is. Built exactly as God showed on the mountain, it speaks of the God "in [whose] light do we see light" (Ps 36:9). The almond blossoms are the first flowers of spring, life waking from winter, so even the lampstand blossoms. It points to Jesus, "the light of the world" (John 8:12), and to his people, the lampstands of Revelation (Rev 1:20), called to shine — not with light of their own making, but bearing his, fueled by the oil of the Spirit. Where God dwells, there is light, and his servants see by it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25-29 — The Incense Altar, Oil, and Incense
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally the golden altar of incense is made, together with the holy anointing oil and the fragrant incense, blended "as by the perfumer." The altar of prayer, the oil of consecration, the incense of worship — all completed exactly as commanded. Every vessel of approach to God is now ready.
verseByVerse.theology: The incense altar (prayer, Ps 141:2; Rev 8:3-4), the anointing oil (the Spirit's consecration, 1 John 2:20), and the holy incense are all made to God's specification. Prayer, the Spirit, and worship are not human inventions but God's provisions for drawing near — and all find their fulfillment in Christ, our Intercessor (Heb 7:25) and the Anointed One.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the altar of prayer, the oil of anointing, and the sweet incense were finished, and the means of approaching God stood ready.

Now: our prayers rise as incense (Rev 8:3-4), our lives are consecrated by the Spirit's anointing — all of it opened to us through Christ, in whom we draw near.

verseByVerse.quote: He made the altar of incense of acacia wood... and overlaid it with pure gold... He made the holy anointing oil also, and the pure fragrant incense, blended as by the perfumer.
verseByVerse.commentary: The last pieces are finished: the golden altar of incense, and with it the holy anointing oil and the fragrant incense, blended "as by the perfumer." With these, every vessel for approaching God is complete — the altar where prayer would rise like sweet smoke (Ps 141:2; Rev 8:3-4), the oil that would consecrate priests and furniture as set apart for God (a sign of the Spirit, 1 John 2:20), and the incense reserved wholly for his presence. None of these means of drawing near is a human invention; each is God's own provision, made to his design. Prayer, consecration, and worship come to us not as ideas we devised but as gifts God gave — and all of them find their true home in Christ, our great Intercessor (Heb 7:25) and the Anointed One, through whom alone we come near. The furnishings are ready; now the tent itself must be raised.

38.title: The Altar, the Court, and the Reckoning
38.text: <sup>1</sup>He made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood... <sup>8</sup>He made the basin of bronze and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting. <sup>21</sup>These are the records of the tabernacle... as they were recorded at the commandment of Moses.
38.overview:
The construction continues with the bronze altar of burnt offering, the bronze laver, and the courtyard with its hangings — the outer elements of the sanctuary where sacrifice is made and the priests are washed. Then comes a careful accounting of all the gold, silver, and bronze used in the work. Every detail is recorded, every ounce of precious metal accounted for. This is stewardship and integrity in the service of God: the leaders give a transparent reckoning of the people's offerings.

One tender detail shines out: the bronze laver is made "from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered at the entrance of the tent of meeting." The women give up their mirrors — instruments of self-regard and vanity in the ancient world — to be melted down into the basin where the priests wash to serve God. What a picture of consecration: surrendering the tools of self-focus to become instruments of cleansing for worship. As MacArthur observes, devotion to God transforms what we treasure, turning even our vanities into vessels of service.

The bronze altar at the entrance reminds us again that the way to God begins with sacrifice; the laver reminds us that those who draw near must be clean. And the meticulous accounting of materials teaches that the work of God is to be done with integrity and transparency, every gift faithfully stewarded. The same care God demanded in the design, his servants display in the reckoning — for all of it is done before the face of God, who sees and weighs every offering.

sections.title: The Bronze Altar and Laver
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the bronze altar of burnt offering with its horns, utensils, and grating, and the bronze laver. The altar stands at the entrance, where sacrifice is made; the laver provides water for the priests' cleansing. Together they declare the order of approach to God: first atonement (the altar), then cleansing (the laver), before entering his presence. There is no shortcut to God; the way runs through sacrifice and purification.

A tender detail shines out: the laver is made "from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting." The women surrender their bronze mirrors — instruments of self-regard in the ancient world — to be melted into the basin where priests wash for service. What a picture of consecration: the tools of vanity transformed into vessels of cleansing for worship. Devotion to God reorders what we treasure, turning even our self-focus into instruments of his service.

sections.title: The Court of the Tabernacle
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the courtyard with its hangings of fine twined linen on bronze-based pillars with silver hooks and fillets, and the screen for the gate woven in blue, purple, and scarlet. The court sets apart the sacred space and provides the one appointed entrance. All the pegs of the tabernacle and the court are of bronze. The boundary declares that God's dwelling is holy ground, entered only through the appointed way.

The single gate, beautifully woven, reminds us that there is one way into the presence of God — fulfilled in Christ, who declares, "I am the door" (John 10:9) and "I am the way" (John 14:6). The white linen surrounding the court speaks of the purity God requires, provided not by the worshiper's own righteousness but through the sacrifice within. Access to God is real, but on his terms, through his appointed means.

sections.title: The Reckoning of the Materials
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends with a careful accounting of all the gold, silver, and bronze used in the tabernacle, recorded "at the commandment of Moses" under the oversight of the Levites. Every talent and shekel is tallied. The silver comes from the atonement money, the half-shekel paid by each man counted in the census. The leaders give a transparent reckoning of the people's offerings, leaving no room for suspicion of mismanagement.

This meticulous accounting teaches that the work of God is to be done with integrity and transparency. Those entrusted with the people's gifts are accountable for every ounce. Paul echoes this principle in his careful handling of the collection for the saints, "taking precaution so that no one should blame us... for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man" (2 Cor. 8:20-21). The same care God demanded in the design, his servants display in the reckoning — for all is done before the face of God who sees every gift.

sections.title: Atonement, Cleansing, and Integrity
sections.commentary:
The chapter holds together the order of approach to God (altar then laver — atonement then cleansing) and the integrity of God's work (every ounce of material accounted for). To draw near to God we must come through sacrifice and purification; to serve God we must handle his work with transparency and faithfulness.

The altar and laver point to Christ, through whose sacrifice and cleansing we approach the Father. The women's surrendered mirrors, melted into the laver, show how devotion to God transforms what we treasure. And the meticulous reckoning anticipates Paul's care with the saints' gifts, "aiming at what is honorable... in the sight of man" (2 Cor. 8:21). All our worship and service are done before the face of the God who sees.

38.theology:
The order of approach to God. The bronze altar (atonement) and laver (cleansing) at the entrance declare that we come to God through sacrifice and purification — fulfilled in Christ.

Consecration transforms what we treasure. The women give their mirrors to make the laver — devotion to God turns even the tools of vanity into instruments of his service.

Integrity in God's work. Every ounce of material is accounted for; the work of God is done with transparency and faithful stewardship (cf. 2 Cor. 8:20-21).
38.examples:
Then: Bezalel built the bronze altar and laver — made from the women's surrendered mirrors — and the court with its one appointed gate, and the leaders gave a careful, transparent reckoning of every gift the people had offered.

Now: We approach God only through sacrifice and cleansing, fulfilled in Christ, the one door and the one way. Devotion to God reorders our treasures, and the work of God is to be done with integrity and transparency — for all our giving and serving is done before the face of the God who sees.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-8 — The Bronze Altar and the Basin of Mirrors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great bronze altar of burnt offering is made, and then the bronze basin — and here comes one of the tenderest details in the whole account: the basin was made "from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent." The women gave up their bronze mirrors, the very tools of self-regard, and those mirrors became the place where the priests washed to serve God. Vanity melted down into cleansing.
verseByVerse.theology: The women's mirrors (v.8) — instruments of looking at oneself — become the basin for washing, a striking picture of consecration: what was once used for self-admiration is surrendered and transformed for God's service. Real devotion gives up not only surplus but the things closest to self. And the altar comes first on the way in — no approach to God but through sacrifice (Eph 5:2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the women handed over their mirrors, and the glass of vanity became the basin of cleansing at the door of God's house.

Now: true devotion surrenders even the things we clutch for ourselves, and God transforms them for his service. What we lay down, he takes up and makes holy.

verseByVerse.quote: He made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood... and overlaid it with bronze... He made the basin of bronze and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verseByVerse.commentary: The bronze altar of burnt offering is made first — for it stands at the entrance, and there is no way in to God but past the place of sacrifice (Eph 5:2). Then the bronze basin for washing. And here the text pauses for a detail so tender it is easy to miss: the basin was made "from the mirrors of the ministering women." In the ancient world a polished bronze mirror was a prized possession, the very instrument of looking at oneself. And the women gave them up. They handed over the tools of self-regard, and those mirrors were melted down into the basin where the priests would wash their hands and feet to serve the Lord. Think of what that means. The glass of vanity became the vessel of cleansing. What had been used to gaze at self was surrendered and transformed for the worship of God. This is the shape of real devotion: it gives up not merely the leftovers but the things nearest to self, and God takes what we lay down and makes it holy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The courtyard is made — the hangings of fine linen on their bronze posts with silver hooks, enclosing the sacred space, with the colorful screen for the single gate on the east. The white wall that separates the holy from the common, and the one gate that offers a way in, are built exactly as commanded.
verseByVerse.theology: The linen wall (purity, Rev 19:8) marks the boundary of the holy; the single gate declares access is real but exclusive — one door into the presence of God, fulfilled in the One who says, "I am the door" (John 10:9). The court holds two truths together: God is set apart, and God has opened a way in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the white linen wall rose around the tabernacle with its single eastern gate — holiness marked off, and yet a way in provided.

Now: there is one way to God, standing open like a door (John 10:9). The boundary is real; the entrance is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And he made the court. For the south side the hangings of the court were of fine twined linen, a hundred cubits... And the screen for the gate of the court was embroidered with needlework in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen... All the pegs for the tabernacle and for the court all around were of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary: The workers raise the courtyard: a wall of brilliant white linen hung on bronze posts with silver hooks, enclosing the sacred space, and on the east side the one embroidered gate. The message of the court, built exactly as God commanded, is the same as ever. The white linen wall marks a boundary between the holy and the common; to come near, one must cross into cleanness (cf. Rev 19:8). And there is only one gate — not many entrances to suit every preference, but a single door. That is not narrowness for its own sake but grace with an address, the very picture Jesus claims: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). Two truths stand together in this quiet courtyard: God is holy, set apart from sinners; and God has graciously opened a way in. One gate — but wide open to all who will come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21-31 — The Reckoning of the Metals
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The account closes with a careful tally of all the gold, silver, and bronze used — an audit of the whole offering. The silver came from the census "ransom" of every counted man, and it became the hundred bases on which the tabernacle stood. Even the bookkeeping preaches: God's house rested, quite literally, on the price of redeemed lives, and everything given was faithfully accounted for.
verseByVerse.theology: The public accounting (v.21) models integrity and transparency in handling what is given to God (cf. 2 Cor 8:20-21). And the theology is in the numbers: the silver from every man's "ransom" (30:12-16) became the bases — the whole structure grounded on atonement money. God's dwelling stands on redemption; the church is "built on... Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Eph 2:20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: every talent of gold and shekel of silver was counted and recorded, and the ransom silver became the foundation of God's house.

Now: what is given to God is to be handled with honesty "not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of man" (2 Cor 8:21) — and the whole church still rests on the one foundation of redemption in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the records of the tabernacle... The silver from those of the congregation who were counted... a beka a head (that is, half a shekel...)... The hundred talents of silver were for casting the bases of the sanctuary... And the bronze that was offered was seventy talents.
verseByVerse.commentary: The building account ends, fittingly, with an audit — a careful public reckoning of every talent of gold, silver, and bronze that was given and used. There is integrity here worth imitating: what the people offered to God was counted and recorded openly, nothing lost, nothing hidden, so that all could see it was handled faithfully (cf. 2 Cor 8:20-21). But there is theology in the numbers, too. The silver came from the census, the half-shekel "ransom for his life" that every counted man had paid (30:12-16). And that ransom silver became the hundred bases — the very foundations on which the tabernacle's frames stood. So the dwelling of God rested, board by board, on the price of redeemed lives. Even the foundations preached the gospel: sinners could have a God dwelling among them only because a ransom had been paid. The church still stands on that one foundation, "Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Eph 2:20). Everything is ready now. The tent has only to be raised.

39.title: As the LORD Had Commanded Moses
39.text: <sup>32</sup>Thus all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished, and the people of Israel did according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses; so they did. <sup>42</sup>According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work. <sup>43</sup>And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them.
39.overview:
This chapter completes the priestly garments and brings the entire construction to its conclusion — and its dominant note is a refrain repeated like a drumbeat: "as the LORD had commanded Moses." Again and again, after each piece of work, the text says it was done exactly as the LORD commanded. The phrase appears seven times in this chapter, hammering home the theme of complete, faithful, joyful obedience. The people did all the work precisely according to God's word.

What a contrast to the golden calf! There, the people did exactly what they wanted; here, they do exactly what God commanded. The covenant broken by self-will is now honored by glad obedience. The repeated refrain is the language of a redeemed people delighting to do God's will — not grudgingly, but completely, down to the last detail. As Calvin noted, true worship consists not in human inventiveness but in conformity to God's revealed will.

And then the climactic scene: "Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them." The language deliberately echoes Genesis 1, where God "saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good," and then rested and blessed. The completion of the tabernacle is a kind of new creation — a finished work, inspected and blessed. As Christ would cry from the cross, "It is finished," so here the work of building God's dwelling is finished, and Moses pronounces blessing. The redeemed have built a home for God among them, exactly as he commanded, and it is good.

sections.title: The Priestly Garments Completed
sections.commentary:
The skilled workers make the priestly garments: the ephod of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet; the engraved onyx stones bearing Israel's names on the shoulder pieces; the breastpiece with its twelve precious stones; the robe with its bells and pomegranates; and the gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" for the turban. After each item, the refrain sounds: "as the LORD had commanded Moses." Every garment is made in precise obedience to God's design.

The garments that carry Israel's names on the high priest's shoulders and heart, and the plate declaring "Holy to the LORD," all point to Christ, our Great High Priest, who bears us into God's presence and is himself holy (Heb. 9:24). The careful, obedient crafting of these garments — "as the LORD had commanded" — declares that the way of mediation is appointed by God, not invented by man. We come to God only through the mediator he has provided, ultimately Christ himself.

sections.title: The Work Finished
sections.commentary:
"Thus all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished, and the people of Israel did according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses; so they did." The text then lists every completed component — the tent, the furnishings, the Ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the laver, the court, the garments — all brought to Moses. The refrain "as the LORD had commanded Moses" sounds again and again, a drumbeat of faithful obedience.

What a contrast to the golden calf, where the people did exactly as they pleased! Here they do exactly as God commanded, down to the last detail. The covenant broken by self-will is honored by glad obedience. The repeated refrain is the language of a redeemed people delighting to do God's will completely. This is the fruit of grace: not grudging compliance but joyful, thorough conformity to the will of the God who saved them.

sections.title: Moses Inspects and Blesses
sections.commentary:
The chapter reaches its climax: "According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work. And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them." The language deliberately echoes the creation account, where God "saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good," then rested and blessed.

The completion of the tabernacle is presented as a kind of new creation — a finished work, inspected and pronounced good, and crowned with blessing. As Christ would one day cry from the cross, "It is finished," so here the work of building God's dwelling is complete. The redeemed have, in obedience to God's word, built a home for God among them, and Moses blesses them. The God who created the world to dwell with man, and who redeemed a people to dwell among them, now has a dwelling prepared — pointing forward to the day when, in Christ, the dwelling of God is with man forever (Rev. 21:3).

sections.title: Glad Obedience as Worship
sections.commentary:
The drumbeat refrain of the chapter — "as the LORD had commanded Moses," sounded again and again — is the language of glad, complete obedience. What a reversal from the golden calf, where the people did exactly as they pleased! Here a redeemed people delight to do God's will down to the last detail. Obedience is not the enemy of grace but its fruit.

And the closing scene echoes creation: Moses sees the finished work, finds it done as commanded, and blesses the people — as God saw his creation "very good," then blessed and rested. The completion of God's dwelling is a new-creation moment, anticipating the greater finished work of Christ, who cried "It is finished," that God might dwell with his people forever.

39.theology:
Complete, joyful obedience. The refrain "as the LORD had commanded Moses" sounds throughout — the redeemed delight to do God's will completely, in contrast to the self-will of the golden calf.

Worship by God's design. Both the priestly garments and the structure are made exactly as commanded; the way of mediation and worship is appointed by God, fulfilled in Christ.

A finished work, inspected and blessed. The completion echoes creation — Moses sees, it is done as commanded, and he blesses, anticipating Christ's "It is finished."
39.examples:
Then: The priestly garments and the whole tabernacle were completed exactly "as the LORD had commanded Moses," and Moses inspected the finished work, saw it was done as commanded, and blessed the people — a new-creation scene of faithful obedience.

Now: Grace produces glad, complete obedience — not the self-will of the golden calf but the joyful conformity of a redeemed people to God's will. The finished tabernacle, inspected and blessed, points to the greater finished work of Christ, who cried "It is finished" so that God might dwell with us forever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The skilled workers make the holy garments exactly as God commanded Moses: the ephod with the tribes' names on the shoulders, the breastpiece with its twelve stones over the heart, the blue robe with bells and pomegranates, the tunics, the turban, and the golden plate engraved "Holy to the LORD." Seven times in this chapter the refrain sounds — "as the LORD had commanded Moses." The clothing that lets a sinner serve the Holy One is complete, down to the last thread.
verseByVerse.theology: The drumbeat "as the LORD had commanded Moses" (repeated throughout chs 39-40) is the theme of obedient completion: every detail done God's way. The garments carry the tribes on the priest's shoulders (strength) and heart (love), and crown him "Holy to the LORD" — all fulfilled in our High Priest, who bears us and presents us holy to God (Heb 7:25; Jude 24). The priest is clothed for service; we are clothed in Christ (Gal 3:27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: every garment was made precisely as God commanded, and the golden plate "Holy to the LORD" was set on the turban — the priest fully clothed to serve.

Now: we come to God clothed not in ourselves but in Christ (Gal 3:27), carried on the shoulders and heart of our High Priest, presented holy before the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: From the blue and purple and scarlet yarns they made finely woven garments, for ministering in the Holy Place. They made the holy garments for Aaron, as the LORD had commanded Moses... And they made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and wrote on it an inscription, like the engraving of a signet, 'Holy to the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The craftsmen make the holy garments, and as they finish each one the text keeps repeating a single phrase like a drumbeat: "as the LORD had commanded Moses." Seven times in this chapter it sounds. The ephod with the twelve tribes engraved on its shoulder-stones; the breastpiece with its twelve jewels worn over the heart; the blue robe hemmed with golden bells and pomegranates; the tunics, the turban, and the golden plate stamped "Holy to the LORD" — all made exactly, faithfully, to God's word. Every garment preaches the same gospel it did when commanded: the priest carries his people on his shoulders (strength) and over his heart (love), and is crowned with holiness so that Israel may be accepted. It is all fulfilled in our great High Priest, who bears us on his strength, treasures us in his love, and presents us "blameless before the presence of his glory" (Jude 24). And the refrain matters. Faithful service is not creative improvisation but glad obedience — doing what God said, the way God said it. What God commands, his people, gifted by his Spirit, carry out to the letter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32-43 — The Work Finished, and Moses Blessed Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: "Thus all the work of the tabernacle... was finished." Every piece is brought to Moses, and he inspects it all — and finds that they had done it "as the LORD had commanded... so had they done it." Then Moses blesses them. The scene deliberately echoes creation: God finished his work, saw all he had made, and blessed it. A new creation in miniature, a place where God will dwell, is complete — and it is very good.
verseByVerse.theology: The language echoes Genesis 1-2: the work "finished," Moses "saw" all of it, and "blessed them" (vv.32, 43; cf. Gen 1:31; 2:1-3). The tabernacle is a new-creation space, a corner of the world reordered for God's presence. Completed obedience ends in blessing — and it points forward to the day the true Temple would say, "It is finished" (John 19:30), and to the new creation where God dwells with man (Rev 21:3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the finished work was laid before Moses, found faithful in every detail, and Moses blessed the people — obedience crowned with blessing.

Now: the work that finally secures God's dwelling with us was finished at the cross (John 19:30), and the blessing rests on all who are in Christ, awaiting the new creation where God is with his people forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished, and the people of Israel did according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses; so they did. And they brought the tabernacle to Moses... According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work. And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Thus all the work... was finished." Every curtain, frame, vessel, and garment is carried to Moses, and he inspects it all — and finds it done exactly "as the LORD had commanded." Then "Moses blessed them." Listen closely to that language, because it is not accidental. It is the language of Genesis. There, God finished his work, God saw everything he had made, and God blessed (Gen 1:31; 2:1-3). Here, the work is finished, Moses sees it all, and Moses blesses. The tabernacle is a new creation in miniature — a small corner of a fallen world set back in order, made fit for God to dwell in, and pronounced good. What began in disaster at the golden calf ends in blessing, because grace restored what sin had wrecked, and obedience completed what grace began. And it all leans forward. One day the true Temple, God among us in the flesh, would finish the greater work and cry, "It is finished" (John 19:30) — and open the way to the new creation where "the dwelling place of God is with man" (Rev 21:3). The tent is built. Now only one thing remains: will God come to fill it?

40.title: The Glory of the LORD Filled the Tabernacle
40.text: <sup>34</sup>Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. <sup>35</sup>And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. <sup>38</sup>For the cloud of the LORD was on the tabernacle by day, and fire was in it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys.
40.overview:
The book of Exodus reaches its glorious climax. The tabernacle is erected, exactly as God commanded, on the first day of the first month — a new beginning, a new year, a new creation. Moses sets up every piece in its appointed place: the Ark behind the veil, the table and lampstand and altar of incense in the Holy Place, the bronze altar and laver in the court. And once more the refrain sounds, "as the LORD had commanded Moses," seven times over. The dwelling place of God among his people is ready.

And then — the climax of the entire book: "the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." The Shekinah glory, the visible presence of God, descends and fills the tent so fully that even Moses cannot enter. The God who came down to deliver his people from Egypt has now come down to dwell among them. The book that began with a people enslaved in a foreign land ends with God himself dwelling in their midst, leading them by cloud and fire through all their journeys. The whole movement of Exodus has been toward this moment: God with his people.

And this is only the beginning of the story. The glory that filled the tabernacle would one day fill the incarnate Christ, in whom "the Word became flesh and dwelt [tabernacled] among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). At Pentecost the glory would fill the temple of the church by the Spirit. And in the end, the glory will fill the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man," and there will be no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb" (Rev. 21:3, 22). The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us — now and forevermore.

sections.title: The Tabernacle Erected
sections.commentary:
God commands Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month — a new beginning, like a new creation. Moses is to place the Ark behind the veil, set up the table and lampstand and altar of incense, position the bronze altar and laver, erect the court, and anoint the tabernacle and the priests, consecrating them for service. Everything is to be ordered exactly as God directs, each object in its appointed place.

The first day of the first month signals a fresh start: God is establishing his dwelling among his people as the inauguration of a new era. The careful ordering and anointing of every element, and the consecration of the priests, prepares the way for God's glory to descend. All is made ready for the holy God to take up residence among his redeemed people — the goal toward which the entire book has been moving.

sections.title: Moses Obeys in Every Detail
sections.commentary:
Moses does everything "as the LORD had commanded him" — the refrain sounds seven times in this section as each element is set in place: the frames, the Ark and the testimony, the veil, the table and its bread, the lampstand and its lamps, the golden altar of incense, the screen, the bronze altar with its offerings, the laver for washing, and the court. "So Moses finished the work." The completion echoes both creation ("God finished his work") and anticipates Christ's "It is finished."

The relentless repetition of "as the LORD had commanded" crowns the book's theme of joyful, complete obedience. From the broken covenant of the golden calf, God has brought his people to faithful conformity to his will. The dwelling of God is prepared not by human creativity but by humble obedience to God's revealed word. Moses finishes the work, and all stands ready for the glory to descend. The pattern of a finished work preparing for God's presence points to the finished work of Christ that opens the way into God's eternal presence.

sections.title: The Glory Fills the Tabernacle
sections.commentary:
Then comes the climax of the entire book: "the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." The Shekinah glory, the visible presence of God, descends and fills the tent so fully that even Moses cannot enter. The God who came down to deliver his people now comes down to dwell among them.

The book that began with a people enslaved in a foreign land ends with God himself dwelling in their midst, leading them by cloud by day and fire by night through all their journeys. This is the goal toward which all of Exodus has moved: God with his people. And it is only the beginning. The glory that filled the tabernacle would one day fill the incarnate Christ, in whom "the Word became flesh and dwelt [tabernacled] among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). At Pentecost the glory filled the temple of the church by the Spirit. And in the end, the glory will fill the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man," and there is no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb" (Rev. 21:3, 22). The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us — now and forevermore. To this end he brought us out; to this end he brought us in: that he might be our God, and we his people, dwelling in his glorious presence forever.

sections.title: The Goal of the Whole Book: God With Us
sections.commentary:
The final scene is the goal toward which the entire book has moved: "the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." The book that opened with a people enslaved in a foreign land closes with God himself dwelling in their midst, leading them by cloud and fire through all their journeys. From bondage to glory, from groaning to the Shekinah presence — this is the arc of redemption.

And it is only the beginning. The glory that filled the tabernacle filled the incarnate Christ, in whom "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14); it filled the church at Pentecost by the Spirit; and it will fill the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man," with no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb" (Rev. 21:3, 22). The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us — now and forevermore. He brought us out that he might bring us in.

40.theology:
God dwells with his people. The glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle — the climax of Exodus. The God who came down to deliver comes down to dwell. "I will dwell among them" is fulfilled.

A finished work and a new creation. "Moses finished the work" on the first day of the first month echoes creation and points to Christ's finished work that opens the way into God's presence.

The trajectory of glory. The tabernacle glory points to Christ who tabernacled among us (John 1:14), to Pentecost, and finally to the New Jerusalem where God dwells with man forever (Rev. 21:3).
40.examples:
Then: Moses erected the tabernacle exactly as God commanded, and the glory of the LORD descended and filled it so fully that even Moses could not enter. The God who redeemed his people from Egypt now dwelt in their midst, leading them by cloud and fire.

Now: The whole book has moved toward this: God with his people. The glory that filled the tabernacle filled the incarnate Christ, fills the church by the Spirit, and will fill the New Jerusalem forever. The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us. He brought us out that he might bring us in — to dwell in his glorious presence, our God forever, world without end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-16 — Command to Raise the Tabernacle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month — a new beginning, almost a year after the exodus. He is told exactly how to arrange every piece, to anoint it all, and to wash and clothe and consecrate Aaron and his sons. And the chapter's quiet refrain begins: "Moses did everything just as the LORD had commanded him." The day of God's coming has almost arrived.
verseByVerse.theology: The tabernacle is raised on "the first day of the first month" (v.2), a fresh new-year beginning — God making all things new for his dwelling among his people. The careful anointing and consecration set everything apart as holy. Obedience precedes glory: only when all is done "as the LORD commanded" does the presence descend. God comes to a house prepared his way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: on a new year's first day, Moses obeyed God's word to the letter, setting each thing in its place, anointing and consecrating all.

Now: God still comes to fill what is prepared according to his word. Obedience is the pathway on which his presence arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: On the first day of the first month you shall erect the tabernacle of the tent of meeting... Then you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall wash them with water... This shall be a perpetual priesthood throughout their generations. This Moses did; according to all that the LORD commanded him, so he did.
verseByVerse.commentary: God commands the tabernacle to be raised "on the first day of the first month" — a new year, a new beginning, nearly a year after Israel left Egypt. There is a fresh-start feeling to it, as if God is making all things new for the moment he comes to dwell. He tells Moses precisely how to arrange every piece — ark, veil, table, lampstand, altars, basin, court — and to anoint it all, and to wash, clothe, and consecrate Aaron and his sons for a perpetual priesthood. And the chapter's gentle refrain begins to sound: "This Moses did; according to all that the LORD commanded him, so he did." Notice the order. First the careful, obedient preparation; then, only then, the glory. God comes to fill a house made ready his way, not ours. Everything is being set in place for the great arrival. The tent stands assembled, consecrated, waiting. All that remains is for God himself to come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Piece by piece, Moses raises the tabernacle: the frames, the ark and veil, the table, the lampstand, the golden altar, the screen, the bronze altar, the basin, the court. Seven times over, the account repeats, "as the LORD had commanded Moses." And then the last line: "So Moses finished the work." Everything is in place. The obedience is complete.
verseByVerse.theology: The sevenfold "as the LORD had commanded Moses" (vv.19-32) and the closing "So Moses finished the work" (v.33) again echo the seven days of creation and God's finished work (Gen 2:1-2). Ordered, complete obedience prepares the place for God's presence. What God commands, God's servant carries out fully — and the finished work opens the way for glory to come.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses set up each piece exactly as commanded and "finished the work" — a house fully ordered for the coming of God.

Now: the finished work that opens God's presence to us is Christ's, not ours; yet we still order our lives by his word, preparing the way for him to be at home among us.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was erected. Moses erected the tabernacle. He laid its bases, and set up its frames, and put in its poles, and raised up its pillars... as the LORD had commanded Moses... So Moses finished the work.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now Moses raises the tabernacle piece by piece, and the writer walks us through it slowly, almost reverently: the bases and frames, the ark carried into the Most Holy Place behind the veil, the table and the lampstand, the golden altar of incense, the screen at the door, the bronze altar and the basin, the court all around. And after each stage comes the same refrain, seven times over: "as the LORD had commanded Moses." Seven — the number of completeness, the number of the creation week. Then the final line: "So Moses finished the work." It is deliberately the language of Genesis, where "God finished his work" (Gen 2:2). A new-creation space stands complete, every piece in its God-appointed place, the whole of it a monument to obedient faith. Nothing is left undone, nothing done a different way than God commanded. The house is finished, ordered, waiting. And a finished, prepared place is exactly where the glory of God loves to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34-38 — The Glory Fills the Tabernacle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And then it happens. "The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." So overwhelming is the presence that even Moses cannot enter. The God who spoke from a burning bush, who thundered on Sinai, now comes down to dwell in the midst of his people — and there he stays. The cloud by day and fire by night would lead them on every stage of their journey. The book that began in the darkness of slavery ends in the blazing glory of God dwelling with his people. This is the goal of redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: The glory-cloud filling the tabernacle (vv.34-35) is the climax of Exodus and the answer to its great longing: "that I may dwell in their midst" (25:8). The same glory would fill Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 8:10-11), take flesh in Christ, who "tabernacled among us" full of glory (John 1:14), fill the church as God's temple at Pentecost (Acts 2; 1 Cor 3:16), and at last fill the new creation, where "the glory of God gives it light" (Rev 21:23). The guiding cloud and fire (vv.36-38) promise that the God who dwells with his people also leads them home.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the glory of God came down and filled the tent, and his cloud and fire led Israel through every stage of the journey — God present, God leading, God at home among them.

Now: the same God dwells in his people by the Spirit (1 Cor 3:16) and leads them still, pressing toward the day when "the dwelling place of God is with man," and "they will see his face" (Rev 21:3; 22:4). The story of the exodus ends where all of Scripture is heading: God with us, forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle... For the cloud of the LORD was on the tabernacle by day, and fire was in it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys.
verseByVerse.commentary: And then — glory. The moment the whole book has been straining toward finally comes: "the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." So dense, so weighty, so overwhelming is the presence of God that even Moses — Moses, who spoke with God face to face, who climbed into the fire on Sinai — cannot enter. God has come down to live among his people, and there he settles, at home in their midst. Remember where this book began: a people crushed under slavery, groaning in the dark, crying out to a God who seemed far away. And here is where it ends — the glory of that same God blazing in the center of the camp, his cloud over them by day and his fire among them by night, leading them onward through every stage of the journey. This is the goal of the exodus, and the goal of all redemption. God did not rescue Israel merely to free them; he rescued them to dwell with them. That glory would fill Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 8:11); it would take flesh and "tabernacle among us" in Christ, full of glory (John 1:14); it would fill the church by the Spirit (1 Cor 3:16); and it will at last fill the new creation, where "they will see his face" and need no other light (Rev 21:23; 22:4). The book closes not with a full stop but with a moving cloud — God dwelling with his people, and leading them home. That is the whole hope of the Bible, and it is ours in Christ. God with us, forever.
